trace.situation: The jacket cooling water (JCW) expansion tank level has been slowly dropping over several watches, with no visible external leakage in the engine room bilges. trace.trigger: Expansion tank low-level alarm on the engine control room panel

procedures.action: Check for visible leaks at stuffing boxes, cylinder cover cooling bores, and pipe flanges along the JCW manifold
procedures.why: Small gasket or flange leaks are the most common cause of gradual inventory loss and are easiest to locate first

procedures.action: Verify the deaerating tank alarm device and vent pipe are functioning and not blocked
procedures.why: A blocked vent can mask air/steam ingress that would otherwise trigger an early warning of internal leakage

procedures.action: Top up the expansion tank with treated, inhibited water of matching concentration and continue to monitor level trend
procedures.why: Replacing lost water with untreated water would dilute the nitrite-borate inhibitor and risk corrosion

procedures.action: If level continues to drop with no external leak found, prepare to inspect cylinder liner O-rings and cooling water space during next port stay
procedures.why: Internal leakage into the crankcase or exhaust gas space is possible if no external source is identified

constraints: Expansion tank volume must be at least 10% of total JCW system volume
Expansion tank located min. 15 m above top of exhaust gas valves
Low-level alarm set above vent pipe termination point
regulations: Everllence JCW system design requirement for expansion tank volume and height
warnings: Continued undetected loss can starve the jacket water pump and cause overheating of cylinder liners
Topping up with untreated water repeatedly will dilute inhibitor below protective concentration
outcomes: If uncorrected, pump cavitation and loss of cooling flow can lead to liner cracking from overheating
If corrected, inventory stabilizes and liner cooling integrity is confirmed

trace.situation: During a routine engine room round, the deaerating tank alarm device activates, indicating an abnormal volume of air or gas entering the jacket cooling water circuit. procedures.action: Reduce engine load immediately and notify the bridge/chief engineer

procedures.action: Check JCW outlet temperature per cylinder unit for abnormal spikes

procedures.action: Take a cooling water sample and test for combustion by-products (e.g., hydrocarbon sheen, pH shift, soot)

outcomes: If ignored, progressive liner cracking can lead to in-cylinder flooding, hydraulic lock, and major engine damage
If detected and investigated promptly, damage can be confined to a single unit with a planned repair

trace.situation: The jacket cooling water outlet temperature has drifted upward over several hours, approaching the 85°C setpoint ceiling, despite steady engine load. procedures.action: Manually override or force the valve toward the cooler side while monitoring temperature response

outcomes: If uncorrected, continued high outlet temperature promotes scale deposition and reduced cooling effectiveness, risking liner overheating
If corrected, stable 85°C outlet temperature is restored, protecting liner and piston ring condition

procedures.action: Increase testing frequency to confirm inhibitor stabilizes at target concentration after redosing

trace.situation: After a plate-type jacket water cooler was opened for cleaning, a small internal gasket leak developed between the seawater/LT side and the freshwater JCW side, allowing chloride-bearing cooling water to cross-contaminate the jacket water circuit. procedures.action: Drain, flush, and refill the JCW system with fresh treated water once the leak is repaired

trace.situation: The central LT cooling water temperature control valve has been left at a setpoint below the required 10°C minimum, apparently adjusted during cold weather operation without being reset. trace.trigger: Scavenge air cooler condensate drain showing unusually high water accumulation during rounds

procedures.action: Check the central cooling water temperature control valve setpoint against the required minimum of 10°C
procedures.why: The setpoint is often mistakenly lowered during cold climate transits and not restored, allowing excessive condensation at the scavenge air cooler

procedures.action: Reset the setpoint to minimum 10°C, or 4°C above ambient seawater temperature for flow-controlled pump setups

procedures.action: Verify scavenge air cooler condensate drain traps are functioning correctly and not blocked
procedures.why: Even with correct temperature, drains must be functional to prevent water carryover into cylinders

procedures.action: Monitor scavenge air temperature and humidity trend after adjustment to confirm condensation reduces to normal levels

constraints: Central cooling water temperature control valve setpoint: minimum 10°C (required for EGR/EcoEGR engines)

regulations: Everllence central cooling water system temperature requirement
warnings: Excessive condensate carryover into the cylinders can wash away lubricating oil film and cause abnormal liner wear or corrosion
Ignoring this condition over time risks water-induced cylinder liner scuffing
outcomes: If uncorrected, continued condensate ingestion accelerates liner wear and increases risk of cylinder corrosion
If corrected, scavenge air cooler operates within design parameters and condensate drain load returns to normal

EGR and EcoEGR engine types require strict adherence to the 10°C minimum setpoint

trace.situation: The jacket water circulating pump exhibits a drop in discharge pressure and an audible rattling noise during normal running, with the engine JCW inlet pressure approaching the minimum guidance value stated for engine inlet connection K. procedures.action: Verify expansion tank water level and elevation versus the required minimum 15 m above the exhaust gas valves

procedures.action: Inspect the pump impeller and casing for cavitation erosion damage once isolated

warnings: Continued pump cavitation erodes the impeller and can lead to sudden loss of cooling water flow

outcomes: If uncorrected, impeller erosion worsens until pump output can no longer meet engine cooling demand, risking overheating trip

trace.situation: Prior to a port departure after a four-day stay, the engine was started with jacket cooling water temperature below the recommended 50°C minimum because the preheater had been switched off to save fuel. procedures.action: Switch to the cold-engine load-up procedure (Table 12.01.02) for the remainder of the load increase

procedures.action: Verify the preheater system and its temperature sensor are functioning for future port stays

constraints: Minimum JCW temperature before start: 50°C (gradual increase to 20°C acceptable only under exceptional circumstances per Table 12.01.02)

trace.situation: The jacket cooling water expansion tank level has been slowly dropping across several watches without any corresponding increase in makeup water logged, suggesting an undetected internal or external leak somewhere in the JCW piping or components.

procedures.why: Restores the designed mixing mechanism for the inhibitor.

procedures.action: Re-dose inhibitor after flow is restored and monitor concentration rise over the following days.

constraints: Dosing tank requires a continuous small jacket water flow for proper inhibitor mixing

trace.situation: The jacket cooling water expansion tank level is rising toward the high-level/overflow alarm, with investigation pointing to a possible internal leak path from a freshwater generator installed in the JCW circuit adding unaccounted volume to the system.

procedures.action: Check venting pipes at the expansion tank for obstruction causing abnormal level readings.
procedures.why: Rules out a false indication caused by blocked venting rather than true excess volume.

procedures.action: If a leak is confirmed, isolate the freshwater generator from the JCW circuit and arrange repair of the shell/tube or gasket.
procedures.why: Stops the unintended volume addition and prevents further dilution/contamination of the treated jacket water.

procedures.action: Drain excess volume to the designated freshwater drain tank and verify inhibitor concentration afterward.
procedures.why: Restores correct tank level and allows reassessment of chemical treatment following dilution.

constraints: Expansion tank high-level alarm is set at the overflow pipe, defining the top of the 10% volume margin
Expansion tank must be designed open to atmosphere with venting pipes terminating below the low-level alarm point

warnings: Repeated overflow events waste treated, inhibitor-dosed water and may indicate a developing freshwater generator leak that could later reverse and contaminate the FWG product water
outcomes: If uncorrected, continued overflow wastes treated water and inhibitor, and the underlying leak may worsen
If corrected, tank level stabilizes and the FWG leak path is eliminated

A freshwater generator installed in the JCW circuit is a potential cross-contamination path if its heat exchanger develops a leak

trace.situation: Following replacement of the central cooling water pump with a higher-capacity unit, flow velocity in sections of external cooling water piping now exceeds the 3.0 m/s design maximum because orifice plates were not resized accordingly, leading to accelerated erosion-corrosion at bends and tee connections.

procedures.action: Calculate actual flow velocity in the affected piping sections based on new pump capacity and pipe bore.
procedures.why: Quantifies whether the 3.0 m/s design limit is being exceeded and by how much.

procedures.action: Review and resize orifice plates or lockable adjustable valves per the original design intent for flow distribution and differential pressure.
procedures.why: Restores intended flow distribution and reduces velocity to within design limits.

procedures.action: Repair or replace eroded piping sections identified during the survey.
procedures.why: Prevents pipe wall perforation and loss of cooling water containment.

procedures.action: Re-survey wall thickness at the affected locations after corrective action to confirm the erosion rate has stabilized.
procedures.why: Verifies the corrective action has addressed the root cause.

constraints: Max external pipe water velocity for central cooling water and seawater is 3.0 m/s
Orifices must create flow distribution and differential pressure matching the central cooler at nominal pump capacity
regulations: Everllence central cooling water piping velocity design limits
warnings: Continued operation above the velocity limit accelerates erosion-corrosion and can lead to sudden pipe wall perforation and flooding risk in the engine room
outcomes: If uncorrected, accelerated wall thinning can progress to pipe failure and uncontrolled water ingress
If corrected by resizing orifices, erosion rates return to normal and piping integrity is preserved
key_facts: Maximum design water velocity for central cooling water and seawater piping is 3.0 m/s
Orifice plates or lockable adjustable valves are required to maintain correct flow distribution after any pump capacity change

trace.situation: The engine was started and loaded toward higher power without confirming jacket cooling water had reached the minimum temperature required by the cold-engine load-up procedure, risking thermal shock to cylinder liners and accelerated cold corrosion, particularly given high-sulphur fuel in use.
trace.trigger: Load increase proceeding while jacket cooling water temperature remains below 50°C, or subsequent liner inspection reveals abnormal wear pattern

procedures.action: Halt further load increase immediately and hold at current load.
procedures.why: Prevents additional thermal and mechanical stress while jacket water is still below the minimum safe temperature for further loading.

procedures.action: Allow jacket water temperature to reach at least 50°C before resuming any load increase, per the cold-engine load-up table.
procedures.why: The manual requires reaching 50°C before further loading when starting from a cold condition, to limit thermal stress and cold corrosion risk.

procedures.action: Resume loading only according to the documented time intervals (e.g., 80-90% SMCR over 60 minutes for most FPP plants) once the temperature threshold is met.
procedures.why: Gradual, time-controlled loading minimizes thermal expansion mismatch and associated leakage/wear risk.

procedures.action: Review engine control system logs to confirm the load-up table compliance and record the deviation for future reference.
procedures.why: Supports root-cause analysis and prevents recurrence through crew awareness or procedure reinforcement.

constraints: Minimum jacket water temperature of 50°C should be reached before start-up under normal conditions; 20°C is acceptable only under exceptional circumstances, with mandatory restricted loading until 50°C is reached
Load-up time intervals per engine type and bore must be followed as tabulated (e.g., 80-90% SMCR speed over 60 or 30 minutes depending on engine type)
regulations: Everllence load-up procedure tables 12.01.01 and 12.01.02
warnings: Loading the engine before reaching minimum jacket water temperature risks mechanical overload, overheating, and cold corrosion, especially with high-sulphur fuel
outcomes: If the procedure continues to be ignored, repeated thermal shock accelerates cylinder liner wear and increases risk of leakage from differential thermal expansion
If the documented load-up procedure is followed, mechanical and corrosion risks associated with cold starts are minimized
key_facts: Cold-engine load-up tables require reaching 50°C jacket water temperature before loading beyond the initial gradual increase stage
Time intervals in the load-up tables are additive, e.g., 60 + 90 minutes for a full 80% to 100% SMCR speed increase on FPP plants

procedures.action: Compare current orifice/valve settings against original commissioning records or design documentation.
procedures.why: Confirms whether settings have drifted or were incorrectly restored after recent maintenance.

procedures.action: If flow or pressure drop instrumentation is available per unit, measure actual values and compare to the design differential pressure referenced to the cooler at nominal flow.
procedures.why: Quantifies the imbalance and confirms which units are under-supplied.

procedures.action: Readjust the lockable orifice valves to restore the correct flow distribution across all cylinder units.
procedures.why: Directly corrects the root cause of localized overheating by restoring design flow balance.

procedures.action: Monitor exhaust gas temperature deviation across units after adjustment to confirm balance has been restored.
procedures.why: Verifies the corrective action was effective.

constraints: Orifices or lockable adjustable valves must create flow distribution and differential pressure matching the cooler at nominal jacket water pump capacity

warnings: Unresolved flow imbalance can cause localized overheating, scuffing, or accelerated wear on the under-cooled units
outcomes: If uncorrected, the affected unit(s) experience accelerated liner/piston wear from chronic local overheating
If corrected, flow is rebalanced and exhaust/liner temperatures normalize across all units

Exhaust gas temperature deviation between cylinders with similar load is a common early indicator of cooling flow imbalance

procedures.action: Open the vent valve or automatic deaerating valve at the exhaust valve cooling water manifold connection.
procedures.why: Releases trapped air that is blocking proper water circulation at that point in the manifold.

procedures.action: Run the engine at low/reduced load while continuing to bleed air to the expansion tank.

procedures.action: Verify the venting pipe is correctly routed to either the fore or aft end of the manifold discharge pipe per the original design.
procedures.why: Confirms the venting arrangement itself was not altered or omitted during the recent maintenance work.

procedures.action: Confirm the affected unit's exhaust valve cooling outlet temperature normalizes before returning to full load.
procedures.why: Verifies the air pocket has been fully cleared and normal cooling flow restored.

constraints: Venting pipe for the cooling water manifold of the exhaust gas valve must be arranged at either the fore or aft end of the manifold discharge pipe, opposite the jacket water pump discharge end

warnings: An uncleared air pocket at the exhaust valve cooling manifold risks localized overheating leading to exhaust valve seat burning or valve seizure
outcomes: If uncorrected, the trapped air pocket can cause recurring localized overheating and exhaust valve damage
If properly vented, cooling flow is restored uniformly and the temperature spike resolves

procedures.why: Reduces stagnation-related fouling and crevice corrosion risk going forward.

procedures.action: Review the trend data across multiple quarterly reports to confirm a genuine degrading pattern rather than a single anomalous result.

procedures.why: Confirms the extent of accumulated contamination and identifies any areas needing additional cleaning.

procedures.action: Refill with fresh treated water, dose inhibitor to the upper end of the recommended range, and resume weekly testing with renewed diligence.
procedures.why: Restores baseline water chemistry and re-establishes proper monitoring discipline going forward.

Weekly, quarterly, and annual testing/maintenance regime must be followed as documented

warnings: Deferring the annual flush allows accumulated deposits and degraded water chemistry to promote under-deposit corrosion and reduced heat transfer, even if nitrite levels appear nominally acceptable
outcomes: If the flush continues to be deferred, accumulated sludge and declining pH will progressively worsen corrosion and fouling throughout the system

trace.situation: During a routine inspection, the duty engineer notices that one lubricating quill on a liner shows no visible oil wetting trace after unit activation test, while adjacent quills show normal wetting. procedures.action: Stop the engine or reduce load as operationally possible and visually inspect the affected lubricating quill and non-return valve for carbon blockage or seizure.
procedures.why: A blocked quill or stuck non-return valve prevents oil delivery to that segment of the liner, causing dry running at that point.

procedures.action: Remove and clean or replace the non-return valve and quill, checking for coked oil or carbon bridging.
procedures.why: Carbon deposits from poor combustion or degraded cylinder oil are the most common cause of quill blockage.

procedures.action: After replacement, run a controlled load increase while monitoring liner wall temperatures and scavenge drain inspection for that unit.
procedures.why: Confirms oil distribution and lubrication has been restored before returning to normal service.

constraints: Cylinder oil must reach all lubricating quills; feed rate must not fall below 0.6 g/kWh minimum per Everllence guidance

outcomes: Uncorrected: localized scuffing, ring land damage, and potential piston seizure on the affected unit
Corrected: even oil film distribution restored, preventing abnormal wear and avoiding unplanned unit overhaul

trace.situation: The vessel switched from HFO to VLSFO operation but the crew failed to update the pilot/fuel sulphur content on the MOP, causing the ACOS2 system to continue calculating a sulphur equivalent based on the old high-sulphur value. procedures.action: Verify and correct the sulphur content entry for the current fuel on the MOP/ECS.

procedures.action: Cross-check actual bunker sulphur content against the entered value using the bunker delivery note or a sulphur test kit.
procedures.why: Ensures the correction is based on the actual fuel being combusted, not an assumed value.

procedures.action: Monitor drain oil analysis and piston underside inspection over the following days to confirm BN levels normalize and deposit formation stops.
procedures.why: Confirms that lubrication strategy correction has resolved the over-alkaline dosing condition.

outcomes: Uncorrected: ring groove deposit build-up, bore polishing, and increased cylinder oil consumption without wear benefit
Corrected: lubrication strategy matches actual fuel sulphur content, restoring normal cylinder condition and consumption

trace.situation: The ACOS2 three-way switching valve failed to change position from high-BN to low-BN oil after the engine completed a changeover to low-sulphur fuel, leaving the engine running continuously on high-BN oil regardless of the auto control mode selection.

procedures.action: Check the feedback signals ZS8261/ZS8262 against the commanded control signal XC8260 to confirm valve position mismatch.
procedures.why: Feedback discrepancy identifies whether the fault is in the valve actuator, solenoid, or control signal wiring.

procedures.action: Inspect the pneumatic actuator, solenoid valve, and control air supply for the three-way valve for sticking, loss of control air, or solenoid coil failure.

procedures.action: Manually verify correct valve operation by cycling control mode (High BN/Low BN) from the MOP and confirm physical valve position matches feedback before returning to Auto mode.
procedures.why: Confirms the fault is cleared and the automatic switching logic is functioning correctly.

Valve position feedback must match commanded control signal before releasing to Auto mode

outcomes: Uncorrected: persistent lubrication/fuel mismatch leading to abnormal cylinder condition trends and increased oil consumption

trace.situation: The engine has been running for several weeks with the cylinder oil feed rate set below the minimum recommended value in an attempt to reduce lubricant consumption costs, resulting in insufficient oil film on the liner during high-load operation.

procedures.action: Review current cylinder oil feed rate setting against the latest Everllence Service Letter minimum feed rate guideline for the engine type and operating condition.
procedures.why: The minimum feed rate is specifically set to ensure sufficient oil reaches all lubrication points under the given load and fuel condition.

procedures.action: Increase the feed rate to at least the documented minimum (never below 0.6 g/kWh) and monitor liner condition and ring wear trend over subsequent running hours.
procedures.why: Restoring adequate feed rate re-establishes the oil film needed to prevent metal-to-metal contact.

procedures.action: Conduct a borescope inspection of accessible liners/piston rings to assess the extent of any wear or scuffing that occurred during the under-dosing period.
procedures.why: Determines whether physical damage has already occurred that requires further repair beyond simply correcting the feed rate.

constraints: Minimum cylinder oil feed rate must not be less than 0.6 g/kWh as per Everllence guidance

trace.situation: Following a lubricant supplier change, the vessel began using a Cat. I cylinder oil with lower detergency on an engine originally designed and operated with Cat. II oil, resulting in gradually increasing piston crown and ring belt deposits and early signs of bore polish.
trace.trigger: Piston inspection during scheduled overhaul shows increased carbon deposits and localized bore polishing compared to previous inspection using Cat. II oil

procedures.action: Confirm the current cylinder oil specification and category against the engine's Mark/design recommendation (Cat. II recommended for Mk.9 and higher).
procedures.why: Using a lower-category oil with insufficient detergency on an engine designed for Cat. II performance can allow deposit accumulation that the lubrication strategy was designed to prevent.

procedures.action: Arrange to revert to an NOL-approved Cat. II cylinder oil matching the engine's design recommendation and fuel sulphur content.
procedures.why: Restores the cleaning/detergency performance required to keep pistons, rings, and liners clean as intended by the original engine design basis.

procedures.action: Monitor piston and ring belt condition at subsequent inspections to confirm the deposit trend reverses after reverting to the correct oil category.
procedures.why: Confirms the corrective action has resolved the developing bore polish and deposit issue before it leads to ring sticking or increased oil consumption.

constraints: Cat. II cylinder oils are recommended for Mk.9 engines and higher due to their superior detergency and cleaning performance
Cylinder oil selection remains the responsibility of the owner/operator to prevent damage to the engine
regulations: Everllence Service Letter SL2022-728 cylinder oil category recommendations (Section 9.01)
warnings: Continued use of a lower-detergency oil category than recommended can progress from bore polish to ring sticking and loss of compression sealing, increasing oil consumption and wear
outcomes: Uncorrected: progressive bore polishing and deposit buildup, risking ring sticking and increased lubricating oil consumption
Corrected: appropriate detergency restored, halting deposit progression and maintaining piston/liner cleanliness
key_facts: Cat. II cylinder oils have superior detergency and cleaning ability compared to Cat. I oils and are recommended for Mk.9 engines and higher
Cylinder oils must keep pistons, piston rings, ring grooves, ringlands, and liners clean as a core design requirement
It remains the owner/operator's responsibility to select a suitable cylinder oil for the engine type

known_issue.detection_method: piston/ring belt inspection during scheduled overhaul

trace.situation: A timing fault in the ME-ECS cylinder lubrication control logic caused the Alpha lubricator injection timing to drift relative to piston position, resulting in oil being injected when the rings were not passing the lubricating orifices, significantly reducing effective lubrication despite normal commanded feed rate.
trace.trigger: Persistent rising trend in piston ring friction/wear indicators or unusually high cylinder oil consumption without a corresponding improvement in cylinder condition

procedures.action: Verify the ME-ECS cylinder lubrication timing signal against the engine's actual crank angle/piston position reference for the affected unit(s).
procedures.why: Injection timing must be synchronized with the piston ring passing the lubricating orifices during the upward stroke for oil to be effectively applied.

procedures.action: Correct or recalibrate the timing reference signal or replace the faulty sensor/control module causing the drift.
procedures.why: Restores correct synchronization between lubricator injection and piston ring position, ensuring oil is deposited where it can form a protective film.

procedures.action: Conduct a borescope inspection of the affected unit(s) to assess ring and liner condition, and monitor drain oil consumption trend post-correction to confirm effective lubrication has been restored.
procedures.why: Confirms both that the control fault has been fixed and that no lasting wear damage requires further repair.

constraints: Cylinder lubricating oil must be injected while the piston rings pass the lubricating orifices during the upward stroke for effective film formation
Control of the Alpha lubricators is integrated in the ME-ECS and depends on accurate piston position/timing reference
regulations: Everllence ME-ECS cylinder lubrication control system design description (Section 9.01/9.02)
warnings: A timing drift fault can cause high oil consumption with poor lubrication effectiveness simultaneously, masking the underlying problem if only consumption is monitored without inspecting actual wear condition
outcomes: Uncorrected: continued poor lubrication effectiveness despite normal or high oil consumption, risking progressive ring/liner wear
Corrected: injection timing restored, re-establishing effective oil film formation and normalizing wear trend
key_facts: Cylinder lubricating oil is only effective when injected as the piston rings pass the lubricating orifices during the upward stroke
The ME-ECS integrates control of the Alpha Cylinder Lubricators including injection timing
High oil consumption alone does not confirm effective lubrication if injection timing has drifted

How do I verify that lubricator injection timing is correctly synchronized with piston ring position?

known_issue.failure_mode: ME-ECS lubricator injection timing drift relative to piston position
known_issue.detection_method: rising wear trend despite normal consumption; crank angle/timing signal verification

trace.situation: During a fuel changeover from high-sulphur to low-sulphur operation, the ACOM system's small mixing volume design caused a brief but repeated oscillation between ordered BN values due to fluctuating sulphur equivalent calculation near the changeover threshold, leading to inconsistent cylinder oil quality being delivered over a short period.
trace.trigger: ACOM ordered BN value displayed on the operating panel shows rapid repeated changes within a short time window during changeover

procedures.action: Review the sulphur equivalent calculation inputs (fuel sulphur content, pilot fuel percentage, engine load) for instability or noise during the changeover period.
procedures.why: Oscillating or noisy input values near a switching threshold can cause the control logic to repeatedly recalculate and change the ordered BN.

procedures.action: If instability is confirmed, extend the changeover period or apply a stabilization delay/filter on the sulphur equivalent input (per manufacturer guidance) to prevent rapid BN oscillation.
procedures.why: Smoothing the input or extending the changeover timeline prevents the mixing system from repeatedly hunting between BN values, which can reduce blend accuracy.

procedures.action: Monitor drain oil BN consistency after the changeover is complete to confirm the mixing system settled to a stable, appropriate BN value.
procedures.why: Confirms that the oscillation has resolved and the cylinder oil delivered is consistent with the final operating fuel condition.

constraints: ACOM mixing volumes are intentionally kept small to enable fast changeover response, which can make the system sensitive to rapidly changing sulphur equivalent inputs
Fuel changeover procedures should allow sufficient time for the sulphur equivalent calculation to stabilize
regulations: Everllence ACOM system design description regarding fast-response mixing volumes (Section 9.01)
warnings: Rapid BN oscillation during changeover can cause a short period of inconsistent cylinder oil quality, which, if combined with other stressors, can locally affect liner condition
outcomes: Uncorrected: recurring short-term BN inconsistency at every fuel changeover event, creating cumulative risk to cylinder condition over many changeovers
Corrected: stabilized changeover procedure ensures consistent, appropriate BN delivery throughout the transition
key_facts: ACOM mixing volumes are kept small specifically to allow fast changeover between cylinder oil BN values
The sulphur equivalent calculation depends on fuel sulphur content, pilot fuel percentage, and engine load, all of which can fluctuate during changeover
Fuel changeover procedures should be planned to allow stable transition of the sulphur equivalent calculation

known_issue.failure_mode: ACOM BN oscillation during fuel changeover due to sulphur equivalent input instability
known_issue.detection_method: rapid repeated changes in ACOM ordered BN display during changeover monitoring

trace.situation: During a planned lubricator overhaul, maintenance personnel inadvertently cross-connected the control air supply lines for two adjacent cylinder units' lubricator actuators, causing one unit's lubricator to fail to actuate on command while the adjacent unit's lubricator over-actuated, resulting in uneven cylinder oil distribution across the two units after the engine was restarted.
trace.trigger: Post-maintenance functional test shows one unit's lubricator not responding to test signal while an adjacent unit shows unexpectedly high stroke activity

procedures.action: Halt further load increase and perform a full functional test of each lubricator unit individually, tracing control air and electrical signal routing against the as-built diagram.
procedures.why: Cross-connected lines will cause one unit's command to actuate the wrong lubricator, which must be identified before safe operation can resume.

procedures.action: Correct the air/signal line connections to match the correct unit assignment and re-test each lubricator individually for correct one-to-one response.
procedures.why: Ensures each cylinder's lubricator responds only to its own designated control signal, restoring correct, independent oil delivery per unit.

procedures.action: Conduct a full load test with close monitoring of both previously affected units' liner temperatures and drain oil condition before returning to normal unmanned operation.
procedures.why: Confirms the correction is effective and no wear has resulted from the period of incorrect/uneven lubrication.

constraints: Each cylinder's lubricator must respond only to its own designated control signal from the ME-ECS
Post-maintenance functional testing of all affected units is mandatory before returning the engine to normal service
regulations: Everllence maintenance and commissioning verification requirements for Alpha Cylinder Lubricators after overhaul (Section 9.02 reference)
warnings: Returning the engine to service without resolving a cross-connected lubricator control fault risks under-lubrication of one unit and potential damage from uncontrolled over-dosing on another
outcomes: Uncorrected: one cylinder starved of lubrication while another receives excess oil, risking both wear on the starved unit and deposit/wet-stacking issues on the over-dosed unit
Corrected: each lubricator correctly linked to its designated cylinder, restoring intended even distribution across all units
key_facts: Each cylinder liner has its own dedicated set of lubricating quills and lubricator actuation signal from the ME-ECS
Post-overhaul functional testing must confirm one-to-one correspondence between control signal and physical lubricator response
Cross-connection during maintenance is a known human-factor risk when working on adjacent, visually similar lubricator units

What functional test should be performed on each lubricator unit before returning the engine to service after overhaul?
Why is individual functional testing of each lubricator required even if the overall feed rate reading looks normal?

known_issue.failure_mode: cross-connected lubricator control signals post-maintenance causing uneven cylinder oil distribution
known_issue.detection_method: post-maintenance functional test of individual lubricator response to command signal

trace.situation: One of the two parallel engine control units (ECU) develops an internal hardware fault. The hot-standby ECU is designed to take over instantly, but a transfer fault alarm appears, indicating the handover was not clean and a brief control discontinuity occurred.
trace.trigger: ECU-A fault alarm with 'ECU transfer fault' indication on MOP

procedures.action: Confirm which ECU is currently active and that governor, injection and exhaust valve timing functions are stable.
procedures.why: Verifies the engine is safely running on the healthy unit before any further action is taken.

procedures.action: Do not attempt to reset or re-power the faulty ECU while the engine is running.
procedures.why: An uncontrolled reset could disturb the active control loop or trigger a second transfer event.

procedures.action: Schedule replacement of the faulty ECU module using the hot-swap procedure at a suitable opportunity.
procedures.why: ECU modules are designed to be replaced without stopping the engine, restoring full redundancy.

procedures.action: Monitor closely for repeat faults on the remaining ECU and prepare contingency for local/manual control.
procedures.why: Loss of the second ECU would remove automatic remote control entirely.

constraints: No single control system failure may be permitted to stop the engine
ECU modules must be replaceable without stopping the engine
regulations: Classification society redundancy requirement for unattended machinery space control systems
warnings: If the remaining ECU also fails, automatic remote control and governor function will be lost, requiring immediate transfer to local/manual control
outcomes: If uncorrected: risk of total loss of automatic engine control if the second ECU degrades
If corrected: full redundancy restored with no interruption to engine operation
key_facts: Two ECUs operate in parallel, one as hot standby for the other
ECU failure does not require engine stoppage for module replacement
ECU handles governor, start/stop sequencing, fuel injection and exhaust valve timing

known_issue.detection_method: MOP alarm for ECU transfer fault

procedures.action: Confirm via MOP diagnostics which CCU failed and that the automatic cutout has been correctly applied.

procedures.action: Reduce load if necessary and monitor remaining cylinders for increased thermal and mechanical loading.

procedures.action: Plan CCU replacement at the earliest safe opportunity.
procedures.why: All CCUs are identical and hot-swappable, restoring full cylinder operation without further risk.

constraints: Engine may continue to run with one cylinder cut out but at reduced power and increased loading on remaining units
warnings: Extended running with a cylinder cut out at high load risks thermal overload of the remaining cylinders
outcomes: If uncorrected: prolonged unbalanced running accelerates wear on remaining cylinders
If corrected: full cylinder operation and balanced load distribution restored

A CCU failure automatically cuts out only the affected cylinder, engine continues running on remaining units

outcomes: If uncorrected: increased risk of degraded scavenge air control if further ACU failures occur

trace.situation: AC input to engine control system power supply A is lost, for example due to a switchboard or breaker fault, causing the supply to switch to its internal UPS battery backup.
trace.trigger: Alarm: 'Power supply A - AC power fail / UPS battery mode'

procedures.action: Investigate the upstream AC supply (switchboard breaker, distribution panel) feeding power supply A.
procedures.why: Identifies and allows correction of the root cause of the AC loss.

procedures.action: Confirm power supply B remains fully healthy and is not affected.
procedures.why: The ECS requires both independent supplies; B must continue supporting control functions while A is on battery.

procedures.action: Restore AC input to supply A as soon as possible and monitor battery state of charge in the meantime.
procedures.why: Battery backup has limited duration; prolonged battery operation risks eventual loss of supply A entirely.

constraints: ECS requires two separate power supplies (A and B) each with battery backup
ME-ECS power supplies must only feed ME-ECS components, not other DC systems
warnings: If power supply B is also lost while A remains on battery, loss of ECS control functions becomes a realistic risk
outcomes: If uncorrected: eventual battery depletion leads to loss of power supply A entirely
If corrected: normal dual-supply redundancy restored
key_facts: Power supply A: input 100-240V AC, 45-65Hz, output 24V DC with UPS battery backup
Alarms include AC power fail, UPS battery mode, batteries not available

procedures.action: Inspect and test the battery backup fuse on power supply B.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the fuse has physically failed or there is an underlying overcurrent condition.

procedures.action: Replace with a fuse of correct rating only, and verify no unauthorized loads are connected to the ME-ECS supply.
procedures.why: The supply must only feed ME-ECS components; extraneous loads can cause recurring overcurrent and fuse failure.

procedures.action: Verify output voltage remains stable at 24V DC after fuse replacement.
procedures.why: Confirms the supply is restored to full protected operation.

constraints: ME-ECS power supplies must be isolated from other DC systems; only ME-ECS components permitted on these supplies
warnings: Operating with no battery backup available on supply B leaves the ECS vulnerable to an unprotected power loss if AC input is interrupted
outcomes: If uncorrected: any AC interruption on supply B will immediately affect ECS without battery buffering
If corrected: full backup protection restored

Fuse fail alarm indicates loss of battery backup availability, not necessarily loss of AC supply

trace.situation: One leg of the redundant ethernet-based control network connecting the MOP screens to the controllers fails, likely due to cable damage or a faulty switch, leaving only a single communication path active.
trace.trigger: Alarm: 'Control network redundancy lost'

procedures.action: Inspect cabling, connectors and network switches/media converters along the affected path, particularly noting total cable length.
procedures.why: Physical damage, moisture ingress or excessive cable run are common causes of network path loss.

procedures.action: Verify cable run does not exceed the 100 m copper ethernet distance limit between engine and engine room.
procedures.why: Exceeding this limit causes signal degradation that can masquerade as a hard failure.

procedures.action: Restore the failed path before any further network degradation occurs on the remaining path.
procedures.why: With only a single active path, any additional fault would isolate the MOP screens from the controllers.

constraints: Maximum cabling distance for copper-based ethernet between engine and engine room is 100 m
warnings: If the remaining single network path also fails, communication between MOP and the control units will be lost, removing crew visibility and command capability
outcomes: If uncorrected: total loss of control network communication is possible if the remaining path fails
If corrected: full network redundancy restored
key_facts: MOP-A and MOP-B connect to controllers via a redundant ethernet-based network
Copper ethernet cabling is distance-limited to 100 m between engine and engine room

warnings: Loss of both MOP screens would remove the crew's command and monitoring interface entirely, requiring reliance on LOP only

procedures.action: Abort the transfer attempt and confirm the ECR MOP retains active control before proceeding further.

procedures.action: Attempt the transfer again after resetting the LOP control request, observing for correct handshake confirmation.

procedures.action: If the fault persists, restrict control transfers to ECR/bridge only and schedule LOP repair before relying on it for engine-side work.

trace.situation: The mechanically driven hydraulic power supply pump fails during normal running, while one electrically driven start-up pump remains available as a standby. The hydraulic system continues to supply the HCUs at reduced redundancy, relying on the backup pump configuration.
trace.trigger: HPS mechanical pump low-flow or pressure alarm with automatic standby pump activation

procedures.action: Confirm hydraulic system pressure has stabilised on the standby electric pump.

procedures.action: Reduce engine load if hydraulic pressure shows any instability on the standby pump alone.
procedures.why: Running on a single pump without further backup increases vulnerability to a complete hydraulic supply loss.

procedures.action: Inspect the failed mechanical pump drive coupling, relief valve, and suction strainer for the cause of failure.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the fault is mechanical wear, blockage, or a relief valve malfunction.

procedures.action: Repair or replace the failed pump component as soon as practicable, restoring full multi-pump redundancy.
procedures.why: The HPS design relies on multiple pumps for redundancy; running on the sole remaining pump leaves no further backup.

constraints: HPS must maintain the required 300 bar hydraulic oil pressure to the HCUs at all times

outcomes: If uncorrected, continued single-pump operation risks complete loss of hydraulic power supply and an engine shutdown

trace.situation: At engine start, one of the two electrically driven start-up hydraulic pumps fails to prime or build pressure, delaying or preventing the engine from reaching the hydraulic pressure needed for a successful start sequence.
trace.trigger: HPS start-up sequence timeout alarm or failure to reach minimum hydraulic pressure before start attempt

procedures.action: Check the ACU assigned to control that start-up pump for a fault code.
procedures.why: ACUs control the electrically driven start-up pumps, and a control fault may prevent proper pump activation.

procedures.action: Manually activate the second electric start-up pump if not already running.
procedures.why: The system is designed with two start-up pumps; switching to the healthy one allows the start sequence to proceed.

procedures.action: Inspect the failed pump's motor, suction strainer, and non-return valve for mechanical faults.
procedures.why: A blocked strainer or faulty non-return valve are common causes of a pump failing to build pressure despite running.

procedures.action: Do not attempt to start the engine until confirmed hydraulic pressure is established via at least one functioning start-up pump.
procedures.why: Starting without adequate hydraulic pressure can result in incomplete or failed fuel injection and exhaust valve timing.

constraints: Minimum hydraulic pressure must be established before the start sequence is permitted to proceed
regulations: Everllence start sequence interlock requirements for HPS pressure confirmation
warnings: Attempting to override the pressure interlock to force a start without adequate hydraulic pressure risks incomplete valve actuation and potential mechanical damage
outcomes: If uncorrected, repeated failed start attempts may occur or the engine may be unable to start at all
If the faulty pump is corrected or the alternate pump is used, normal start sequence timing is restored

ACUs control the electrically driven hydraulic oil pumps of the HPS unit

procedures.action: Contact Everllence technical support and class surveyor to assess compatibility and required corrective action.
procedures.why: Panel compatibility with the remote control and safety system is a class and maker requirement, not a discretionary choice.

procedures.action: Replace with an approved panel or apply the maker's compatibility patch before returning to full automatic reliance.
procedures.why: Restores guaranteed correct shutdown/slowdown signal transfer to the ECS.

constraints: Only Everllence-approved shutdown/slowdown panels may be used with the ME control system
The remote control system and safety system must be verified compatible

trace.situation: A faulty sensor feeding the independent engine safety system generates an erroneous critical value reading, triggering a non-cancellable shutdown signal to the ECS even though the underlying engine condition is actually normal.
trace.trigger: Unexpected non-cancellable shutdown executed by the ECS with no corroborating abnormal trend on other related parameters

procedures.action: Do not attempt to restart the engine until the shutdown cause has been investigated and confirmed as a false signal.
procedures.why: A non-cancellable shutdown is designed to prevent restart until the safety condition is cleared; bypassing this risks masking a real fault.

procedures.action: Cross-check the triggering parameter against redundant or nearby sensors and logged trend data.
procedures.why: Helps distinguish a genuine critical condition from a single faulty sensor reading.

procedures.action: Inspect and test the specific sensor and its wiring/signal conditioning for calibration drift, moisture ingress, or connector faults.
procedures.why: Faulty sensors are a common cause of spurious safety system shutdowns that do not reflect actual engine conditions.

procedures.action: Replace or recalibrate the faulty sensor and have the safety system reset by authorised personnel before clearing the shutdown.
procedures.why: Ensures the shutdown signal path is restored to accurate operation before engine restart is permitted.

constraints: The safety system is independent of the ECS and its shutdown signals must fulfil classification society and Everllence requirements
Non-cancellable shutdowns must not be bypassed without proper investigation

If the faulty sensor is identified and corrected, normal reliable safety system operation is restored

procedures.action: Verify via the AMS and MOP that the original alarm condition has genuinely cleared and is reading within normal limits consistently, not just momentarily.

procedures.action: Check whether the slowdown cancellation requires manual acknowledgement at the AMS or MOP.

procedures.why: A persistent slowdown despite a cleared condition may indicate a signal path or logic fault rather than a genuine engine condition.

procedures.action: Escalate to engineering support if the slowdown cannot be cleared through normal means, documenting the parameter history.
procedures.why: Ensures proper diagnosis of whether this is an ECS/AMS interface fault requiring technical correction.

procedures.action: If repeated attempts fail, use the LOP as a fallback and report the remote control system fault for technical investigation.

procedures.why: Confirms whether blowers are failing to start/stop at the correct load thresholds as commanded by the SCU.

procedures.action: If automatic control is unreliable, manually control the auxiliary blowers to maintain adequate scavenge air pressure for the current load.
procedures.why: Prevents insufficient scavenge air supply, which could affect combustion quality and increase thermal loading.

procedures.action: Repair the faulty ACU/SCU component and verify correct automatic blower sequencing is restored across a range of load changes before returning to full automatic operation.
procedures.why: Ensures reliable scavenge air pressure control is re-established for all engine operating conditions.

constraints: Scavenge air pressure must be adequate for the current engine load to ensure proper combustion and thermal loading
regulations: Everllence requirement for correct auxiliary blower sequencing relative to engine load via SCU
warnings: Insufficient scavenge air pressure at a given load can lead to incomplete combustion, increased exhaust temperatures, and risk of thermal overload on affected cylinders
outcomes: If uncorrected, unreliable scavenge air control can degrade combustion efficiency and increase exhaust temperature spread between cylinders
If the ACU/SCU fault is corrected, scavenge air pressure control is restored to match engine load reliably
key_facts: ACUs control auxiliary blowers and the scavenge air control unit (SCU)
Auxiliary blower status for 'Auxiliary system ready' is one of the required inputs for the remote control system

chapter_title: Engine Control System -- synthesized domain knowledge

trace.situation: The 'Auxiliary system ready' interlock signal, compiled from multiple inputs including turning gear disengaged status, main starting valve position, and control air valve states, fails to clear even though all individual auxiliary systems appear physically ready, preventing the engine from being started.
trace.trigger: Engine start sequence blocked with 'auxiliary system not ready' indication despite apparent normal status of all prerequisite systems

procedures.action: Check each individual input contributing to the 'Auxiliary system ready' signal: turning gear disengaged, main starting valve open, sealing air valve open, air spring valve open, auxiliary blowers running, and HPS ready.
procedures.why: The composite ready signal depends on multiple discrete inputs, any one of which being stuck or miswired will block the overall signal.

procedures.action: Physically verify the turning gear is fully disengaged and its position switch is functioning correctly.
procedures.why: A faulty or misaligned turning gear position switch is a common cause of a false 'not ready' signal even when the gear is actually disengaged.

procedures.action: Check main starting valve and control air valve position feedback switches for correct operation and signal continuity to the ECS.
procedures.why: A failed position switch or broken wiring on any one valve can hold the composite ready signal false indefinitely.

procedures.action: Repair or replace the faulty position switch or wiring identified, then confirm the 'Auxiliary system ready' signal clears before attempting to start.
procedures.why: Ensures the interlock accurately reflects true system readiness before allowing an engine start.

constraints: Engine start must be blocked until 'Auxiliary system ready' is confirmed true from all required subsystems
regulations: Everllence start interlock requirement for auxiliary system readiness confirmation
warnings: Bypassing the 'Auxiliary system ready' interlock without confirming all auxiliary systems are genuinely ready risks starting the engine with turning gear engaged or valves incorrectly positioned, which can cause severe mechanical damage
outcomes: If uncorrected, the engine remains blocked from starting despite being otherwise ready, delaying operations
If the faulty input switch or wiring is repaired, the start interlock correctly clears and normal starting is restored
key_facts: 'Auxiliary system ready' combines inputs from fuel oil, lube oil, and cooling water systems plus ECS inputs: turning gear disengaged, main starting valve open, sealing air valve open, air spring valve open, auxiliary blowers running, and HPS ready
All these inputs must be true simultaneously before the start sequence can proceed

known_issue.failure_mode: false 'Auxiliary system ready' interlock block due to faulty position switch or wiring
known_issue.detection_method: engine start sequence blocked with composite auxiliary readiness status showing not ready despite individually confirmed system status

trace.situation: One or more Alpha cylinder lubricator quills on a liner become partially or fully blocked by carbonised oil residue (carbon bridging), reducing or stopping oil delivery through those specific orifices while the remaining quills on the same liner continue to lubricate normally.
trace.trigger: Localized rise in scavenge drain oil iron content from one unit, or an uneven black/dry patch found on the liner wall during a scheduled scavenge port inspection.

procedures.action: Run a manual lubricator test shot and visually/instrumentally verify oil discharge at each individual quill on the affected cylinder.
procedures.why: Confirms exactly which quill(s) are blocked versus delivering normally before any disassembly is attempted.

procedures.action: Remove the blocked quill non-return valve assembly and clear carbon bridging using OEM-approved tools, replacing the non-return valve if scored.
procedures.why: Carbon bridging obstructs the metered oil path; only approved clearing methods avoid enlarging the orifice and over-dosing later.

procedures.action: Inspect the liner wall and piston ring running surface through the scavenge port for scuffing, glazing or dry patches before returning to full load.
procedures.why: Identifies wear already caused by localized oil starvation so load can be limited until condition is confirmed safe.

procedures.action: Temporarily increase the cylinder oil feed rate on the affected unit per OEM guidance until the quill repair is verified effective over several running hours.
procedures.why: Compensates for reduced lubrication coverage and protects the liner until normal dosing is confirmed restored.

constraints: Minimum cylinder oil feed rate must not be less than 0.6 g/kWh per Service Letter guidance
Oil must be delivered via quills during the piston ring upward stroke through non-return valves as per design
regulations: Everllence Service Letter on cylinder oil feed rate
Class requirement for liner condition monitoring during surveys
warnings: If left unresolved, localized dry friction can progress to liner scuffing and ring breakage within hours at full load, risking a cylinder unit shutdown
Do not ream blocked quills with oversized tools as this permanently alters the metered dose
outcomes: If not corrected: liner scoring, ring land wear, and potential piston seizure on the affected unit
If corrected: uniform lubrication restored and progressive wear arrested
key_facts: Cylinder oil is introduced via lubricating quills timed to the piston ring upward stroke
Non-return valves at each quill prevent backflow of combustion gas into the lubricator
ME-ECS integrates and times lubricator control
Minimum feed rate per Service Letter is 0.6 g/kWh

trace.situation: A cylinder oil non-return valve at a lubricating quill sticks in the open position, allowing combustion gas and pressure to act back into the lubricator feed line instead of metering oil only on the upward ring stroke, causing erratic or excessive oil discharge at that point.
trace.trigger: Alpha lubricator feedback alarm for abnormal injection pressure, or visible excessive oil wetting/streaking at one lubricating point noted during a routine piston inspection.

procedures.action: Isolate the affected lubricator feed line at the quill and confirm with a pressure test whether the non-return valve holds pressure in the closed direction.
procedures.why: Determines whether the valve seat or spring has failed, allowing reverse flow or gas blow-back.

procedures.action: Remove and replace the faulty non-return valve with an OEM spare, checking seat condition and spring tension before refitting.
procedures.why: A stuck-open valve cannot meter oil correctly and risks gas ingress into the lubricator supply line.

procedures.action: Check surrounding quills and liner surface for oil flooding or dry patches caused by the faulty metering.
procedures.why: Confirms whether uneven lubrication has already caused localized wear requiring load restriction.

procedures.action: Log the event and increase monitoring frequency of lubricator feedback signals on that cylinder for the next several running hours.
procedures.why: Verifies the repair is effective and no secondary valve is developing the same fault.

constraints: Non-return valves must only allow flow into the cylinder during the piston ring upward stroke
Lubricator control signals are supervised by ME-ECS and must show consistent feedback per injection cycle
regulations: Manufacturer maintenance manual requirement for periodic non-return valve inspection/renewal
warnings: Continued operation with a stuck-open non-return valve risks combustion gas blow-back into the cylinder oil supply system, a fire/explosion hazard
Uneven oil flooding at one point can mask under-lubrication elsewhere on the same liner
outcomes: If not corrected: gas blow-back contamination of cylinder oil supply and localized liner wear from oil flooding/starvation imbalance
If corrected: proper one-way metered lubrication restored and gas path hazard eliminated
key_facts: Cylinder oil is pumped into the cylinder via non-return valves timed to the ring upward stroke
Non-return valves prevent combustion gas from entering the lubricator feed system
ME-ECS monitors lubricator injection via feedback signals

known_issue.detection_method: lubricator feedback pressure anomaly / visual oil flooding at quill

trace.situation: The ACOS2 three-way ball valve actuator fails to switch pneumatically between high-BN and low-BN cylinder oil, leaving the engine running on the wrong BN grade relative to the current fuel sulphur content and operating mode.
trace.trigger: ZS8261/ZS8262 valve position feedback alarm mismatch with the commanded XC8260 signal on the ME-ECS, or cylinder condition monitoring showing unexpected drain oil BN trend.

procedures.action: Check control air supply pressure and the solenoid valve (3/2 type) operation feeding the pneumatic actuator.
procedures.why: Loss of control air or a failed solenoid is the most common cause of the actuator not responding to the ECS command.

procedures.action: Manually verify actual three-way valve position against the ECS feedback signals ZS8261/ZS8262.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the fault is in the valve itself, the feedback wiring, or the actuator mechanism.

procedures.action: If the actuator is mechanically seized, isolate, repair or replace it, noting that spring return defaults to high-BN oil in fail-safe.
procedures.why: Restores correct automatic switching function matched to sulphur equivalent and load.

procedures.action: Until repaired, manually select the correct BN control mode on the MOP matching current fuel/pilot fuel sulphur content.
procedures.why: Prevents prolonged operation on an unmatched BN oil that could cause cold corrosion or excessive deposit formation.

constraints: Three-way valve fail-safe position must default to high-BN oil on loss of control air
BN selection must match sulphur equivalent per cylinder lubrication strategy
regulations: Everllence Service Letter cylinder lubrication guideline for BN selection matched to fuel sulphur
warnings: Running low-BN oil on high-sulphur fuel can cause cold corrosion and rapid liner wear
Running high-BN oil continuously on low-sulphur fuel promotes excessive deposit build-up and bore polishing
outcomes: If not corrected: mismatched BN leads to either corrosive wear or deposit-related scuffing depending on direction of error
If corrected: automatic BN switching matched to actual fuel sulphur content resumes, protecting liner condition
key_facts: ACOS2 uses a pneumatically actuated three-way ball valve with spring return to high-BN oil as fail-safe
Valve position feedback signals are ZS8261 (low-BN) and ZS8262 (high-BN)
Control signal XC8260 commands low-BN selection when closed

trace.situation: During dual-fuel operation the crew enters an incorrect pilot fuel sulphur percentage into the main operating panel (MOP), causing the ACOS2/ACOM system to calculate an incorrect sulphur equivalent and select or mix the wrong cylinder oil BN.
trace.trigger: Drain oil analysis BN trend inconsistent with the expected fuel sulphur content, or a cross-check of MOP input against bunker delivery note sulphur data reveals a discrepancy.

procedures.action: Cross-check the pilot fuel sulphur percentage entered on the MOP against the current bunker delivery note (BDN) certificate value.
procedures.why: The sulphur equivalent calculation depends entirely on the accuracy of this manually entered value.

procedures.action: Correct the MOP sulphur input to match the verified BDN value for the fuel in use.
procedures.why: Restores correct automatic BN selection/mixing matched to actual combusted sulphur content.

procedures.action: Review recent drain oil analysis trends for signs of under- or over-dosed BN during the incorrect input period.
procedures.why: Determines whether corrective inspection of liners/rings is warranted before resuming normal operation.

procedures.action: Establish a watch-standing procedure requiring sulphur input verification at every fuel/pilot fuel change.
procedures.why: Prevents recurrence of the same input error on future fuel changes.

constraints: Sulphur equivalent calculation is based on engine load, pilot fuel amount, and pilot fuel sulphur content entered manually on MOP
BN selection/mixing must track the calculated sulphur equivalent, not nominal fuel type alone
regulations: Everllence cylinder lubrication strategy guideline matching cylinder oil to fuel sulphur content
warnings: An uncorrected sulphur input error can persist for days, causing cumulative wear or deposit damage before being detected by drain oil trend review
Incorrect BN selection in DF operation risks cold corrosion if actual sulphur equivalent is higher than assumed
outcomes: If not corrected: continued mismatch between oil BN and actual acid load, risking liner/ring damage
If corrected: sulphur equivalent calculation and automatic BN control restored to design intent
key_facts: Sulphur equivalent in DF operation accounts for engine load, pilot fuel quantity, and pilot fuel sulphur content
The crew must manually input pilot fuel sulphur content on the MOP
ACOS2/ACOM automatically calculate sulphur equivalent from this input

trace.situation: Electrical heat tracing on the cylinder oil supply pipeline between the heating tank and the engine fails, allowing the oil to cool below its design minimum temperature, increasing viscosity and degrading atomisation and metering accuracy at the lubricator quills.
trace.trigger: Cylinder oil supply temperature alarm low, or irregular lubricator injection behaviour noted during cold weather/low ambient conditions.

procedures.action: Check the electrical heat tracing circuit breaker, terminal box connections, and tracing cable continuity at the engine connection point.
procedures.why: A tripped breaker or open circuit in the tracing cable is the most common cause of pipeline cooling.

procedures.action: Verify the heating tank temperature and element operation to rule out a tank-side heating fault as well.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the fault is isolated to the pipeline tracing or extends to the heating tank heater element.

procedures.action: Restore tracing power and re-insulate any damaged sections of pipe lagging found during the inspection.
procedures.why: Heat tracing and insulation together maintain the oil above its design minimum viscosity temperature along the entire run to the engine.

procedures.action: Monitor cylinder oil feed rate and lubricator performance for several hours after restoring tracing to confirm normal metering has resumed.
procedures.why: Confirms viscosity has returned to within the recommended 18.5–21.9 cSt at 100°C range equivalent for proper dosing.

constraints: Design minimum cylinder oil temperature in the tank is 25°C
Entire pipeline from heating tank to engine must be fitted with insulation and electrical heat tracing
regulations: Everllence system design requirement for heat tracing and insulation on cylinder oil supply lines
warnings: Cold, high-viscosity cylinder oil can cause erratic or reduced delivery at the lubricator quills, risking localized starvation
Prolonged low temperature operation may require increasing heating element size per the design formula if not corrected
outcomes: If not corrected: poor oil atomisation and inconsistent dosing increase wear risk across multiple cylinders
If corrected: oil viscosity and flow characteristics return to design range, restoring reliable lubricator metering
key_facts: Design minimum cylinder oil temperature in the tank is 25°C
Recommended cylinder oil viscosity is 18.5–21.9 cSt at 100°C with VI min. 95
Heat tracing cable connects to a terminal box at the engine
Heating tank capacity is approximately 40 litres

trace.situation: Cylinder oil feed rate is set below the OEM minimum guideline (configured ACC factor too low) relative to current fuel sulphur content, resulting in chronic under-lubrication across all units rather than a single-cylinder fault.
trace.trigger: Fleet-wide or engine-wide rising trend in drain oil iron content across multiple cylinders despite normal individual quill/valve function.

procedures.action: Retrieve the current feed rate setting and ACC factor configured in the ME-ECS and compare against the latest OEM Service Letter guideline for the fuel sulphur in use.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the configured feed rate falls below the recommended minimum for current operating conditions.

procedures.action: Adjust the feed rate/ACC setting upward to meet or exceed the minimum of 0.6 g/kWh or the current Service Letter recommendation, whichever is higher.
procedures.why: Restores adequate oil film thickness to protect liner and rings against the acid and friction loads present.

procedures.action: Review recent drain oil analysis and scavenge port inspection results across all units for early scuffing or wear indicators.
procedures.why: Determines if any units require closer monitoring or temporary feed rate boost above minimum before trend stabilises.

procedures.action: Document the configuration change and notify technical superintendent/OEM service for confirmation the new setting matches the latest guideline.
procedures.why: Ensures the correction aligns with the most current official feed rate recommendation, which is periodically revised.

constraints: Minimum cylinder oil feed rate must not be less than 0.6 g/kWh
ACC factor nominally between 0.2–0.4 g/kWh per % sulphur, as per design basis
regulations: Everllence Service Letter on minimum cylinder oil feed rate
warnings: Sustained under-dosing across the engine can lead to simultaneous multi-cylinder liner wear and increases risk of a cascading seizure event
Feed rate changes should be verified against the latest Service Letter as guidance is periodically updated
outcomes: If not corrected: accelerated, widespread liner and ring wear requiring premature overhaul
If corrected: feed rate restored to protective minimum, arresting the wear trend
key_facts: Minimum cylinder oil feed rate is 0.6 g/kWh regardless of calculated ACC x S value
Feed rate = ACC [g/kWh] x S[%], with ACC normally 0.2–0.4
Continuous drain oil analysis is used to optimise feed rate and safeguard against wear

trace.situation: The engine operates for an extended period on low-BN cylinder oil at low load or with high-sulphur fuel present (e.g., incorrect sulphur equivalent calculation or operator override), allowing sulphuric acid formed from combustion to attack the liner surface faster than the oil's alkalinity can neutralise it.
trace.trigger: Drain oil analysis shows abnormally high acid number / low residual BN, or liner wall inspection reveals a characteristic honed, glassy-grey corrosive wear pattern rather than normal polishing.

procedures.action: Confirm actual fuel sulphur content and current load against the cylinder oil BN currently selected or mixed.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the BN in use is too low for the acid load being generated at the current operating condition.

procedures.action: Switch to high-BN cylinder oil (manually if required) and/or adjust ACOM mixing target BN upward.
procedures.why: Higher BN oil provides greater alkalinity reserve to neutralise the sulphuric acid formed from combustion.

procedures.action: Inspect affected liners and piston rings at the next opportunity for cold corrosion patterns (grey/matte honing marks, pitting).
procedures.why: Determines extent of damage already done and whether liner/ring renewal is required.

procedures.action: Review low-load operating procedures to ensure adequate cylinder oil BN and feed rate are maintained during extended slow steaming or manoeuvring.
procedures.why: Low load combined with low BN oil is a known high-risk combination for cold corrosion.

constraints: Cylinder oil BN must be matched to sulphur equivalent of combusted fuel per lubrication strategy
Cat. II 100/140 BN oils are intended mainly for high-sulphur fuel applications
regulations: Everllence lubrication strategy guideline matching cylinder oil BN to fuel type and sulphur content
warnings: Cold corrosion can progress to severe liner wear and ring breakage within a relatively short running period if uncorrected
Low engine load combined with mismatched low-BN oil significantly increases cold corrosion risk
outcomes: If not corrected: accelerated liner wear, ring groove wear, and potential piston ring collapse from cold corrosion
If corrected: acid neutralisation restored, halting further corrosive wear
key_facts: Cylinder oils neutralise acids and oxidation products via their base number (BN)
100 and 140 BN Cat. II oils are mainly used for high-sulphur fuel applications
Cold corrosion produces a characteristic grey, honed liner wear pattern distinct from abrasive wear

known_issue.failure_mode: cold corrosion from BN/sulphur mismatch
known_issue.detection_method: drain oil acid number trend and liner wall visual inspection

trace.situation: Prolonged operation with excessively high cylinder oil feed rate or overly high detergency BN oil relative to actual fuel sulphur content causes excessive deposit formation and bore polishing on the liner, reducing the oil film retention and increasing lubricating oil consumption from the crankcase side.
trace.trigger: Increasing lube oil consumption trend combined with a shiny, mirror-like polished band observed on the liner during a scavenge port inspection.

procedures.action: Review recent cylinder oil feed rate and BN selection history against actual fuel sulphur content over the preceding weeks.
procedures.why: Confirms whether over-dosing or BN mismatch (too high) is the driver of excess deposit/polishing rather than a mechanical fault.

procedures.action: Reduce the feed rate toward the OEM-recommended optimum (not below the 0.6 g/kWh minimum) and/or correct BN selection to match actual sulphur equivalent.
procedures.why: Lowers detergent/alkalinity oversupply that is stripping the liner's protective oxide/oil film and causing polishing.

procedures.action: Inspect piston rings for reduced ring tension or flattened running surfaces consistent with bore polish.
procedures.why: Confirms the extent of ring/liner interaction damage requiring possible ring renewal.

procedures.action: Monitor liner wall roughness and lube oil consumption trend over subsequent running hours to confirm the corrective dosing arrests further polishing.
procedures.why: Validates that the adjusted feed rate/BN restores a honing pattern rather than a mirror-polished surface.

constraints: Feed rate adjustments must still respect the 0.6 g/kWh minimum
Cylinder oil must keep liners clean without stripping the protective running-in surface finish
regulations: Everllence guideline on optimising cylinder oil feed rate via drain oil analysis
warnings: Bore polishing increases lube oil consumption and can progress to loss of ring sealing if not corrected
Over-correction (too low feed rate) risks swinging into under-lubrication wear instead
outcomes: If not corrected: continued bore polishing, rising lube oil consumption, and eventual loss of compression/ring sealing
If corrected: liner surface finish and oil retention restored, consumption trend normalises
key_facts: Cylinder oil feed rate optimisation relies on continuous drain oil analysis
Excess detergency/BN can strip the liner's protective running surface, causing bore polish
Feed rate minimum remains 0.6 g/kWh even when reducing from an over-dosed condition

known_issue.detection_method: rising lube oil consumption trend and scavenge port visual inspection

trace.situation: Water ingress into the cylinder oil storage tank (via a faulty tank vent, condensation, or contaminated bunkering) causes emulsification of the cylinder oil, degrading its lubricating and acid-neutralising properties before it reaches the lubricators.
trace.trigger: Routine tank sounding/sample shows free water or a cloudy emulsified sample, or lubricator supply pressure fluctuates abnormally.

procedures.action: Sound and sample the affected storage/service tank bottom, draining any free water via the sloped tank bottom drain.
procedures.why: The tank design intentionally slopes to the bottom for water drainage; water must be removed before oil is drawn for lubrication.

procedures.action: Send an oil sample for laboratory analysis to confirm water content and emulsion stability before returning the tank to service.
procedures.why: Visual clearing does not confirm the oil's lubricating and BN properties have not been compromised.

procedures.action: Inspect the tank vent pipe and filling arrangements for the source of water ingress.
procedures.why: Prevents recurrence by addressing the entry point (damaged vent head, poor bunkering practice, etc.).

procedures.action: If contamination is confirmed significant, isolate the tank and switch to the alternate cylinder oil tank/grade while the affected tank is drained and cleaned.
procedures.why: Protects the engine from receiving degraded cylinder oil during the cleanup period.

constraints: Tank bottoms must be sloped for easy water drainage per design
Tall, slim tank design is intended to optimise settling of contaminants
regulations: Shipboard bunkering and tank sounding procedures per SMS/PMS requirements
warnings: Emulsified cylinder oil can cause erratic lubricator metering and reduced film strength, increasing scuffing risk
Undetected water contamination can mask itself until lubricator malfunction symptoms appear at the engine
outcomes: If not corrected: degraded lubrication performance and possible lubricator metering faults across multiple units
If corrected: oil quality restored and lubrication reliability maintained
key_facts: Cylinder oil storage/service tanks are designed tall and slim with sloped bottoms to aid water settling and drainage
Routine tank sounding and sampling is part of safeguarding lubrication quality
Two separate tanks are normally arranged for the two cylinder oil grades
