known_issue.detection_method: tank sounding/sampling and lubricator supply pressure irregularity

trace.situation: The ACOM Coriolis flowmeter used for sulphur-equivalent based BN mixing drifts or fails, causing the mixed cylinder oil BN delivered to the engine to deviate from the calculated target without an immediately obvious alarm.
trace.trigger: Drain oil BN measurement inconsistent with the ACOM-reported mixed BN value, or an ACOM system flow deviation/consistency alarm on the ME-ECS.

procedures.action: Compare the ACOM system's reported mixed BN and flow values against an independent drain oil BN sample result.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the discrepancy originates from the flowmeter/mixing calculation rather than an operational cause.

procedures.action: Inspect and, if necessary, recalibrate or replace the Coriolis-type flowmeter per OEM procedure.
procedures.why: The Coriolis meter is specifically required for accurate mass flow measurement at the very low flow rates involved in cylinder lubrication.

procedures.action: Switch ACOM to manual BN mode and enter a verified target BN while the flowmeter fault is resolved.
procedures.why: Maintains correct cylinder oil BN delivery independent of the faulty automatic mixing calculation.

procedures.action: Review recent drain oil trends to assess whether any period of incorrect mixed BN caused measurable liner/ring wear.
procedures.why: Determines if follow-up inspection is warranted before resuming full automatic control.

constraints: Only a Coriolis-type flowmeter can be used in the heating-tank-to-engine or service-tank-to-heating-tank locations due to low flow accuracy requirements
ACOM mixed BN must remain within the range bounded by the two stored cylinder oil BN grades
regulations: OEM ACOM system design and flowmeter type requirement
warnings: An undetected flowmeter drift can silently deliver incorrect BN oil for an extended period before drain oil analysis reveals the discrepancy
Reverting to manual mode without verifying the correct target BN can itself introduce dosing errors
outcomes: If not corrected: continued delivery of incorrect BN oil risking either cold corrosion or deposit-related wear depending on direction of error
If corrected: automatic BN mixing accuracy restored, matching actual fuel sulphur equivalent
key_facts: ACOM mixes two fully formulated cylinder oils to an optimum BN based on calculated sulphur equivalent
A Coriolis-type mass flowmeter is recommended due to low differential pressure and no built-in non-return function
ACOM mixing volumes are kept small for fast changeover response

trace.situation: A cylinder lubricator pump unit (Alpha lubricator) develops a mechanical fault such as a stuck or worn plunger, causing zero or significantly reduced oil delivery to one or more cylinders served by that unit, independent of quill condition.
trace.trigger: ME-ECS lubricator fault/no-injection alarm for a specific unit, or a sudden drop in that cylinder's logged oil consumption versus commanded dose.

procedures.action: Confirm the fault via ME-ECS lubricator diagnostic data, checking commanded versus actual injection feedback for the affected unit.
procedures.why: Distinguishes a pump mechanical fault from a control signal or quill-side issue.

procedures.action: Inspect and, if required, overhaul or replace the lubricator pump plunger/element per OEM maintenance instructions.
procedures.why: A stuck or worn plunger cannot deliver the commanded metered dose and must be mechanically restored.

procedures.action: Verify oil delivery is restored by test-firing the repaired unit and confirming feedback matches command.
procedures.why: Confirms the repair effectively restores metering before resuming normal load on that cylinder.

procedures.action: Reduce load or monitor the affected cylinder closely until lubrication is confirmed fully restored.
procedures.why: Protects the liner from running under-lubricated while the repair is completed and verified.

constraints: Lubricator control and injection timing is integrated in the ME-ECS and must match the piston ring upward stroke

A command-feedback mismatch alarm should never be silenced without physical verification of oil delivery
outcomes: If not corrected: localized dry-running wear leading to possible piston seizure on the affected unit
If corrected: metered lubrication restored and unit protected from starvation wear

Lubricator injection is timed to occur during the piston ring upward stroke
A command-feedback mismatch is the primary indicator of a mechanical lubricator fault

trace.situation: The cylinder oil supply filter (250 micron absolute fineness) becomes progressively clogged with sludge or wear debris, restricting flow from the service/heating tank toward the lubricators and reducing available injection pressure.
trace.trigger: Gradually falling cylinder oil supply pressure trend noted on ME-ECS monitoring, or increased lubricator low-pressure alarms across multiple units simultaneously.

procedures.action: Check differential pressure across the cylinder oil filter and compare against the clean/dirty filter reference values.
procedures.why: Confirms filter clogging as the cause of reduced supply pressure rather than a lubricator or pump fault.

procedures.action: Isolate and clean or renew the filter element, verifying it meets the 250 micron absolute fineness specification.
procedures.why: Restores design flow capacity to the lubricators and heating tank supply line.

procedures.action: Inspect the removed filter debris for abnormal wear metal content, sending a sample for analysis if significant.
procedures.why: Clogging caused by wear debris rather than normal sludge may indicate an upstream mechanical problem requiring further investigation.

procedures.action: Re-establish normal supply pressure and confirm lubricator injection pressure feedback returns to normal range across all units.
procedures.why: Confirms the corrective action has fully restored the lubrication supply system.

constraints: Cylinder oil filter fineness must be 250 μm absolute

regulations: OEM component specification for cylinder oil filter fineness
warnings: A clogged filter affecting multiple cylinders simultaneously is a higher-severity event than a single quill blockage and should be treated as engine-wide risk
Ignoring a rising differential pressure trend risks a sudden flow restriction event during manoeuvring
outcomes: If not corrected: progressive reduction in lubrication supply pressure across multiple cylinders, risking widespread under-lubrication
If corrected: design flow and pressure restored, protecting all cylinders uniformly

Filter is located in the supply path between storage/service tank and heating tank/engine

trace.situation: The cylinder oil heating tank level falls below the low-level alarm setpoint (LS 8212 AL) due to a transfer pump fault or valve mis-alignment, risking air entrainment into the gravity-fed supply line to the lubricators.
trace.trigger: Low-level alarm LS 8212 AL activates on the heating tank, or lubricator supply pressure becomes unstable/pulsating.

procedures.action: Immediately check the transfer pump from the service/storage tank to the heating tank for operation and correct valve line-up.
procedures.why: A stopped pump or mis-aligned valve is the most common cause of the heating tank not replenishing.

procedures.action: Restore the transfer pump operation or correct valve alignment, then confirm the heating tank level rises and the alarm clears.
procedures.why: Re-establishes the gravity head needed to maintain stable lubricator supply pressure and prevent air ingress.

procedures.action: Check the vent pipe for blockage if the tank is not filling despite a running transfer pump.
procedures.why: A blocked vent can prevent proper tank filling even with the pump running correctly.

procedures.action: Monitor lubricator injection pressure feedback across all units after level recovery to confirm no air remains entrained in the supply line.
procedures.why: Air entrainment can cause erratic dosing even after the level alarm clears, requiring venting/bleeding of the line.

constraints: Heating tank bottom must be minimum 2000 mm above the engine connection 'AC' to maintain gravity head
Low-level alarm LS 8212 AL must be acted upon promptly to avoid supply interruption
regulations: OEM GVA (Guidance Values for Automation) tag requirement for heating tank low-level alarm
warnings: Running the heating tank dry can introduce air into the lubricator supply line causing multi-cylinder dosing irregularities
Delayed response to the low-level alarm risks a full interruption of cylinder lubrication supply
outcomes: If not corrected: air entrainment and eventual loss of cylinder oil supply to the lubricators, risking engine-wide under-lubrication
If corrected: stable gravity-fed supply restored, maintaining consistent lubricator dosing

Heating tank bottom must be at least 2000 mm above the engine inlet connection 'AC' for correct gravity feed

trace.situation: A single cylinder oil transfer pump shared between the two BN grades experiences an interlock failure between suction/discharge valves, allowing unintended blending of high-BN and low-BN cylinder oils in the service/heating tanks.
trace.trigger: Unexpected BN value in drain oil analysis that does not match either nominal stocked grade, or a tank sample showing an intermediate BN inconsistent with the selected control mode.

procedures.action: Stop the shared transfer pump immediately and verify the position of all suction/discharge valves against the interlock logic.
procedures.why: Prevents further cross-contamination while the interlock fault is diagnosed.

procedures.action: Repair or replace the failed interlock mechanism between the two valve sets before resuming transfer operations.
procedures.why: The interlock exists specifically to prevent simultaneous opening of both grades' valves, which causes blending.

procedures.action: Sample and analyse the affected service/heating tank to determine the actual resulting BN and whether it remains usable or must be downgraded/discarded.
procedures.why: Determines whether the blended oil can still be used (e.g., as a lower BN stock) or must be disposed of to avoid incorrect dosing.

procedures.action: Review the control mode selection logic (Auto/High BN/Low BN) to ensure it reflects the actual verified BN now in the tank.
procedures.why: Prevents the ECS from assuming a nominal BN that no longer matches the blended tank contents.

constraints: If one transfer pump is used for both cylinder oils, suction/discharge valves must be interlocked to prevent unintended blending
Separate storage/service tanks are normally required for the two BN grades
regulations: OEM system design requirement for transfer pump valve interlock when a shared pump is used
warnings: Blended BN oil of unknown concentration can result in either under- or over-alkalinity relative to what the ECS assumes is being delivered
Continuing to operate on an unverified blended tank risks systemic wrong-dosing across all cylinders
outcomes: If not corrected: engine-wide incorrect BN dosing with unpredictable cold corrosion or deposit risk
If corrected: segregation of the two cylinder oil grades restored, ensuring BN selection matches actual tank contents
key_facts: A shared transfer pump for both cylinder oils requires interlocked suction/discharge valves
Cylinder oil storage/service tanks are normally arranged separately per BN grade
Drain oil BN analysis is the primary means of detecting unintended blending

trace.situation: The ACOS2 timer (Max./Force functions) is misconfigured, allowing the engine to run on low-BN cylinder oil for longer than intended without switching to high-BN for the scheduled cleaning cycle, leading to progressive cylinder deposit build-up.
trace.trigger: A scavenge port inspection reveals heavier-than-normal carbon deposits on piston crown/ring lands despite nominal feed rate, or a review of timer logs shows the Max./Force criteria have not triggered a switch for an unusually long period.

procedures.action: Review the ACOS2 timer configuration (Max. and Force day values and feed rate thresholds) in the ME-ECS against the OEM-recommended cleaning cycle guidance.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the timer settings themselves, rather than a hardware fault, are allowing excessive low-BN running time.

procedures.action: Correct the Max./Force timer day values and/or feed rate thresholds to match the current Service Letter recommendation for cylinder cleanliness management.
procedures.why: Restores the intended periodic switch to high-BN oil needed to control deposit build-up.

procedures.action: Force a manual switch to high-BN oil for an extended period to perform a corrective cleaning cycle on the affected units.
procedures.why: Actively removes accumulated deposits that built up during the extended low-BN period.

procedures.action: Re-inspect via scavenge port after the cleaning cycle to confirm deposit levels have reduced to normal.
procedures.why: Validates that the timer correction and cleaning cycle have been effective.

constraints: The Max. timer switches to high-BN oil if either the low-BN feed rate threshold or configured day count is exceeded
The Force timer requires both the feed rate and day criteria to be met before switching to high-BN oil
regulations: Everllence Service Letter / circular letter guidance on cylinder oil BN switching cycles for cleanliness
warnings: Excessive deposit build-up can eventually cause ring sticking or bore polishing if not periodically cleaned with high-BN operation
Misconfigured timers may not generate any alarm, relying on periodic log review or inspection to detect
outcomes: If not corrected: progressive piston/ring land deposit build-up risking ring sticking and blow-by
If corrected: periodic high-BN cleaning cycles resume, maintaining piston and liner cleanliness

trace.situation: Drain oil analysis across multiple cylinders shows a gradual upward trend in iron content over several weeks without any single acute event, indicating a slow-developing generalized wear condition rather than a sudden fault.
trace.trigger: Routine periodic drain oil sample results show a steady increase in iron (Fe) ppm trend across consecutive sampling intervals, flagged during trend review.

procedures.action: Compile the drain oil iron trend data across all cylinders over the recent sampling history and identify whether the increase is uniform or concentrated on specific units.
procedures.why: Distinguishes a systemic cause (feed rate, oil quality, BN mismatch) from a localized mechanical issue on specific cylinders.

procedures.action: Cross-check feed rate settings, current BN selection, and recent fuel sulphur history against the trend onset.
procedures.why: Identifies whether a change in operating condition or dosing coincides with the start of the wear trend.

procedures.action: Schedule a scavenge port visual inspection of the units showing the highest trend increase to assess liner/ring condition directly.
procedures.why: Confirms whether physical wear is occurring at a rate consistent with the oil analysis trend.

procedures.action: Adjust feed rate, BN selection, or investigate cylinder oil supply quality as indicated by the combined trend and inspection findings.
procedures.why: Targets the corrective action at the actual root cause identified rather than applying a generic fix.

constraints: Continuous drain oil sample analysis is required to optimise feed rate and safeguard against wear per OEM guidance
Trend analysis, not single-sample values, should drive corrective decisions
regulations: Everllence guidance on continuous cylinder condition monitoring via drain oil analysis
warnings: A slow-developing trend can be overlooked if only single-point sample values are reviewed instead of the trend over time
Delayed response to a confirmed rising trend risks progression to acute scuffing or ring damage
outcomes: If not corrected: gradual wear progresses to a point where acute cylinder damage (scuffing, ring breakage) occurs
If corrected: root cause addressed before wear progresses to a critical stage, extending component life

trace.situation: The vent pipe from the cylinder oil heating tank (or ACOM BN mixing tank) becomes partially blocked, restricting pressure equalisation during filling and causing oil overflow or erratic level readings at the tank.
trace.trigger: Oil observed weeping/overflowing from the heating tank vent arrangement, or inconsistent/unstable level indication reported during routine tank filling.

procedures.action: Inspect the vent pipe routing for kinks, debris blockage, or incorrect valve closure along its length.
procedures.why: A blocked or restricted vent prevents proper air displacement during tank filling, causing pressure build-up and overflow.

procedures.action: Clear the blockage or correct valve alignment, ensuring the vent pipe is open to atmosphere as designed.
procedures.why: Restores normal pressure equalisation, allowing stable, accurate level readings and preventing overflow.

procedures.action: On twin-engine installations, confirm each engine's heating tank/ACOM tank has its own separate, unobstructed vent pipe.
procedures.why: Shared or cross-connected vent pipes between engines can cause cross-interference in pressure equalisation.

procedures.action: Clean up any spilled cylinder oil and verify no contamination has entered nearby electrical equipment or bilges.
procedures.why: Addresses the immediate safety/environmental consequence of the overflow event.

Twin-engine plants require a separate vent pipe from each engine's heating tank or ACOM mixing tank

Unstable level readings caused by vent blockage can mask a genuine low-level condition
outcomes: If not corrected: recurring overflow events and unreliable level monitoring risking undetected supply interruption
If corrected: stable, accurate tank level indication and elimination of overflow risk

Twin-engine plants must have separate vent pipes per engine to avoid cross-interference

trace.situation: An incompatible cylinder oil brand without an Everllence No Objection Letter (NOL) is bunkered and used, resulting in poor detergency performance and the formation of sludge/varnish deposits in the piston ring grooves and ring lands over subsequent running hours.
trace.trigger: Unusual sludge/varnish deposits found in piston ring grooves during a routine piston overhaul, inconsistent with the expected cleanliness performance of the nominally specified BN oil.

procedures.action: Verify the cylinder oil brand and grade currently in use against the latest Everllence NOL list (Cat. I/Cat. II tables) for the engine's Mk. designation.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the oil in use has actually been tested and approved for this engine type and BN category.

procedures.action: If the oil is unverified or lacks an NOL, arrange for a compatible, OEM-approved cylinder oil to be bunkered as soon as practicable.
procedures.why: Non-approved oils may lack the specific detergency and alkalinity performance validated for this engine design.

procedures.action: Inspect piston ring grooves, ring lands, and piston crown for sludge/varnish accumulation during the next available access.
procedures.why: Determines the extent of cleanliness-related damage requiring mechanical cleaning or ring renewal.

procedures.action: Document the incident and notify the technical superintendent/owner to review bunkering procurement controls for cylinder oil.
procedures.why: Prevents recurrence by tightening supplier verification against the NOL list before future bunkering.

constraints: Only Cat. I or Cat. II cylinder oils with a valid Everllence NOL should be used for the applicable Mk. engine design
Responsibility for ensuring suitable lubricants are used rests with the owner/operator per OEM disclaimer
regulations: Everllence Service Letter SL2022-728 listing Cat. I and Cat. II NOL cylinder oils
warnings: Use of a non-approved cylinder oil voids the basis for OEM performance expectations and may not be covered under warranty/liability provisions
Sludge/varnish build-up can progress to ring sticking and loss of ring sealing if not addressed
outcomes: If not corrected: continued use of an unsuitable oil leads to progressive ring groove fouling and potential ring sticking
If corrected: switching to an NOL-approved oil restores expected cleanliness performance

Owner/operator bears responsibility for ensuring suitable fuel and lube oil use per OEM disclaimer

trace.situation: A cylinder oil consumption flowmeter (used for daily consumption/feed rate reporting) drifts or fails low, causing the reported cylinder oil consumption to appear normal while actual delivered dosage to one or more lubricators is below the commanded rate.
trace.trigger: Discrepancy noted between the logged daily cylinder oil consumption figure and the physically measured tank level drop during a routine sounding reconciliation.

procedures.action: Cross-check the flowmeter-reported daily consumption against a manual tank sounding-based consumption calculation.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the flowmeter reading is drifting from actual physical consumption.

procedures.action: Inspect and recalibrate or replace the flowmeter per OEM procedure, noting that a Coriolis-type meter is required at low-flow installation points.
procedures.why: Restores accurate mass flow measurement needed for correct feed rate reporting and ECS dosing verification.

procedures.action: Review recent drain oil analysis and scavenge port condition on all units to check for any under-dosing wear indicators that went unflagged due to the faulty reading.
procedures.why: Determines if the undetected under-dosing period caused measurable wear requiring further action.

procedures.action: Re-establish manual tank sounding cross-checks on a defined interval until flowmeter reliability is re-confirmed.
procedures.why: Provides an independent verification method while confidence in the flowmeter is restored.

constraints: Flowmeter locations between service tank and heating tank, or heating tank and engine, can produce unreliable readings due to very low flow and require a Coriolis-type meter
Reported consumption data is used to safeguard against wear and must reflect actual delivered dosage
regulations: OEM component specification requiring Coriolis-type flowmeters at low-flow cylinder oil measurement points
warnings: Reliance on a drifting flowmeter without periodic sounding cross-checks can mask an extended under-dosing condition
Low-flow installation points are inherently prone to measurement unreliability and require extra verification diligence
outcomes: If not corrected: undetected under-dosing continues, risking liner/ring wear without any apparent consumption anomaly
If corrected: accurate consumption reporting restored, re-enabling reliable feed rate verification

trace.situation: During a fuel-sulphur changeover (e.g., entering/leaving an Emission Control Area) the ACOS2/ACOM system responds slower than the actual fuel sulphur transition on board, resulting in a temporary mismatch between the cylinder oil BN delivered and the fuel actually being combusted.
trace.trigger: A documented fuel changeover procedure timestamp shows fuel sulphur content changed before the cylinder oil BN switch/mix was confirmed complete in the ECS.

procedures.action: Monitor the ACOS2 valve position feedback or ACOM mixed BN value in real time throughout the fuel changeover sequence.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the cylinder oil BN transition is keeping pace with the fuel sulphur transition or lagging behind.

procedures.action: If a lag is detected, manually select the correct BN mode (or enter the correct target BN on ACOM) ahead of or during the changeover rather than relying solely on automatic switching.
procedures.why: Reduces the duration of BN/sulphur mismatch during the changeover window.

procedures.action: Extend the changeover duration if necessary to allow the three-way valve/mixing system to fully stabilise on the new BN before sulphur content fully transitions.
procedures.why: Matches established fuel changeover best practice of allowing adequate time for all dependent systems, including cylinder lubrication, to adjust.

procedures.action: Record the changeover timing and BN transition data in the engine log for review against the vessel's fuel changeover procedure.
procedures.why: Provides traceability and supports procedure refinement to avoid repeat mismatches on future changeovers.

constraints: Cylinder oil BN switching must be coordinated with, not simply follow, the fuel sulphur changeover sequence
ACOS2 is a simpler system intended for longer changeover periods; ACOM is designed for faster-responding fuel switches
regulations: Vessel's documented fuel changeover procedure (ECA compliance) and OEM lubrication strategy guidance
warnings: A prolonged BN/sulphur mismatch during ECA entry/exit can cause a short but repeated cold corrosion or deposit risk if changeovers are frequent
ACOS2-equipped vessels operating in trades with frequent short changeovers may be structurally unable to keep pace and should consider ACOM
outcomes: If not corrected: repeated short-duration BN/sulphur mismatches accumulate wear risk over many changeover events
If corrected: cylinder oil BN transition properly coordinated with fuel changeover, minimising mismatch exposure
key_facts: ACOS2 is the standard system suited to longer changeover periods
ACOM is the advanced option designed for faster-responding fuel switches
Fuel changeover procedures must account for cylinder lubrication BN transition timing, not just fuel system flushing

trace.situation: A lubricator quill orifice becomes eroded/enlarged over time due to abrasive cat-fine or wear-particle laden cylinder oil, causing over-delivery of oil at that point and localized oil flooding on the liner, wasting oil and risking deposit formation at the flooded area.
trace.trigger: A specific lubricating point shows persistent oil wetting/streaking beyond normal pattern during visual inspection, combined with higher than expected cylinder oil consumption on that unit relative to others.

procedures.action: Confirm the specific quill location showing excess oil delivery via visual inspection and compare consumption data for that cylinder against the fleet/engine average.
procedures.why: Localizes the issue to a specific orifice rather than a general over-dosing condition.

procedures.action: Remove the affected quill assembly and measure/inspect the orifice for erosion/enlargement against OEM tolerance.
procedures.why: Confirms orifice wear as the root cause of excess, uncontrolled oil delivery at that point.

procedures.action: Replace the worn quill/orifice component with a new OEM part.
procedures.why: Restores the design metering rate for that lubricating point.

procedures.action: Investigate upstream cylinder oil cleanliness (filter condition, storage tank settling) as a possible source of abrasive particles causing the erosion.
procedures.why: Addresses the root cause of orifice erosion to prevent recurrence on other quills.

constraints: Lubricating orifices are precision-metered and must remain within OEM tolerance for correct dosing
Cylinder oil filter fineness of 250 μm is intended to protect downstream metering components from larger particulates
regulations: OEM Alpha lubricator component tolerance specification (Section 9.02)
warnings: Localized over-delivery wastes cylinder oil and can promote deposit formation at the flooded point, offsetting the apparent benefit of extra lubrication
Orifice erosion found on one quill warrants inspection of others for early-stage wear
outcomes: If not corrected: continued excess oil consumption and potential deposit-related issues at the affected point
If corrected: design metering rate restored, consumption normalised, and deposit risk reduced

Abrasive particulates in cylinder oil can erode orifice tolerances over time
250 μm filter fineness is intended to protect system components including metering orifices

trace.situation: One of the two redundant engine control units (ECU-A) develops an internal fault while the engine is running under remote control. The hot-standby ECU-B must take over governor, start/stop sequencing and injection timing functions without any interruption to engine operation.
trace.trigger: ECU-A fault/watchdog alarm on MOP with automatic changeover indication to ECU-B

procedures.action: Confirm on MOP that ECU-B has taken over control and engine speed/load response is unaffected.
procedures.why: The system is designed so failover is bumpless; confirming this verifies redundancy functioned as intended and no slowdown was triggered.

procedures.action: Do not attempt to reset or swap ECU-A while underway unless manufacturer procedure confirms it is safe at current load.
procedures.why: Hot-swapping a controller is supported without stopping the engine, but premature intervention during an active fault condition could interrupt the standby path.

procedures.action: Log the fault code and schedule replacement of the defective ECU module at the next safe opportunity (port stay or reduced load).
procedures.why: Running on a single ECU removes redundancy; a second failure would leave the engine without electronic governing.

procedures.action: Notify classification society/owner's superintendent of the redundancy loss per SMS reporting requirements.
procedures.why: Loss of single-failure tolerance is a reportable condition under unattended machinery space requirements.

constraints: No single failure may be allowed to stop the engine (ECS design requirement)
ECU replacement must be possible without stopping the engine
regulations: Classification society requirements for redundancy in unattended machinery spaces (UMS)
warnings: If ECU-B subsequently fails before ECU-A is repaired, the engine will lose electronic control entirely, risking an uncontrolled shutdown
outcomes: If not corrected: vessel operates with no control redundancy, exposed to total loss of remote control on second failure
If corrected: full redundancy restored, engine continues normal unattended operation
key_facts: The ME control system uses two ECUs in parallel, one as hot standby
Any controller can be replaced without stopping the engine
Failover between ECUs is designed to be seamless, without affecting engine performance

trace.situation: A cylinder control unit (CCU) on one cylinder fails, losing control of the electronic fuel injection valve, exhaust valve actuator and starting air valve for that unit. The engine control system automatically cuts out the affected cylinder to protect the engine from erratic injection or valve timing.
trace.trigger: CCU fault alarm for specific cylinder with 'cylinder cut-out' status shown on MOP

procedures.action: Verify on MOP which cylinder has been cut out and confirm the remaining cylinders are compensating evenly (no abnormal exhaust temperature spread).
procedures.why: Automatic cut-out prevents uncontrolled injection, but load must be verified as properly redistributed to avoid overloading adjacent units.

procedures.action: Reduce engine load if running near MCR to keep mean indicated pressure within balanced limits across remaining cylinders.
procedures.why: Running all cylinders near full load with one unit cut out increases thermal and mechanical load on the healthy units.

procedures.action: Inspect CCU wiring, connectors and power supply to the affected cylinder for loose connections or moisture ingress before replacing the module.
procedures.why: Many CCU faults originate from connector corrosion or cable damage rather than internal electronics failure.

procedures.action: Replace the faulty CCU module at the earliest safe opportunity; the engine does not need to be stopped for this.
procedures.why: CCUs are hot-swappable by design, restoring full cylinder operation without interrupting the voyage.

constraints: Cylinder cut-out is automatic and cannot be overridden if CCU communication is lost
Engine must not be run at MCR for extended periods with a cylinder cut out
regulations: Everllence CCU replacement procedure for hot-swappable modules
warnings: Continued running at high load with an unbalanced cylinder configuration risks thermal overload of adjacent units and increased vibration
outcomes: If not corrected: reduced power availability, uneven thermal loading, potential damage to compensating cylinders
If corrected: cylinder restored to normal firing, full power availability regained
key_facts: Each cylinder has its own CCU controlling fuel injection, exhaust valve actuation and starting air valves
CCU failure automatically cuts out only the affected cylinder
All CCUs are identical and interchangeable

procedures.why: Erratic ACU signals can cause blower hunting, risking insufficient scavenge air at low load or during maneuvering.

procedures.why: Maintaining adequate scavenge air pressure is critical for combustion stability and turbocharger surge avoidance.

procedures.action: Replace the faulty ACU module without stopping the engine per the hot-swap design.
procedures.why: Restores full automatic auxiliary control and removes the risk of cascading control instability.

Scavenge air pressure must remain within normal limits for the given load
regulations: Everllence auxiliary control unit redundancy design requirement
warnings: Unstable blower control during maneuvering can cause momentary loss of scavenge air pressure, risking incomplete combustion or turbocharger surge
outcomes: If not corrected: continued erratic blower cycling, potential combustion instability and increased exhaust temperature spread
If corrected: stable auxiliary control restored, normal scavenging and engine response

Four ACUs are used for redundancy of auxiliary functions

trace.situation: Power supply A to the ECS enters UPS battery mode following loss of the AC input, while power supply B remains healthy. The control system continues to operate normally on the surviving supply, but the loss of input power redundancy is a precursor condition that needs attention before batteries deplete.
trace.trigger: Power supply A 'AC power' alarm and 'UPS battery mode' alarm on MOP

procedures.action: Confirm power supply B is still supplying 24V DC normally and that engine control functions are unaffected.
procedures.why: The ECS requires two separate power supplies with battery backup; as long as B is healthy, control integrity is maintained.

procedures.action: Check the AC input breaker, fuse, and cabling feeding power supply A for a tripped breaker or loose connection.
procedures.why: Most AC input loss events are caused by upstream breaker trips or loose terminals rather than internal supply failure.

procedures.action: Monitor UPS battery state of charge and estimated runtime; restore AC input before batteries deplete.
procedures.why: Once the battery backup is exhausted, power supply A will fail completely, leaving the system on only one supply with no further backup on that channel.

procedures.action: Verify that no non-ECS DC loads have been inadvertently connected to supply A or B.
procedures.why: Power supplies must only feed ME-ECS components; extraneous loads can overload the supply and mask the true fault.

constraints: ECS requires two separate power supplies (A and B) with battery backup
Power supplies must be dedicated to ME-ECS components only, not shared with other DC systems

warnings: If AC input is not restored before UPS batteries deplete, power supply A will go fully offline, removing all redundancy on that channel
outcomes: If not corrected: battery depletion leads to total loss of power supply A, leaving ECS on single point of supply
If corrected: redundant power supply restored, full design resilience maintained
key_facts: Power supply A input is 100-240V AC, 45-65Hz, output 24V DC with battery backup
Alarms include AC power loss, UPS battery mode, and batteries not available (fuse fail)
ECS power supplies must be isolated from other ship DC systems

trace.situation: Power supply B's UPS batteries report a 'fuse fail / batteries not available' condition while the unit is still receiving normal AC input. The backup capability for this channel is effectively lost even though the supply itself appears to function normally.
trace.trigger: Power supply B 'batteries not available (fuse fail)' alarm on MOP/AMS

procedures.action: Verify power supply B output voltage and current are still within normal 24V DC range despite the battery alarm.
procedures.why: The alarm indicates loss of backup capability, not necessarily loss of the primary DC output, so immediate control impact may be absent.

procedures.action: Inspect the battery fuse and battery bank for the affected supply at the next safe opportunity.
procedures.why: A blown fuse or degraded battery bank is a common and quickly correctable root cause of this alarm.

procedures.action: Treat the vessel as temporarily operating without battery backup redundancy on supply B and avoid unnecessary electrical switching near the ECS supply circuits.
procedures.why: Without battery backup, any transient AC interruption on this channel will cause an immediate, uncushioned loss of that supply.

procedures.action: Replace the blown fuse or battery module and confirm alarm clears before resuming normal unattended operation status.
procedures.why: Restoring battery backup re-establishes the full two-channel redundancy required for unattended machinery space operation.

constraints: Both power supplies must maintain functioning battery backup for UMS compliance
Fuse fail condition must be cleared before the engine can be certified for unattended operation
regulations: Classification society unattended machinery space (UMS) requirements for control system power redundancy
warnings: A power dip on supply B while batteries are unavailable could cause an unexpected drop of that supply with no cushioning
outcomes: If not corrected: vessel is vulnerable to instantaneous loss of ECS power channel B on any AC disturbance
If corrected: full backup capability restored, compliant with UMS redundancy requirements
key_facts: Power supply B alarms include AC power, UPS battery mode, and batteries not available (fuse fail)
Power supply B output is 24V DC from 110-240V AC input
Battery backup is a mandatory design feature of the ME-ECS

trace.situation: Both ME-ECS power supplies are discovered, during a wiring audit, to be sharing DC distribution with unrelated ship systems due to a yard modification, violating the requirement for dedicated ECS power circuits. trace.trigger: Discovered during routine electrical inspection or after an unexplained nuisance trip on an unrelated DC circuit affecting ECS voltage

procedures.action: Trace all loads connected to ME-ECS power supply A and B distribution boards and identify any non-ECS equipment.
procedures.why: Shared loads can draw unpredictable current and introduce noise or fault propagation into the control system supply.

procedures.action: Plan and execute re-wiring to isolate ME-ECS components onto dedicated circuits, coordinating with yard/electrical engineer during a planned maintenance window.
procedures.why: The manual requires that only ME-ECS components be connected to these supplies to preserve isolation and fault containment.

procedures.action: Until separation is complete, monitor both power supplies closely for voltage fluctuations correlating with switching of the shared non-ECS load.
procedures.why: Early detection of cross-interference allows mitigation before it affects engine control stability.

procedures.action: Document the non-conformance and corrective action for class survey records.
procedures.why: This is a design/installation deviation from manufacturer requirements that may be flagged during class inspection.

constraints: ME-ECS power supplies must be dedicated solely to ME-ECS components
IT (floating) DC system design must not be compromised by external loads
regulations: Everllence ME-ECS power supply isolation requirement
warnings: A fault on the shared non-ECS load could trip or disturb the ECS power supply, risking an unplanned loss of engine control
outcomes: If not corrected: risk of common-mode control system power loss due to external fault propagation
If corrected: ECS power integrity restored to design specification, eliminating cross-system fault risk
key_facts: ME-ECS power supplies are IT (floating) type DC systems with individually isolated outputs
Only ME-ECS components may be connected to power supply A or B
Shared loading is a documented design violation, not a normal operating condition

trace.situation: The redundant ethernet-based control network connecting the MOP screens to the ECUs and CCUs experiences intermittent communication dropouts, likely due to cable degradation or a marginal connection near the maximum allowed 100 m cabling distance between engine and engine room.
trace.trigger: Intermittent 'communication loss' or 'network redundancy degraded' alarm on MOP

procedures.action: Check MOP diagnostics to determine whether only one of the redundant network paths is affected or both.
procedures.why: The network is redundant; if only one path is down, control continues uninterrupted but resilience is reduced.

procedures.action: Measure actual cable run length and inspect connectors/patch panels between the engine and ECR for damage, corrosion, or moisture ingress.
procedures.why: Copper ethernet runs are limited to 100 m; exceeding this or having degraded connectors causes signal attenuation and intermittent faults.

procedures.action: If cable length exceeds specification or condition is poor, plan for fiber media converter installation or cable replacement at next port.
procedures.why: Restoring a compliant, high-integrity physical layer removes the root cause of intermittent dropouts.

procedures.action: In the interim, avoid relying on the single remaining network path for critical maneuvers; keep LOP as a ready backup control station.
procedures.why: With reduced network redundancy, a second independent fault could interrupt control signal flow between MOP and the engine-mounted units.

constraints: Maximum copper ethernet cabling distance between engine and engine room is 100 m
Control network must remain redundant for MOP-to-controller communication
regulations: Everllence ECS network cabling specification
warnings: Loss of both redundant network paths simultaneously would isolate MOP from the engine-mounted control units, forcing reliance on LOP
outcomes: If not corrected: increasing risk of intermittent command loss between MOP and engine, potential for full communication loss under vibration or thermal cycling
If corrected: stable, fully redundant network communication restored

Maximum cabling distance for copper-based ethernet is 100 m between engine and engine room
Network redundancy loss does not stop the engine but reduces fault tolerance

trace.situation: During engine start sequence, one of the two electrically driven start-up pumps in the mechanically driven HPS unit fails to engage, delaying hydraulic pressure build-up to the hydraulic cylinder units (HCU) needed for exhaust valve and fuel injection actuation.
trace.trigger: Delayed 'HPS ready' signal or low hydraulic pressure alarm during start sequence

procedures.action: Check MOP/ACU status for which start-up pump failed to activate and whether the second standby pump engaged automatically.
procedures.why: The system is designed so one of two electric start-up pumps activates at engine start; identifying the failed unit focuses troubleshooting.

procedures.action: Inspect the failed pump's motor starter, ACU command output, and local breaker for a tripped protection device.
procedures.why: Pump non-start is commonly caused by a tripped motor protection breaker or a failed starter contactor rather than the pump itself.

procedures.action: If the standby pump is confirmed healthy and pressure builds normally, proceed with start but flag the failed pump for repair before relying on it as backup again.
procedures.why: Continuing on the healthy pump maintains safe starting capability, but redundancy is now reduced until the fault is fixed.

procedures.action: Do not attempt engine start if neither pump achieves required HPS pressure within the normal start window.
procedures.why: Insufficient hydraulic pressure will prevent proper exhaust valve and fuel injection actuation, risking a failed or irregular start.

constraints: HPS must reach required pressure before engine start is permitted
Mechanically driven HPS unit relies on one of two electric start-up pumps during starting
regulations: Everllence HPS start sequence requirement (Chapter 8 reference)
warnings: Attempting to start the engine with inadequate hydraulic pressure can cause incomplete or irregular fuel injection and exhaust valve timing, risking cylinder damage
outcomes: If not corrected: unreliable or failed engine starts, potential damage from irregular valve/injection timing
If corrected: normal reliable hydraulic pressure build-up restored for starting
key_facts: One of two electrically driven start-up pumps activates automatically at engine start in the mechanically driven HPS layout
HPS supplies high-pressure oil to HCUs for fuel injection and exhaust valve actuation
HPS unit size and capacity vary by engine type

trace.situation: On an engine fitted with an electrically driven HPS unit, one of the main hydraulic oil pumps trips during normal running at sea, reducing available hydraulic flow margin to the HCUs. The remaining pumps maintain system pressure, but redundancy is now reduced for a multi-cylinder engine at high load.
trace.trigger: HPS pump trip alarm with hydraulic system pressure remaining nominal but pump running status showing one unit stopped

procedures.action: Confirm from ACU/MOP that overall hydraulic header pressure remains within normal operating range despite the tripped pump.
procedures.why: Multiple pump configuration with standby units is designed to maintain pressure on loss of one pump; confirming this verifies the system is still safely supplying the HCUs.

procedures.action: Check the tripped pump's motor overload, ACU control signal, and local relief valve for abnormal operation.
procedures.why: Pump trips are frequently caused by motor overload protection activating due to a developing mechanical fault or electrical fault in the drive.

procedures.action: Avoid further load increase until the cause of the trip is identified and either the pump is restarted or confirmed to be safely isolated.
procedures.why: At high engine load, losing a second pump could drop hydraulic pressure below the level needed for reliable HCU operation across all cylinders.

procedures.action: Restart the tripped pump locally if the fault is cleared and protection reset is safe, otherwise keep it isolated and plan repair in port.
procedures.why: Restoring full pump redundancy returns the HPS to its designed fault-tolerant configuration.

constraints: HPS multiple-pump configuration must maintain required pressure to HCUs under all normal loads
Loss of a second pump concurrent with first failure risks inadequate hydraulic supply
regulations: Everllence HPS redundancy design requirement for electrically driven supply (Fig. 16.01.02b)
warnings: If a second HPS pump fails while the engine remains at high load, hydraulic pressure to the HCUs may become insufficient, risking irregular fuel injection and exhaust valve timing across multiple cylinders
outcomes: If not corrected: reduced redundancy margin, increased risk of a cascading hydraulic pressure failure under high load
If corrected: full pump redundancy restored, system operating within designed safety margins
key_facts: Electrically driven HPS units use multiple pumps with standby units for redundancy
Control of engine and electrically driven pumps is divided between the ACUs
HPS pressure for HCU operation is typically around 300 bar in common supply systems

known_issue.detection_method: Pump trip alarm with hydraulic header pressure monitored via ACU/MOP

trace.situation: MOP-A screen, one of the two redundant main operating panel computers in the ECR, freezes and becomes unresponsive to touch input while MOP-B remains fully functional. Engine commands and parameter displays are unaffected because the system is designed with two independent panels.
trace.trigger: MOP-A screen unresponsive or blank display reported by watchkeeping engineer

procedures.action: Switch all engine monitoring and command activity to MOP-B and confirm full functionality of engine commands, status displays, and running mode selection.
procedures.why: MOP-B is a fully capable redundant unit able to perform all MOP-A functions without interruption to engine control.

procedures.action: Attempt a controlled restart of the MOP-A computer per manufacturer procedure, without disturbing MOP-B or the underlying ECUs.
procedures.why: MOP screens are standard marine-approved PCs and a software/OS fault can often be cleared by a controlled reboot without affecting engine operation.

procedures.action: If MOP-A does not recover after restart, report it as out of service and schedule replacement/repair of the PC hardware or touch screen.
procedures.why: Operating with only one MOP removes display/command redundancy, which should be restored as soon as practicable.

procedures.action: Avoid simultaneous critical commands from a single MOP during maneuvering until the second unit is restored, maintaining heightened watch on the single active screen.
procedures.why: With only one MOP operational, there is no backup command path if that unit also fails during a critical maneuver.

constraints: Two redundant MOP screens must be available in the ECR for crew command and monitoring
Loss of one MOP does not stop the engine but reduces operational redundancy
regulations: Everllence MOP redundancy design requirement
warnings: If MOP-B also fails while MOP-A remains down, the crew loses the primary command/monitoring interface in the ECR and must revert to LOP
outcomes: If not corrected: reduced monitoring/command redundancy, single point of failure risk for ECR control
If corrected: full dual-MOP redundancy restored for command and monitoring
key_facts: Both MOP screens are marine-approved PCs with touch screen located in the ECR
MOP-A and MOP-B can be used simultaneously or as primary/backup
MOP failure does not directly affect ECU/CCU engine control functions

trace.situation: The local operating panel (LOP) on the engine shows discrepant speed and status readings compared to the ECR MOP during a planned transfer of control to local operation for maintenance, raising concern about reliability of basic start/stop/speed functions available at the LOP.
trace.trigger: Discrepancy noted between LOP displayed engine speed/status and MOP displayed values during pre-transfer check

procedures.action: Before transferring control, cross-check LOP displayed values (speed, direction, key alarms) against MOP and local tachometer/instrumentation.
procedures.why: The LOP is a redundant control station and must show consistent core data before it can be trusted for actual engine command during maintenance work on the ECR.

procedures.action: If discrepancy is confirmed, do not transfer control to LOP; keep control at ECR/bridge and report the LOP display fault.
procedures.why: Commanding the engine from a panel with unverified or incorrect displayed data risks incorrect manual intervention during maneuvering or maintenance.

procedures.action: Investigate LOP signal wiring and local sensor/transmitter inputs feeding the LOP display independently of the main ECU data path.
procedures.why: LOP indications may be fed through a different signal path than MOP; a local sensor or wiring fault is a likely root cause.

procedures.action: After repair, re-verify matching display values across LOP, MOP, and bridge telegraph before returning the LOP to available-for-use status.
procedures.why: Confirms the redundant control station is trustworthy again before being relied upon in an emergency or maintenance scenario.

constraints: LOP must provide reliable start, stop, speed control, reversing and key engine data as a substitute control station
LOP, MOP, and bridge displays must show consistent core engine parameters
regulations: Everllence LOP functional requirement as redundant control station
warnings: Using the LOP for actual engine command while displayed data is unverified could lead to an unintended speed or direction command
outcomes: If not corrected: LOP cannot be trusted as backup control station, undermining the three-station control redundancy (bridge/ECR/local)
If corrected: LOP restored as a verified, reliable backup control station
key_facts: LOP is normally mounted on the engine and provides basic start, stop, speed control, and reversing functions
LOP is a redundant substitute for the previous engine-side control console
Core engine data must match across bridge, ECR, and LOP displays

trace.situation: The safety system's shutdown and slowdown panel, supplied by a third-party vendor, is found to be sending shutdown signals that are not properly recognized by the ECS due to a compatibility mismatch introduced after a software update to the remote control system.
trace.trigger: Shutdown signal from safety panel not acknowledged by ECS, or unexpected inconsistent slowdown/shutdown behavior following a software update

procedures.action: Verify the exact software/firmware versions on both the remote control system and the shutdown/slowdown panel against the latest Everllence compatibility matrix.
procedures.why: The remote control system and safety system must be compatible per manufacturer requirement; a version mismatch after an update is a common cause of signal misinterpretation.

procedures.action: Perform a manual function test of shutdown and slowdown signal paths (cancellable and non-cancellable) with the engine at rest or low load under controlled conditions.
procedures.why: Confirms whether critical safety signals correctly reach the ECS before the vessel returns to normal service relying on this safety chain.

procedures.action: If incompatibility is confirmed, revert the recent software update or apply the manufacturer-approved compatible version before further operation.
procedures.why: Only Everllence-approved panel and software combinations are permitted; using unapproved or mismatched versions compromises the safety shutdown function.

procedures.action: Report the finding to class and the equipment supplier, and suspend reliance on the automated shutdown path until verified, using manual emergency stop procedures as an interim safeguard.
procedures.why: A non-functioning shutdown signal path is a critical safety gap requiring class and class-approved supplier involvement.

constraints: The remote control system and safety system (shutdown/slowdown panel) must be compatible
Only Everllence-approved shutdown/slowdown panels may be used
regulations: Everllence approval requirement for shutdown/slowdown panels (Lyngsø Marine, Kongsberg, Nabtesco, Mitsui Zosen Systems Research)
Classification society requirements for independent safety system function
warnings: If a genuine critical shutdown condition occurs while this incompatibility persists, the engine may fail to shut down automatically, risking catastrophic damage
outcomes: If not corrected: safety shutdown function unreliable, risking failure to protect engine during a genuine critical event
If corrected: verified, compliant shutdown/slowdown signal path restored

Only Everllence-approved panels (Lyngsø Marine, Kongsberg Maritime, Nabtesco, Mitsui Zosen Systems Research) are permitted
Remote control and safety systems must be verified compatible

trace.situation: The bridge-to-engine telegraph system intermittently fails to transfer speed and direction commands to the ECS, causing a delay between bridge lever movement and actual engine response during port maneuvering.
trace.trigger: Noticeable lag or non-response between bridge telegraph lever movement and engine speed/direction change, with no corresponding ECS fault alarm

procedures.action: Immediately transfer control to ECR or attempt a repeat command from the bridge telegraph to confirm whether the fault is repeatable.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the issue is a transient signal glitch or a persistent fault requiring station transfer for safety during maneuvering.

procedures.action: If delay persists, transfer active control to ECR manual command and inform the bridge/pilot of the change in control station.
procedures.why: Maneuvering safety takes priority; ECR control bypasses the faulty telegraph signal path while troubleshooting continues.

procedures.action: Check telegraph/speed-setting unit wiring, network connection, and power supply at both bridge and ECR stations for intermittent faults.
procedures.why: Telegraph signal transfer relies on the same control network infrastructure; a marginal connection or module fault is a likely cause.

procedures.action: Test full telegraph response range (ahead/astern/stop, full speed range) at each station before returning control to bridge for continued maneuvering.
procedures.why: Full verification ensures the fault is fully cleared before resuming normal bridge-controlled operation, especially in a maneuvering area.

constraints: Telegraph system must reliably transfer speed and direction commands from bridge, ECR, or LOP to the ECS
Control station transfer must be clearly communicated between bridge and engine room
regulations: Everllence telegraph/remote control system functional requirement
warnings: Delayed or failed telegraph commands during close-quarters maneuvering can result in loss of timely speed/direction control, risking collision or grounding
outcomes: If not corrected: continued unpredictable delay in engine response to bridge commands during maneuvering, elevated collision/grounding risk
If corrected: reliable, immediate telegraph command transfer restored for safe maneuvering
key_facts: The telegraph system transfers speed and direction commands from bridge, ECR, or LOP to the ECS
ECR and LOP are provided with combined telegraph and speed-setting units
Telegraph command path is distinct from, but dependent on, the overall control network

trace.situation: The slowdown system repeatedly issues spurious slowdown requests to the ECS during steady-state full-load operation, despite no corresponding abnormal parameter being shown on the alarm and monitoring system (AMS), suggesting a false signal or logic fault in the slowdown request path.
trace.trigger: Unexplained slowdown command received by ECS with no corroborating AMS alarm for an exceeded service limit

procedures.action: Record the exact slowdown trigger source and timestamp from the ECS log, and cross-reference with AMS alarm history for the same period.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the request originated from AMS or an internal ECS slowdown logic fault, directing troubleshooting to the correct subsystem.

procedures.action: If the request is cancellable, acknowledge/cancel it per normal procedure while confirming no genuine abnormal condition exists via direct parameter check.
procedures.why: Prevents unnecessary loss of power while ensuring a real limit excursion is not being masked by assuming it is false.

procedures.action: Inspect the specific sensor or AMS input channel implicated by the slowdown logic for calibration drift, wiring fault, or intermittent short.

trace.situation: During pre-start checks, the 'auxiliary system ready' interlock remains unsatisfied even though fuel oil, lube oil, and cooling water systems all report normal status, preventing the engine start sequence from proceeding.
trace.trigger: Engine start sequence blocked with 'auxiliary system not ready' indication on MOP despite normal fuel/lube/cooling status

procedures.action: Check the ECS-side status inputs individually: turning gear disengaged, main starting valve open, control air valve for sealing air open, control air valve for air spring open, auxiliary blowers running, and HPS ready.
procedures.why: The 'auxiliary system ready' signal depends on both remote control system inputs and these specific ECS-side conditions; isolating which one is unsatisfied narrows the fault quickly.

procedures.action: Physically verify turning gear is fully disengaged and its limit switch/position sensor is functioning correctly.
procedures.why: A turning gear engaged or limit switch fault is one of the most common causes of a blocked start interlock despite other systems appearing ready.

procedures.action: Confirm main starting air valve position and control air valves for sealing air and air spring show correct 'open' feedback, checking position sensors and pneumatic supply if not.
procedures.why: These pneumatic interlocks are mandatory preconditions for start; a stuck valve or faulty position sensor will block the sequence even if other systems are healthy.

procedures.action: If auxiliary blowers are not confirmed running or HPS is not confirmed ready, resolve those systems first before reattempting start.
procedures.why: All listed ECS-side conditions must be simultaneously satisfied for the interlock to clear and permit a safe start.

constraints: All auxiliary system ready conditions must be satisfied before start sequence can proceed
Turning gear must be verified disengaged via limit switch before start is permitted

warnings: Bypassing or defeating the auxiliary system ready interlock to force a start risks starting the engine with turning gear engaged or inadequate air/hydraulic supply, which can cause severe mechanical damage
outcomes: If not corrected: engine start remains blocked, delaying departure or maneuvering readiness
If corrected: start interlock clears normally, confirming all preconditions genuinely satisfied for a safe start
key_facts: Auxiliary system ready combines remote control system inputs (fuel, lube, cooling) with ECS-side status (turning gear, starting valve, control air valves, blowers, HPS)

All conditions must be simultaneously true for the interlock to clear

trace.trigger: Rough/uneven engine start with irregular rpm pickup and possible local alarm indicating SAV position fault on affected cylinder

procedures.action: Abort the start attempt immediately if rpm pickup is irregular or stalling is imminent, returning to stop/turning gear condition per normal procedure.

procedures.action: Check MOP/CCU diagnostics for the specific cylinder's SAV position feedback and control signal status.

procedures.action: Inspect the SAV solenoid/actuator and associated control air supply for the affected cylinder for blockage, sticking, or loss of control air pressure.
procedures.why: SAV faults are often caused by mechanical sticking, debris, or control air pressure loss rather than a CCU hardware failure.

procedures.action: If the SAV cannot be restored to normal function immediately, consult manufacturer guidance on whether a start can be safely attempted with that cylinder's starting air function temporarily isolated, understanding the increased risk and reduced starting torque margin.

trace.situation: The engine interface control unit (EICC), which manages the interface between the ECS and surrounding systems such as the alarm/monitoring system and power management system, loses communication, cutting off data exchange with these external systems while the core ECU/CCU engine control continues unaffected.
trace.trigger: Loss of data exchange between ECS and AMS/PMS reported, with no change in direct engine running parameters

procedures.action: Confirm that direct engine control functions (speed, start/stop, cylinder operation) remain fully normal via MOP, independent of the EICC fault.
procedures.why: The EICC handles external interfacing, not core engine control, so verifying unaffected engine operation correctly scopes the fault's impact.

procedures.action: Notify bridge and relevant watchkeepers that AMS/PMS data from the engine may be stale or unavailable until the EICC is restored.

procedures.action: Check EICC power, network connection, and physical mounting location (ECR or engine room) for an obvious fault such as loose cabling or power loss.
procedures.why: EICC faults are frequently caused by connectivity issues rather than internal failure, and are often quickly correctable.

procedures.action: If not quickly resolved, arrange for manual reporting of key engine parameters to bridge/PMS operators as an interim measure until EICC function is restored.
procedures.why: Maintains situational awareness for systems depending on the EICC interface while the underlying fault is being fixed.

constraints: EICC provides the interface between ECS and surrounding ship control systems; its failure does not stop the engine but isolates external data exchange

procedures.action: After safe resolution, review PMS/ECS interface logs with technical support to determine root cause before attempting another automatic phase-in.
procedures.why: Prevents recurrence of a stalled synchronization sequence during a future generator changeover, particularly during critical maneuvering periods.

trace.situation: The PMI auto-tuning function within the engine management services (EMS) begins applying incorrect fuel injection timing adjustments to several cylinders after a sensor calibration drift goes undetected, gradually increasing cylinder pressure imbalance without triggering an immediate alarm.
trace.trigger: Gradual increase in cylinder pressure (Pmax/Pcomp) imbalance noted during routine PMI/CoCoS-EDS review, without a discrete alarm

procedures.action: Pull the latest PMI auto-tuning trend data from CoCoS-EDS and compare cylinder-by-cylinder Pmax/Pcomp values against baseline and class/manufacturer allowable spread.

procedures.action: Suspend automatic PMI auto-tuning adjustments and revert to last known good timing parameters or manual timing settings.
procedures.why: Prevents the faulty auto-tuning algorithm from continuing to apply incorrect corrections based on drifted sensor input.

procedures.action: Check pressure sensors used for PMI feedback on the affected cylinders for calibration drift, fouling, or wiring degradation.
procedures.why: Auto-tuning relies on accurate pressure sensor input; a drifted sensor is a common root cause of progressively worsening cylinder balance.

procedures.action: Recalibrate or replace the faulty sensor(s), then re-enable auto-tuning gradually while monitoring Pmax/Pcomp trends to confirm correction before returning to full automatic operation.
procedures.why: Ensures the underlying sensor fault is fixed before trusting the auto-tuning system again, avoiding recurrence of the imbalance.

trace.situation: Following a control system software update, the engine fails to properly recognize a control station transfer from bridge to ECR, resulting in both stations momentarily showing 'in control' status simultaneously, creating ambiguity over which station's commands the ECS will execute.
trace.trigger: Both bridge and ECR control stations simultaneously indicating 'in control' status following a station transfer attempt after software update

procedures.action: Immediately halt all command inputs from both stations and verify actual control ownership directly from ECU status via MOP diagnostics page.
procedures.why: Conflicting command sources could result in the ECS executing unintended or conflicting speed/direction commands if left unresolved.

procedures.action: Establish control unambiguously at one station using the standard transfer procedure, confirming the other station shows a clear 'not in control' indication before resuming operations.
procedures.why: Only one station should be able to issue commands at a time; this must be positively confirmed before relying on either station.

procedures.action: Document the exact software version and transfer sequence that produced the ambiguous status for reporting to the system supplier/Everllence.

procedures.action: Until the fault is confirmed resolved and verified through repeated transfer tests, restrict control transfers to essential maneuvers only and keep both stations manned to monitor for recurrence.
procedures.why: Reduces risk exposure from a known control-transfer ambiguity while a permanent fix is implemented.

constraints: Only one control station (bridge, ECR, or local) may have command authority over the ECS at any time

trace.situation: The exhaust gas compensator (expansion joint) fitted between the turbocharger gas outlet and the funnel transition piece develops fatigue cracking in the bellows due to repeated thermal cycling and insufficient allowance for engine seating movement. trace.trigger: Visible soot staining and a hissing sound around the compensator bellows, later confirmed by a local high-temperature patch detected by IR scan on the insulation cladding.

procedures.action: Reduce load and, if leakage is severe, stop the engine to inspect the compensator at the turbocharger outlet flange.
procedures.why: Reducing exhaust gas flow and pressure prevents the crack from propagating further and limits hot gas escape into the casing.

procedures.action: Check alignment of the exhaust pipe supports and verify that thermal expansion (DA, DB, DC) is within the values calculated for 20°C to 250°C expansion range.
procedures.why: Misalignment or restricted movement overstresses the bellows beyond its designed elasticity, causing fatigue failure.

procedures.action: Replace the compensator bellows and re-torque the flange bolts to the maker's specified values before restarting.
procedures.why: A cracked bellows cannot safely absorb thermal expansion and will continue to leak or fail completely under full load.

constraints: Compensator must absorb thermal expansion calculated for a temperature rise from 20°C to 250°C
Forces/moments on turbocharger gas outlet flange must not exceed maker's permissible limits per Table 15.06.02

warnings: Continued operation with a leaking compensator risks hot gas impingement on adjacent cabling, insulation ignition, and crew burn injury
outcomes: If uncorrected, bellows rupture can cause a sudden large exhaust gas leak, loss of turbocharger backpressure, and fire risk in the casing
Timely replacement restores gas-tight sealing and prevents escalation to a casing fire
key_facts: Compensators are fitted both between exhaust valve housings and the receiver, and between receiver and turbocharger
Expansion is calculated for a 20°C to 250°C temperature rise

trace.situation: One cylinder's exhaust gas outlet temperature trends significantly higher than the others, indicating a leaking or burnt exhaust valve spindle/seat that is allowing hot gas to bypass proper sealing during the closed period.
trace.trigger: Cylinder exhaust gas temperature deviation alarm for the affected unit, exceeding the normal spread from the mean of all cylinders.

procedures.action: Cross-check the affected cylinder's exhaust temperature against scavenge air temperature and indicator diagram/PMI data to confirm abnormal combustion.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the deviation is due to valve leakage rather than a sensor fault or injection timing issue.

procedures.action: Reduce load if the deviation is severe and schedule inspection of the exhaust valve, seat, and spindle for burning or erosion.
procedures.why: A leaking exhaust valve allows hot gas blow-by, accelerating valve seat erosion and risking valve failure.

procedures.action: Grind or replace the exhaust valve and seat, and verify spindle rotation (if fitted) is functioning correctly before returning to service.
procedures.why: Proper valve rotation and sealing restores even combustion and gas temperature across the cylinder.

constraints: Cylinder exhaust gas temperature deviation from mean should not exceed the maker-specified alarm threshold (typically ±50°C depending on engine type)
Exhaust valve housings are directly connected to the exhaust gas receiver via compensators
regulations: Manufacturer's cylinder exhaust temperature deviation alarm limit per engine operation manual
warnings: Continued operation with a leaking exhaust valve can lead to valve burn-through, piston crown damage, and potential scavenge fire
outcomes: If uncorrected, valve leakage worsens, leading to reduced cylinder power and possible mechanical damage to the valve seat or cage
Timely valve overhaul restores normal exhaust temperature and combustion balance
key_facts: Exhaust gas is led from each cylinder's exhaust valve housing to the common exhaust gas receiver
Temperature deviation alarms are a primary diagnostic tool for individual cylinder exhaust valve condition

question_seeds.text: Why does a leaking exhaust valve produce a high individual cylinder exhaust temperature rather than a low one?
Which other parameters confirm an exhaust valve problem versus a sensor fault?

known_issue.failure_mode: exhaust valve leakage / burnt seat
