trace.situation: The exhaust gas boiler experiences a steadily rising pressure drop across its tube bank due to soot accumulation, exceeding the recommended maximum pressure loss and increasing overall exhaust system backpressure on the engine.
trace.trigger: Boiler differential pressure gauge reading above 150 mm WC at specified MCR, accompanied by a general rise in exhaust gas temperature after the turbocharger.

procedures.action: Operate the boiler soot blowers per schedule or initiate an additional soot blow cycle.
procedures.why: Soot blowing removes loose deposits from boiler tube surfaces, restoring gas flow area.

procedures.action: If soot blowing does not reduce the pressure drop, plan for manual mechanical cleaning of the boiler tube bank at the next opportunity.
procedures.why: Hardened or bridged soot deposits may not respond to blowing alone and require physical removal.

procedures.action: Review combustion quality (fuel injection timing, excess air) to identify the root cause of excessive soot formation.
procedures.why: Addressing poor combustion prevents recurrence of rapid boiler fouling.

constraints: Maximum recommended pressure loss across the exhaust gas boiler is 150 mm WC at specified MCR
Combined pressure loss across silencer and/or spark arrester plus boiler should be considered in the overall backpressure budget
regulations: Manufacturer's exhaust gas boiler design pressure loss limit
warnings: Excessive uncorrected boiler backpressure elevates turbocharger exhaust temperature and raises the risk of a soot fire within the boiler
outcomes: If left unaddressed, rising backpressure can trigger a boiler soot fire and force an emergency shutdown of steam production
Regular soot blowing maintains design pressure loss and protects engine performance
key_facts: Maximum recommended pressure loss across the exhaust gas boiler is normally 150 mm WC at specified MCR
Pressure loss across the boiler must include inlet/outlet transition piece losses

question_seeds.text: What is the maximum allowable pressure loss across the exhaust gas boiler at specified MCR?
How is soot fouling in the exhaust gas boiler distinguished from a silencer blockage?

known_issue.failure_mode: exhaust gas boiler soot fouling / high differential pressure
known_issue.detection_method: boiler differential pressure gauge trend

trace.situation: Accumulated unburned soot deposits inside the exhaust gas boiler ignite spontaneously, producing a sudden rise in boiler gas-side temperature and visible smoke/sparks from the funnel, constituting a boiler soot fire.
trace.trigger: Rapid unexplained rise in exhaust gas boiler outlet temperature well above normal, combined with a sudden increase in boiler differential pressure and smoke from the funnel.

procedures.action: Immediately reduce engine load and stop fuel firing to any auxiliary boiler sharing the uptake, then isolate feedwater/steam circuits as per boiler fire emergency procedure.
procedures.why: Reducing exhaust flow starves the fire of oxygen and heat input while protecting the boiler structure.

procedures.action: Activate the fixed fire-fighting system for the exhaust gas boiler (CO2/steam smothering) if fitted, and do not open boiler doors during the fire.
procedures.why: Opening access doors introduces fresh air and can cause a flashback or explosion.

procedures.action: After the fire is confirmed extinguished and the boiler has cooled, inspect for tube damage, warping, or insulation failure before restoring service.
procedures.why: Soot fires can generate sufficient heat to deform tubes and damage boiler casing, requiring repair before resuming steam production.

constraints: SOLAS requirement for fixed fire extinguishing arrangements on exhaust gas boilers
Maximum boiler pressure loss of 150 mm WC as a preventive fouling control measure
regulations: SOLAS II-2 requirements for exhaust gas boiler fire protection
Class society boiler fire drill and extinguishing system survey requirements
warnings: Opening boiler inspection doors during an active soot fire can cause a backdraft/explosion and severe injury
outcomes: Unmanaged soot fire can destroy boiler tubes, spread to adjacent funnel structure, and force complete loss of waste heat recovery
Prompt isolation and smothering limits damage to boiler internals and allows return to service after inspection
key_facts: Soot fires are a recognized hazard where combustion is poor or boiler cleaning is neglected
Boiler is usually located near the engine top or in the funnel, exposed to continuous hot exhaust flow

question_seeds.text: When is it safe to open the exhaust gas boiler access doors after a suspected soot fire?
Why must the boiler be starved of air rather than doused directly with water during a soot fire?

known_issue.failure_mode: exhaust gas boiler soot fire
known_issue.detection_method: sudden boiler outlet temperature spike, visible smoke/sparks from funnel

trace.situation: The spark arrester fitted as the last component in the exhaust gas system becomes partially blocked by accumulated carbon particles, creating a combined pressure loss with the silencer that exceeds the recommended system limit and raises turbocharger backpressure.
trace.trigger: Overall exhaust system backpressure gauge after the turbocharger reading above the combined 100 mm WC design limit, with a corresponding rise in exhaust gas temperature across all cylinders.

procedures.action: Inspect and clean the spark arrester element, removing accumulated carbon deposits.
procedures.why: A blocked spark arrester restricts gas flow and raises system backpressure above design limits.

procedures.action: Verify the combined pressure loss across silencer and spark arrester against the 100 mm WC limit (or 200 mm WC if no boiler is fitted) after cleaning.
procedures.why: Confirms the system has been restored within the pressure loss budget specified for the exhaust system design.

procedures.action: Investigate combustion quality and fuel injection settings if fouling recurs rapidly.
procedures.why: Frequent spark arrester blockage often indicates poor combustion generating excess particulate loading.

constraints: Combined pressure loss across silencer and/or spark arrester should not exceed 100 mm WC at specified MCR (200 mm WC if no boiler installed)
regulations: Manufacturer's recommended exhaust system backpressure budget
warnings: Excessive backpressure from a blocked spark arrester reduces turbocharger efficiency and can push exhaust temperatures into the high-temperature alarm range across all cylinders
outcomes: If left blocked, sustained high backpressure reduces engine efficiency, raises fuel consumption, and accelerates turbocharger thermal stress
Cleaning restores the designed pressure balance and normal operating temperatures
key_facts: A spark arrester contributes a considerable pressure drop and is the last component in the exhaust gas system
Recommended combined pressure loss across silencer/spark arrester is 100 mm WC at specified MCR

question_seeds.text: What is the combined pressure loss limit for silencer and spark arrester at specified MCR?
How do we distinguish spark arrester blockage from turbocharger turbine fouling as the cause of high backpressure?

known_issue.failure_mode: spark arrester fouling / excess backpressure
known_issue.detection_method: exhaust backpressure gauge reading above design limit

trace.situation: The exhaust gas silencer's internal absorption material has degraded and partially collapsed, obstructing the central flow tube and raising exhaust backpressure beyond the expected ~20 mm WC design loss at MCR.
trace.trigger: A gradual but sustained increase in exhaust backpressure reading above baseline, with no corresponding change in turbocharger speed or cylinder exhaust temperature deviation pattern.

procedures.action: Visually inspect the silencer internals via access panel for collapsed packing or debris obstructing the central tube.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the backpressure rise originates from the silencer rather than the turbocharger or boiler.

procedures.action: Remove collapsed absorption material and restore the design flow area, replacing packing per maker's specification.
procedures.why: Restoring the central tube gas velocity design (~35 m/s) returns backpressure to its design value.

procedures.action: Verify backpressure returns to baseline after repair before resuming normal MCR operation.
procedures.why: Confirms the repair has resolved the obstruction and restored system balance.

constraints: Exhaust gas silencer designed for approximately 35 m/s gas velocity through central tube with ~20 mm WC pressure loss at specified MCR
regulations: Manufacturer's silencer design pressure loss specification
warnings: Ignoring a progressively collapsing silencer can lead to complete flow blockage, forcing an emergency load reduction to protect the turbocharger
outcomes: If uncorrected, the obstruction worsens and backpressure rises further, degrading turbocharger efficiency and increasing fuel consumption
Repair of the silencer internals restores normal exhaust flow and backpressure
key_facts: The exhaust gas silencer is usually of the absorption type
Typical pressure loss across a flow silencer is around 20 mm WC at specified MCR

question_seeds.text: Which component should be checked first when backpressure rises without a change in TC speed or cylinder temperature spread?
Why does silencer packing collapse increase exhaust backpressure over time?

known_issue.failure_mode: silencer absorption material collapse / flow obstruction
known_issue.detection_method: exhaust backpressure trend, visual inspection

trace.situation: A turbocharger journal/thrust bearing begins to wear due to lubrication oil contamination, producing increased vibration and erratic turbocharger speed readings as rotor clearances change under load.
trace.trigger: Turbocharger speed pick-up signal shows abnormal fluctuation and bearing vibration sensor (if fitted) trends upward beyond the normal baseline at steady load.

procedures.action: Reduce load and check turbocharger lubricating oil supply pressure, temperature, and cleanliness (particle count if available).
procedures.why: Bearing wear is commonly driven by contaminated or degraded lubricating oil reducing the oil film.

procedures.action: If vibration or speed fluctuation persists, shut down and inspect the turbocharger bearing housing for scoring, excessive clearance, or metal particles in the oil drain.
procedures.why: Confirms the extent of bearing damage before continuing operation risks a catastrophic rotor seizure.

procedures.action: Replace the affected bearing(s) and flush the turbocharger lubrication system before returning to service.
procedures.why: Worn bearings left in service risk rotor-to-casing contact and total turbocharger loss.

constraints: Turbocharger speed must be continuously monitored via the fitted pick-up for remote indication
Maker's lubricating oil cleanliness and bearing clearance limits must be respected
regulations: Turbocharger manufacturer's bearing inspection and lubrication specification
warnings: Continued running with a worn turbocharger bearing can lead to rotor seizure, blade-to-casing contact, and consequential damage requiring a full turbocharger overhaul or replacement
outcomes: If uncorrected, bearing wear progresses to rotor contact and catastrophic turbocharger failure, potentially damaging the exhaust receiver and casing
Early bearing replacement avoids major turbocharger damage and restores stable speed readings
key_facts: The turbocharger is fitted with a pick-up for monitoring and remote indication of turbocharger speed
Bearing condition directly affects rotor clearance and vibration behaviour

question_seeds.text: What turbocharger speed signal behaviour indicates developing bearing wear rather than a sensor fault?
Why is oil contamination a leading cause of turbocharger bearing failure?

known_issue.failure_mode: turbocharger bearing wear / rotor instability
known_issue.detection_method: speed pick-up signal fluctuation, vibration monitoring

trace.situation: The turbocharger speed pick-up sensor itself fails or its signal cable develops an intermittent connection, causing loss of or erratic remote speed indication without any actual change in turbocharger mechanical condition.
trace.trigger: Turbocharger speed display drops to zero or shows erratic spikes while all other exhaust parameters (temperature, scavenge pressure) remain normal and stable.

procedures.action: Cross-check the indicated speed against engine load, scavenge air pressure, and exhaust temperature trends to determine if the turbocharger is actually behaving abnormally or if only the signal is faulty.
procedures.why: Distinguishes a genuine mechanical fault from an instrumentation fault before taking any load-reduction action.

procedures.action: Inspect the pick-up sensor, its gap setting, and cable connections at the turbocharger housing.
procedures.why: Loose connections or incorrect sensor gap are common causes of erratic or lost speed signals.

procedures.action: Replace the faulty pick-up sensor or repair the cable, then verify stable signal reading before returning the parameter to automatic monitoring.
procedures.why: Restores reliable remote indication needed for control system logic and alarm monitoring.

constraints: Turbocharger speed indication is required for monitoring per the manual's remote indication arrangement
regulations: Manufacturer requirement for functioning turbocharger speed remote indication
warnings: Operating for extended periods without reliable turbocharger speed indication removes a key early-warning parameter for surge or overspeed conditions
outcomes: If left unresolved, a true overspeed or surge event could go undetected until secondary symptoms appear, delaying corrective action
Prompt sensor repair restores full monitoring capability and alarm protection
key_facts: The turbocharger is fitted with a pick-up for monitoring and remote indication of turbocharger speed
Speed indication faults are distinguished from mechanical faults by cross-checking other exhaust parameters

question_seeds.text: How do we confirm a turbocharger speed indication fault is instrumentation-related and not mechanical?
What should be checked first when the turbocharger speed display drops to zero suddenly?

known_issue.failure_mode: turbocharger speed pick-up sensor/cable fault
known_issue.detection_method: loss or erratic behaviour of remote speed indication

trace.situation: Multiple cylinders show a gradual, uniform upward drift in exhaust gas outlet temperature across the whole engine, without individual cylinder deviation, suggesting a systemic cause such as scavenge air cooler fouling or turbocharger efficiency loss rather than a single-cylinder fault.
trace.trigger: Overall average exhaust gas temperature after turbocharger trending upward over several days while individual cylinder deviation spread remains within normal limits.

procedures.action: Check scavenge air pressure and temperature, along with cooling water inlet/outlet temperatures on the scavenge air cooler.
procedures.why: A fouled scavenge air cooler reduces charge air density, raising combustion and exhaust temperatures uniformly across all cylinders.

procedures.action: Verify turbocharger efficiency indicators (speed vs boost pressure ratio) to rule out general turbine/compressor fouling.
procedures.why: A uniformly fouled turbocharger produces a similar whole-engine exhaust temperature rise pattern.

procedures.action: Schedule cleaning of the scavenge air cooler and/or turbocharger as indicated by the diagnosis, then recheck the temperature trend.
procedures.why: Addressing the root system-wide cause restores normal exhaust temperatures across all cylinders simultaneously.

constraints: Exhaust gas temperature after turbocharger should remain within the baseline range established for the given load and ambient condition
regulations: Manufacturer's performance monitoring guideline for whole-engine exhaust temperature trending
warnings: A sustained uniform exhaust temperature rise left undiagnosed can mask the onset of turbocharger or cooler fouling until a hard alarm limit is reached
outcomes: Uncorrected, this trend leads to reduced thermal efficiency, higher fuel consumption, and eventual high-temperature trip conditions
Early root-cause identification and cleaning restores engine efficiency and avoids trip-level temperatures
key_facts: Exhaust gas temperature and flow rate are influenced by ambient conditions and must be assessed relative to baseline, not an absolute fixed number
A uniform whole-engine rise points to a shared system component (cooler/turbocharger) rather than an individual cylinder

question_seeds.text: Why would a uniform rise in all cylinders' exhaust temperature point away from a fuel injection problem?
Which components should be checked first for a whole-engine exhaust temperature drift?

known_issue.failure_mode: systemic exhaust temperature rise / scavenge air cooler or turbocharger fouling
known_issue.detection_method: trend analysis of mean exhaust gas temperature after turbocharger

trace.situation: During a rapid load increase while maneuvering, the turbocharger experiences a surge event marked by a sudden drop in boost pressure accompanied by loud pulsating noise, caused by the compressor operating beyond its stable flow range due to a combination of fouling and aggressive load application.
trace.trigger: Sudden pulsating banging noise from the turbocharger compressor casing with a simultaneous drop in scavenge air pressure during a load ramp.

procedures.action: Immediately reduce the rate of load increase or briefly reduce load to bring the turbocharger back into its stable operating range.
procedures.why: Surge occurs when compressor flow falls below the stall line; reducing demand restores flow above the surge line.

procedures.action: Review the load-up program/rate limiter settings against the maker's recommended acceleration schedule.
procedures.why: Surge during maneuvering is often triggered by exceeding the approved load application rate for the engine/turbocharger combination.

procedures.action: After the event, inspect the compressor for any fouling or mechanical damage that may have lowered the surge margin, and schedule compressor washing if fouling is confirmed.
procedures.why: A fouled compressor has a reduced surge margin, making the unit more susceptible to surge during transients.

constraints: Engine load application rate must follow the maker's approved acceleration/load-up schedule to maintain turbocharger surge margin
regulations: Engine manufacturer's load application program and turbocharger surge margin guidance
warnings: Repeated surge events can cause mechanical damage to compressor blades, rotor, and thrust bearing, potentially leading to sudden turbocharger failure
outcomes: If surge events continue unaddressed, cumulative blade and bearing damage can cause a sudden turbocharger breakdown during critical maneuvering
Adjusting load rate and correcting compressor fouling restores a safe surge margin for maneuvering operations
key_facts: Turbocharger surge is characterized by pulsating flow reversal and is distinct from steady fouling-related performance loss
Compressor washing and controlled load application both help maintain adequate surge margin

known_issue.failure_mode: turbocharger compressor surge during load transient
known_issue.detection_method: pulsating noise and sudden scavenge pressure drop during load change

trace.situation: An exhaust gas receiver support bracket cracks due to thermal fatigue from repeated expansion/contraction cycles, allowing slight sagging of the receiver and placing additional unplanned stress on the adjacent compensators.
trace.trigger: Routine visual inspection during an engine stop reveals a hairline crack at the receiver support bracket weld, with slight visible misalignment of the adjacent compensator.

procedures.action: Restrict engine load and schedule a detailed NDT (dye penetrant or magnetic particle) inspection of the cracked bracket and surrounding welds.
procedures.why: Confirms crack depth and extent before deciding on repair versus full bracket replacement.

procedures.action: Repair or replace the support bracket per the maker's approved welding procedure, ensuring the receiver returns to its designed alignment.
procedures.why: Correct alignment removes the additional stress being placed on the adjacent compensator, preventing secondary failure.

procedures.action: Re-inspect the adjacent compensators for any induced stress damage before returning the engine to full service.
procedures.why: A misaligned receiver can transmit additional load to compensators, risking a secondary gas leak if not checked.

constraints: Exhaust gas receiver support and expansion joints must accommodate the calculated thermal expansion without imposing abnormal loads on compensators
regulations: Class society requirement for structural integrity inspection of exhaust system support structures
warnings: An unrepaired cracked support bracket can progress to a sudden structural failure of the receiver support, risking a major exhaust gas leak
outcomes: If left unrepaired, the crack can propagate, leading to receiver misalignment severe enough to rupture a compensator under load
Prompt bracket repair restores correct alignment and protects the compensators from abnormal stress
key_facts: The exhaust gas receiver equalises fluctuating cylinder pressures before delivering gas to the turbocharger at constant pressure
Receiver movement is accommodated by surrounding compensators designed for specific thermal expansion values

Why is receiver alignment important to the integrity of adjacent compensators?

known_issue.failure_mode: support bracket thermal fatigue crack / receiver misalignment
known_issue.detection_method: visual/NDT inspection during scheduled engine stop

trace.situation: A persistent small gas leak develops at the exhaust valve housing-to-receiver compensator joint due to a degraded gasket, producing a continuous faint hissing sound and slight soot deposition on the surrounding lagging without a significant measurable temperature change.
trace.trigger: Engineer on rounds notices soot streaking and a faint hissing sound at a specific exhaust valve housing joint during normal operation.

procedures.action: Mark the location and monitor for any progression in soot staining or noise over the following watches.
procedures.why: Determines whether the leak is stable (minor seal degradation) or worsening (developing structural issue).

procedures.action: At the next available opportunity, reduce load, allow cooling, and replace the compensator joint gasket/seal.
procedures.why: A degraded gasket is the most common cause of a minor, stable exhaust gas leak at this joint.

procedures.action: Re-torque the joint per the maker's bolt tightening sequence and pressure-test if practical before full reload.
procedures.why: Proper torque sequence prevents uneven sealing stress that could cause a recurrence of the leak.

constraints: All exhaust gas joints must be maintained gas-tight to prevent casing contamination and heat loss
regulations: Manufacturer's joint torque specification for exhaust system flanges
warnings: A minor leak left unaddressed can progress to a larger gas escape, especially if the gasket further degrades under continued thermal cycling
outcomes: If ignored, the leak may enlarge, increasing fire risk from hot gas on nearby components and insulation
Timely gasket replacement restores a gas-tight joint and eliminates the fire/soot hazard
key_facts: Compensators are fitted between the exhaust valve housings and the exhaust gas receiver
Minor gas leaks are often first detected by soot staining rather than instrumentation

question_seeds.text: How should a minor exhaust joint gas leak be monitored before scheduling repair?
What is the typical root cause of a stable, low-level gas leak at an exhaust valve housing joint?

known_issue.failure_mode: degraded gasket / minor gas leak at compensator joint
known_issue.detection_method: visual soot staining and audible hissing during rounds

trace.situation: The turbine casing of the turbocharger develops a through-wall crack due to high-cycle thermal fatigue after years of service, resulting in a slow exhaust gas leak from the casing itself rather than from a joint or compensator.
trace.trigger: A localized hot spot on the turbocharger turbine casing detected by IR thermography during a routine thermographic survey, with no corresponding alarm from standard instrumentation.

procedures.action: Confirm the crack location and extent using dye penetrant testing once the engine is stopped and the casing has cooled.
procedures.why: Determines whether the crack is superficial or through-wall, which dictates whether continued operation is safe.

procedures.action: If through-wall, take the turbocharger out of service and arrange for casing repair or replacement per the maker's approved procedure.
procedures.why: A through-wall crack in the turbine casing risks sudden enlargement under thermal and pressure cycling, leading to major gas leak or casing rupture.

procedures.action: If only one turbocharger is fitted, assess engine derating requirements while awaiting replacement parts; if twin turbochargers are fitted, consider single-TC operation per the maker's guidance.
procedures.why: Managing engine load within the derated/single-TC capability prevents overstressing the remaining system while repairs are arranged.

constraints: Turbine casing structural integrity must be maintained to the turbocharger maker's design pressure and temperature ratings
regulations: Turbocharger manufacturer's casing inspection and repair approval requirement
Class society survey requirement for pressure-retaining casing repairs
warnings: Continued operation with a confirmed through-wall turbine casing crack risks sudden casing failure, releasing high-temperature, high-velocity exhaust gas into the engine room
outcomes: If left unrepaired, the crack can propagate rapidly under cyclic thermal stress, leading to a sudden casing rupture and serious injury/fire risk
Early detection via thermography and planned repair avoids catastrophic casing failure
key_facts: Turbocharger casings are subject to high-cycle thermal fatigue over their service life
Thermographic surveys can detect developing cracks before standard instrumentation shows any deviation

question_seeds.text: How is a turbine casing crack confirmed as through-wall versus surface-only?

known_issue.detection_method: IR thermographic survey detecting localized hot spot

trace.situation: Water washing of the turbocharger compressor is performed incorrectly, with washing water of excessive temperature differential relative to the compressor wheel, resulting in thermal shock cracking of several compressor blades.
trace.trigger: A sudden imbalance vibration and drop in scavenge air pressure occurring shortly after a compressor water wash cycle.

procedures.action: Stop the engine immediately if vibration is significant, and inspect the compressor wheel for visible blade cracking or chipping.
procedures.why: Thermal shock cracking can quickly propagate to blade liberation, risking severe secondary damage to the compressor casing and downstream charge air cooler.

procedures.action: Review the washing procedure used against the maker's specified water temperature, flow rate, and injection duration limits.
procedures.why: Identifies the procedural deviation responsible for the thermal shock, to prevent recurrence.

procedures.action: Replace damaged compressor wheel/blades and re-balance the rotor assembly before returning the turbocharger to service.
procedures.why: Cracked or chipped blades create rotor imbalance that will accelerate bearing wear and risk further failure if not corrected.

constraints: Compressor water washing must be performed within the water temperature and flow parameters specified by the turbocharger maker
regulations: Turbocharger manufacturer's compressor washing procedure specification
warnings: Continuing to run a turbocharger with cracked compressor blades can lead to sudden blade liberation, severely damaging the compressor casing and potentially ejecting debris into the engine room
outcomes: If uncorrected, blade cracks propagate to full blade failure and catastrophic compressor damage
Correcting the washing procedure and replacing damaged blades restores safe turbocharger operation
key_facts: All turbocharger makes are fitted with an arrangement for optional water washing of the compressor side
Washing procedure parameters (temperature, duration) are maker-specific and must be strictly followed

question_seeds.text: Why can incorrect water washing temperature cause compressor blade cracking?

known_issue.failure_mode: compressor blade thermal shock cracking from improper water washing
known_issue.detection_method: post-washing vibration increase and scavenge pressure drop

trace.situation: On an engine fitted with two turbochargers on the exhaust side, one unit begins to underperform relative to the other due to uneven exhaust gas distribution from the receiver, causing one turbocharger to run at a notably lower speed and higher exhaust temperature than its twin.
trace.trigger: A persistent speed and temperature split between the two turbochargers under steady load conditions, beyond the normal balance tolerance.

procedures.action: Verify the split is not due to a sensor calibration discrepancy by comparing both turbochargers' instrumentation against a portable reference where possible.
procedures.why: Rules out an instrumentation fault before investigating mechanical/flow causes.

procedures.action: Inspect the exhaust gas receiver branch ducting and compensators feeding the underperforming turbocharger for partial blockage, fouling, or a sagging/leaking joint.
procedures.why: Uneven gas distribution between parallel turbochargers is most often caused by a flow restriction in one branch.

procedures.action: Clean or repair the affected branch and recheck turbocharger balance under steady load before accepting full MCR operation.
procedures.why: Confirms the flow imbalance has been corrected and that both turbochargers are sharing load as designed.

constraints: Twin-turbocharger engines must maintain balanced gas distribution between units per engine design intent
regulations: Manufacturer's guidance on multi-turbocharger balance monitoring
warnings: Prolonged imbalance overloads the underperforming turbocharger thermally while underutilizing its twin, risking premature failure of the overloaded unit
outcomes: If uncorrected, the overloaded turbocharger experiences accelerated wear and may fail prematurely, forcing single-TC operation
Restoring balanced flow protects both turbochargers and maintains full-rated engine performance
key_facts: If an engine is fitted with two turbochargers, they are always located on the exhaust side of the engine
Balance between multiple turbochargers depends on even distribution from the common exhaust gas receiver

question_seeds.text: Which component is most likely responsible for an exhaust flow imbalance between two turbochargers on the same engine?

known_issue.failure_mode: uneven gas distribution between twin turbochargers
known_issue.detection_method: comparative TC speed and temperature trend between units

trace.situation: Deteriorating fuel quality combined with poor atomization from worn fuel injection nozzles leads to visibly dense black smoke from the funnel and a general rise in exhaust gas opacity, independent of any single component failure in the exhaust system itself.
trace.trigger: Visible black smoke reported from the bridge or by external observation, with no abnormal individual cylinder or turbocharger parameter yet in alarm.

procedures.action: Check fuel oil viscosity, temperature, and quality parameters against the ISO 8217 specification currently in use.
procedures.why: Off-spec fuel viscosity or poor quality directly causes incomplete combustion and visible smoke.

procedures.action: Inspect fuel injection pressure and spray pattern (via indicator cards or injector inspection) for signs of worn nozzles or incorrect injection timing.
procedures.why: Worn nozzles produce poor atomization, a major contributor to smoke even with correct fuel quality.

procedures.action: Adjust fuel treatment (settling, centrifuging, heating) and/or schedule injector overhaul to restore proper combustion and reduce smoke.
procedures.why: Correcting both fuel conditioning and injection equipment addresses the combined root causes of excessive smoke.

constraints: Fuel quality must conform to ISO 8217 specification for the grade in use

regulations: MARPOL Annex VI smoke/particulate emission compliance
ISO 8217 fuel quality standard
warnings: Sustained heavy smoke can trigger port state control action and also indicates accelerated fouling risk to downstream turbocharger and boiler components
outcomes: If uncorrected, continued poor combustion accelerates turbocharger and boiler fouling and risks a MARPOL compliance violation
Correcting fuel treatment and injection equipment restores clean combustion and protects downstream exhaust components
key_facts: Exhaust gas temperature, flow rate, and smoke opacity are influenced by both fuel quality and injection equipment condition
Visible smoke is often an early external indicator before instrumentation shows a clear deviation

question_seeds.text: Why can visible black smoke occur without any single alarm being triggered on the engine instrumentation?

known_issue.detection_method: visual smoke observation, fuel quality and injection pressure check

trace.situation: A loose or corroded turbocharger inlet casing bolt allows a small amount of air/gas bypass around the turbine inlet seal, slightly reducing effective turbine efficiency and causing a minor, hard-to-diagnose drop in available engine power at high load.
trace.trigger: A slight but consistent shortfall in achievable engine load/power relative to the fuel index for the given RPM, without any single alarm being active.

procedures.action: Perform a full engine performance check (shop trial comparison) to confirm the power shortfall is real and not a measurement artifact.
procedures.why: Confirms the deviation is genuine before committing to a turbocharger inspection.

procedures.action: Inspect the turbocharger inlet casing joint bolts and seals for looseness, corrosion, or gas bypass marks (soot streaking).
procedures.why: A loose casing joint allows gas bypass around the turbine, reducing the energy delivered to the rotor and lowering boost pressure for a given fuel rate.

procedures.action: Re-torque or replace the affected bolts/seals per the maker's specification and re-run the performance check to confirm recovery.
procedures.why: Restoring a tight, sealed inlet casing joint recovers full turbine efficiency and engine power capability.

procedures.action: Inspect the pipe run configuration at the engine inlet and confirm whether a bend or an expansion joint is present as required by design.

procedures.action: Arrange installation of an expansion joint or modify the pipe run to include the required bend during the next planned maintenance opportunity.

warnings: Fuel leakage from a cracked high-temperature fuel connection is a serious fire hazard, particularly given the hot surfaces present near the engine

Installing the required expansion joint or bend eliminates the thermal stress source and prevents recurrence

trace.situation: Heat tracing on the fuel oil drain piping between the engine and the drain tanks has failed, allowing heavy fuel oil residue in the drain lines to cool below its pumping temperature and congeal, blocking the drain path from the HCU and pressure booster.

procedures.action: Check jacket cooling water (or steam) tracing supply to the fuel oil drain lines for interruption or valve closure.

procedures.action: Restore tracing flow and, once the line has reheated to above 50°C, verify drain flow resumes normally.

trace.situation: The fuel oil supply pump's built-on overflow valve or the external bypass valve has drifted out of adjustment, disrupting the intended pressure staging between the low-pressure supply circuit and the circulating circuit, resulting in abnormal recirculation and potential cavitation at the circulating pump suction.

procedures.action: Check and re-adjust the built-on supply pump overflow valve to its correct 5 bar setting.

procedures.action: Check and re-adjust the external bypass valve to its correct 4 bar setting.

procedures.action: After adjustment, verify circulating pump suction condition is free of cavitation noise and that supply pump discharge is stable.

Correct valve adjustment restores designed pressure staging and stable fuel delivery to the engine

trace.situation: The fuel oil pipe insulation covering hot fuel lines has been damaged or removed during maintenance and not properly reinstated, resulting in a surface temperature above the 55°C limit in the engine room and an increased risk of fuel vapor ignition from contact with hot bare pipework in case of a later leak.

procedures.action: Reinstate insulation per specification (20 mm mineral wool minimum 150 kg/m3, covered with glass cloth minimum 400 g/m2, or 30 mm if combined with heating pipes) and refit removable pads on flanges and valves.

procedures.action: Confirm spray shields are also correctly refitted over fuel oil pipe assemblies per IMO requirements after insulation work is complete.
procedures.why: Spray shields provide an additional barrier against fuel spray reaching hot surfaces in the event of a leaking joint.

Fuel oil pipe insulation: 20 mm mineral wool (150 kg/m3) with 400 g/m2 glass cloth, or 30 mm if combined with heating pipes
regulations: IMO regulation requiring spray shields on fuel oil and lubricating oil pipe assemblies
Classification society approval requirements for insulation material
warnings: Exposed hot fuel pipe surfaces combined with any future fuel leak significantly increase the risk of an engine room fire
outcomes: If left uncorrected, a subsequent minor fuel leak onto exposed hot pipework could ignite, causing an engine room fire

trace.situation: The fuel oil viscosity at engine inlet has dropped below the 2 cSt minimum because the heater's temperature control loop is not maintaining the required outlet temperature. constraints: Minimum fuel viscosity at engine inlet: 2 cSt (3 cSt or higher preferred)
Recommended viscometer setpoint: 10-15 cSt
regulations: MAN Everllence fuel oil system manual, Section 7.05 viscosity requirements
warnings: Continued operation below 2 cSt risks abnormal wear and seizure in the fuel pump plunger/barrel, leading to loss of cylinder fuelling
Do not attempt to compensate by over-cooling the fuel as this can cause the opposite problem of excess viscosity
outcomes: If uncorrected, abnormal fuel pump wear and potential plunger seizure resulting in cylinder misfiring
If corrected, viscosity returns to the 10-15 cSt normal HFO range and injection equipment wear rate normalises
key_facts: Lower fuel viscosity limit at engine inlet is 2 cSt
Recommended viscosity for distillate fuel is 3 cSt or higher
Steam supply to the heater should be saturated at approximately 7 bar(a)

If corrected, fuel viscosity returns within the 10-15 cSt normal HFO band and injection quality is restored

trace.situation: Catalytic fines (cat fines, Al+Si) concentration in the fuel supplied to the engine has risen above the recommended maximum because the fuel oil separators are not achieving adequate removal efficiency, possibly due to incorrect throttling, low feed temperature, or worn discs.

procedures.action: Verify separator inlet temperature is maintained at the minimum of 98°C.

Do not bypass the separator to maintain engine fuel supply without a confirmed low cat fines result

If corrected, cat fines are reduced to acceptable levels and abnormal wear rates return to normal service life expectations

procedures.action: Once stopped, renew the damaged high-pressure pipe and inspect the spray shield for fire-safety compliance before restart.

Absolute fineness of the main filter: maximum 10 micron

outcomes: If uncorrected, continued fouling can restrict fuel flow enough to trigger low fuel pressure alarms and load limitation
If corrected through timely changeover and cleaning, normal pressure drop and fuel delivery are restored

procedures.action: Inspect the pressure booster top cover seal for damage once the blockage is cleared, and renew if leakage or deformation is found.

constraints: Valves in the engine drain pipe must be locked open and marked, only to be closed when there is no fuel pressure to the engine

Never leave a drain valve closed under normal running conditions
outcomes: If uncorrected, continued backpressure can destroy the top cover seal leading to internal oil contamination and potential loss of hydraulic control pressure in the HCU
If corrected, free drainage is restored and the seal can be inspected and renewed before further damage occurs
key_facts: The manual explicitly states a valve in the engine drain pipe is not acceptable unless locked open and marked
Blocked drains are a documented direct cause of pressure booster top cover seal damage
Any required valve must only be closed when there is confirmed no fuel oil pressure to the engine

trace.situation: The automatic deaerating valve on the fuel oil venting box has stuck closed, preventing release of entrained gas from the surplus fuel recirculated from the engine. Gas accumulation in the low-pressure part of the system can lead to pump cavitation and unstable fuel pressure.

procedures.action: If the valve is found seized, clean or renew it, bearing in mind it must retain liquids while only releasing gas.

constraints: Venting box must be positioned at or above the top of the service tank, or drained to a lower tank if not
Supply pump maintains approximately 4 bar in the low-pressure part to minimize gasification
regulations: MAN Everllence fuel oil system manual, Section 7.05 Fuel oil venting box
warnings: Trapped gas in the circulating system can cause erratic fuel pressure and injection irregularities across multiple cylinders
Do not disable or bypass the automatic deaerating valve permanently as a workaround
outcomes: If uncorrected, gas accumulation can cause circulating pump cavitation and unstable fuel delivery pressure, risking uneven combustion
If corrected, stable fuel pressure and proper gas release are restored, preventing pump cavitation damage
key_facts: The deaerating valve releases gas but retains liquid fuel
The supply pump maintains about 4 bar to help avoid gasification in the venting box temperature range
The venting box size is matched to the maximum circulating pump flow rate

procedures.action: Stop the changeover process immediately and do not introduce further distillate fuel until the blend compatibility is assessed.
procedures.why: Continuing to mix incompatible fuels will worsen flocculation and generate more sludge that can block filters and pumps.

procedures.action: Drain and flush the affected section of piping, venting box, and drain tank of the flocculated mixture.
procedures.why: Removing the unstable blend prevents it from being drawn into the circulating pump and filter, protecting fuel equipment.

procedures.action: Review changeover timing against the engine's recommended slow changeover procedure and ensure adequate time is allowed for the system to fully transition between fuel types.
procedures.why: A controlled, gradual changeover reduces the risk of two incompatible fuel batches being present simultaneously in the same line.

procedures.action: Sample and test the fuel oil for compatibility (e.g., spot test) before resuming normal circulation.
procedures.why: Confirming compatibility before resuming avoids repeating the sludge formation event.

constraints: Everllence recommends constant operation on heavy fuel where practicable, with changeover to diesel oil only as required for operational reasons
Changeover should be managed to avoid blending incompatible residual and distillate fuels of marginal quality
regulations: MAN Everllence fuel oil system manual, Section 7.01 Fuel considerations
warnings: Asphaltene sludge from incompatible blends can rapidly block filters and starve the engine of fuel
Emission control area sulphur restrictions can force changeovers; these must be carefully planned to avoid incompatibility
outcomes: If uncorrected, continued circulation of flocculated fuel can clog filters repeatedly and risk a complete loss of fuel supply
If corrected, the system is flushed clean and future changeovers are planned to avoid repeat incompatibility events

Changeover to diesel oil can be performed at any time, even with the engine stopped

trace.situation: The service tank has not been used for an extended period, allowing settled cat fines and water to concentrate near the tank bottom; without the transfer pump function returning this content to the settling tank, contaminated fuel is being drawn directly to the engine.
trace.trigger: Unexplained rise in cat fines or water content in routine fuel samples taken from the service tank outlet, despite normal separator operation

procedures.action: Confirm how long the current service tank has been in use without replenishment or circulation.
procedures.why: Extended static periods allow heavier contaminants to settle and concentrate near the tank outlet level.

procedures.action: Operate the transfer pump (if fitted) to return service tank content to the settling tank before further use.
procedures.why: This redistributes settled contaminants back through the separator treatment process rather than sending them to the engine.

procedures.action: If no transfer pump is fitted, increase separator duty and sampling frequency while drawing down the affected tank, and consider blending with a fresher batch.
procedures.why: Without a transfer pump, extra separator throughput is the only mitigation to reduce contaminant levels reaching the engine.

constraints: Service tank outlet to supply pumps should remain above any accumulated sediment
Transfer pump function should return service tank content to settling tank after an idle period, per manual recommendation
regulations: MAN Everllence fuel oil system manual, Section 7.01 Note 6 - Transfer pump
warnings: Drawing fuel directly from a long-idle service tank without redistribution risks a cat fines spike reaching the engine undetected
Do not assume separator performance alone will compensate for tank settling issues
outcomes: If uncorrected, abrasive wear from concentrated cat fines can damage fuel pumps, injection valves and liners
If corrected via transfer pump operation, contaminant levels at the engine are normalised before damage occurs

trace.situation: A recently bunkered fuel batch has a specific gravity above the 0.991 threshold, which exceeds the effective cleaning capability of the installed separators unless modern high-efficiency centrifuges or clarifiers are in use, risking inadequate removal of water and solid contaminants.
trace.trigger: Bunker delivery note or fuel sample analysis showing density at 15°C above 0.991 kg/l

procedures.action: Confirm whether the installed separators are rated for high-density fuel (e.g., Alcap, Unitrol, or E-Hidens II type units) before accepting the fuel into service circulation.
procedures.why: Standard gravity-disc separators cannot effectively clean fuel above 0.991 density without modern self-adjusting or high-G technology.

procedures.action: If separators are not rated for high density, segregate the affected batch and blend cautiously with lower-density fuel while monitoring separator performance closely.
procedures.why: Blending can bring the effective density within the separator's design capability, reducing contamination risk.

procedures.action: Increase sampling frequency of treated fuel at the engine inlet to verify water content remains below 0.5% v/v and cat fines remain controlled.
procedures.why: Close monitoring confirms whether the separator is still achieving adequate cleaning despite the challenging fuel density.

constraints: Guiding maximum density at 15°C is 1.010 kg/m3 only if automatic clarifiers are installed; otherwise 0.991 is the practical separation limit

regulations: MAN Everllence fuel oils guiding specification, Section 7.02

warnings: Accepting high-density fuel without confirming separator capability risks delivering water and solids directly to the engine
Standard clarifier-type separators without special design will not adequately treat fuel above 0.991 density
outcomes: If uncorrected, water and solid contaminants bypass the separator and reach the engine, risking injection equipment damage and combustion instability
If corrected, the fuel batch is properly segregated or blended and treated fuel quality at the engine inlet remains within specification
key_facts: The practical separation limit for standard separators is a specific gravity of 0.991 at 15°C

trace.situation: The MDO/MGO cooler fitted ahead of the supply pumps has fouled or lost cooling water flow, allowing low-viscosity distillate fuel to reach the supply pump at an elevated temperature, reducing its viscosity below the 2 cSt minimum required for reliable pump operation.

procedures.action: Clean or backflush the cooler if fouling is confirmed, and verify cooling water supply valves are fully open.

procedures.action: Monitor supply and circulating pump performance (suction pressure, noise, vibration) for signs of cavitation during the fault period.

constraints: Minimum viscosity for reliable pump operation: 2 cSt

Operating pumps below the minimum viscosity for extended periods can cause internal cavitation damage
outcomes: If uncorrected, continued low-viscosity operation risks pump cavitation damage and unstable fuel delivery to the engine
If corrected, fuel viscosity is restored above 2 cSt and normal pump operation resumes without cavitation risk
key_facts: The MDO/MGO cooler exists specifically to protect supply pumps from too-warm, too-low-viscosity distillate fuel
All fuel system pumps, not just engine fuel pumps, require above 2 cSt viscosity to function correctly

trace.situation: The spring-loaded overflow valve on the engine, which maintains constant fuel pressure to the injection pumps across all loads, has drifted out of adjustment, causing fuel pressure to vary abnormally with engine load instead of remaining steady.

procedures.action: Confirm the overflow valve setting against the specified 4-5 bar range (5 bar for built-on supply pump overflow valves, 4 bar for the external bypass valve) relevant to its installation point.

procedures.action: Inspect the valve spring and seat for wear, corrosion, or sludge buildup preventing proper seating.

External bypass valve: adjusted to 4 bar

outcomes: If uncorrected, inconsistent fuel pressure at varying loads can cause uneven cylinder performance and increased exhaust temperature spread

trace.situation: The electrically driven fuel oil supply pump is exhibiting signs of cavitation, evidenced by noise and pressure fluctuation, because the suction piping from the service tank is undersized relative to the discharge piping or a suction strainer is partially blocked.

procedures.action: Verify the suction strainer upstream of the supply pump is clean and not restricting flow.
procedures.why: A partially blocked strainer is the most common and quickly correctable cause of pump suction starvation.

procedures.action: Confirm the suction pipe passage area is at least 50% larger than the pipe between the supply pump and circulating pump, per the design requirement.
procedures.why: Undersized suction piping increases pressure drop at the pump inlet, promoting cavitation regardless of strainer condition.

procedures.action: Check fuel temperature at the pump suction is not excessively high, which can also contribute to gasification and cavitation.

constraints: Suction pipe to supply pump must have minimum 50% larger passage area than the pipe between supply pump and circulating pump

warnings: Prolonged cavitation can cause erosion damage to the supply pump impeller/gears and reduce pump life significantly

trace.situation: During an extended port stay with the engine stopped, the steam heat tracing on the fuel oil supply piping failed, allowing heavy fuel oil in the pipework to cool below its pumping temperature of approximately 50°C and solidify, preventing the circulating pump from re-establishing flow at restart.

procedures.action: Check the steam tracing supply valves and steam trap condition on the affected fuel line sections.
procedures.why: A failed or isolated steam trace is the direct cause of the fuel cooling below pumping temperature during standstill.

procedures.action: If piping is confirmed solidified, apply external or supplementary heating (e.g., temporary steam hose, portable heater) to gradually raise pipe temperature before attempting to run the pump.

procedures.action: Once flow is restored, verify the heat tracing system is fully repaired and operating automatically before any further extended stop.

constraints: HFO pumping temperature in the pipe system: approximately 50°C

warnings: Attempting to force the circulating pump against solidified fuel can trip the pump motor on overload or cause internal mechanical damage

outcomes: If uncorrected, the pump cannot restart and the vessel risks delayed departure while the fuel system is manually thawed and restored
If corrected, heat tracing maintains pumpable fuel temperature through standstill and normal restart capability is preserved

A changeover to diesel oil is recommended for stops expected to exceed five days or during major fuel system repairs
Recommended tracing heat output is about 100 watts per meter of pipe

procedures.action: If no bypass valve exists, prepare to manually isolate and bypass the flowmeter using temporary piping or valves as per the vessel's emergency fuel system procedure.

Any temporary bypass arrangement must be removed and replaced with a proper permanent bypass valve as soon as practicable
outcomes: If uncorrected, continued restriction can escalate to a fuel starvation engine shutdown
If corrected, fuel flow is restored and a permanent bypass valve eliminates recurrence risk
key_facts: The manual specifically requires a safety bypass valve across the flowmeter due to blockage risk
The flowmeter's rated flow should equal the fuel supply pump capacity

procedures.action: Increase separator purge frequency and verify the self-cleaning discharge interval is appropriate for the current water content.

procedures.action: Check settling and service tank drain valves for accumulated free water and drain as required before further use.
procedures.why: Free water settling at the tank bottom can be drawn into the fuel supply if not regularly drained.

procedures.action: If water content remains high despite separator adjustment, reduce engine load and increase monitoring of combustion parameters for signs of water-induced irregular combustion.
procedures.why: Reducing load lowers the risk of water-related injection problems while the root contamination source is investigated.

constraints: Guiding maximum water content in HFO as supplied: 0.5% v/v
Separator should remove both water and solid contaminants down to acceptable limits before fuel reaches the service tank
regulations: MAN Everllence fuel oils guiding specification, Section 7.02

Max differential pressure cooling side of TC cooler is 0.2 bar

warnings: Sustained high TC lube oil temperature accelerates oil oxidation and can reduce the load-carrying capacity of the turbocharger bearing oil film
If temperature is not controlled, turbocharger bearing damage and consequential rotor imbalance can occur
outcomes: If uncorrected, turbocharger bearing wear accelerates and may lead to unplanned turbocharger overhaul

TC lube oil temperature and alarm setpoints are governed by sensor TE 8112 I-AH-AL-Y

trace.situation: Condensate accumulates in the crankcase venting line because the drain cowl near the engine flange is blocked or has not been drained during a period of fluctuating ambient conditions, restricting normal venting and allowing slight pressure buildup inside the crankcase.
trace.trigger: Slightly elevated crankcase pressure reading or oil residue/moisture observed at the vent line drain cowl during routine rounds

procedures.action: Open and drain the condensate drain cowl on the crankcase venting line near the engine flange.
procedures.why: The drain cowl exists specifically to remove condensate buildup that can otherwise restrict the venting line.

procedures.action: Check the venting pipe routing for proper ascending inclination and absence of pipe pockets.
procedures.why: An improperly routed vent line can trap condensate even if the drain cowl is clear, requiring correction of pipe routing or a dedicated pocket drain.

procedures.action: Verify crankcase pressure returns to normal (near atmospheric) after draining, and increase drain cowl inspection frequency going forward.
procedures.why: Confirms the restriction has been cleared and establishes a more appropriate maintenance interval.

constraints: Crankcase venting line must include a drain cowl located as close as possible to the engine flange
Vent piping must be routed with steadily ascending inclination (minimum 5° longitudinal, 15° transverse) to avoid pockets
regulations: Engine builder venting and drain pipe arrangement requirements (Section 8.07)
warnings: A restricted crankcase vent can mask early oil mist detection and allow slow pressure buildup that affects seal integrity
Accumulated condensate in a vent pocket, if not drained, increases the risk of localized corrosion in the vent piping
outcomes: If uncorrected, restricted venting can interfere with crankcase pressure relief and oil mist monitoring accuracy
If corrected, normal crankcase venting and pressure balance are restored

Vent pipe routing requires minimum 5° longitudinal and 15° transverse ascending inclination to avoid pockets

trace.situation: A newly commissioned lubricating oil system fails to meet the specified ISO 4406 cleanliness level after shipyard flushing was reported complete, with particle counts still showing XX/21/18 against the required XX/19/15 for the general lubricating oil system.
trace.trigger: Pall Fluid Contamination Comparator sample result exceeding the acceptance cleanliness level prior to sea trial

procedures.action: Reject the flushing completion certificate and require continued flushing with the engine bypassed.
procedures.why: Proceeding to engine start with oil above the specified cleanliness level risks introducing particulate contamination directly into bearing clearances.

procedures.action: Increase purifier run-time and consider temporarily reducing the main filter mesh size to 10-25 µm with the 6 µm fine filter in the bypass loop.
procedures.why: Finer temporary filtration and increased separator throughput accelerate removal of residual particulate to meet the target cleanliness level.

procedures.action: Re-sample at regular intervals and document results in the flushing log until XX/19/15 (or XX/16/13 for hydraulic/control oil circuits) is consistently achieved.
procedures.why: A documented, repeatable clean result is required before the system is accepted for engine-connected flushing and sea trial.

constraints: Required cleanliness level is ISO 4406 XX/19/15 for the general lubricating oil system and XX/16/13 for ME hydraulic/control oil systems
New oil delivered typically at XX/23/19 per ISO 4406 requires further cleaning before use
regulations: Engine builder flushing and cleanliness specification (Section 8.05)
warnings: Starting the engine with oil above the specified cleanliness level can cause widespread abrasive wear of bearings and hydraulic components
Do not sign off the flushing log until target cleanliness is independently verified
outcomes: If uncorrected, commissioning with contaminated oil risks premature wear of bearings, HCU components, and control valves
If corrected, the system meets specification and the engine can be safely connected for flushing and sea trial

New bunkered oil typically arrives at ISO 4406 XX/23/19 and requires further cleaning

trace.situation: The hydraulic control oil (HCO) filter serving the Alfa Laval or Hydac type filter unit becomes progressively fouled with fine varnish-like deposits from oil oxidation, degrading the responsiveness of the hydraulic cylinder unit (HCU) controlling the exhaust valve.
trace.trigger: Exhaust valve timing deviation alarm or slower-than-normal valve closing response noted during performance monitoring

procedures.action: Check HCO filter differential pressure and inspect/replace the filter element.
procedures.why: A fouled HCO filter restricts flow to the hydraulic cylinder unit, slowing valve actuation response.

procedures.action: Sample hydraulic control oil for varnish potential (e.g., MPC test) and oxidation indicators.
procedures.why: Varnish deposits indicate oil oxidation, which if left unaddressed will continue to foul filters and valve spool clearances.

procedures.action: Verify cleanliness level against the stricter ISO 4406 XX/16/13 requirement for hydraulic/control oil circuits and increase separator/fine filtration if not met.
procedures.why: The hydraulic control system requires a tighter cleanliness standard than the general LO system due to fine clearances in control valves.

constraints: Required cleanliness for ME hydraulic oil and second fuel hydraulic oil systems is ISO 4406 XX/16/13, stricter than the general LO system
RW connection applies specifically to Alfa Laval or Hydac HCO filter installations
regulations: Engine builder hydraulic control oil cleanliness and filtration specification
warnings: Degraded hydraulic control oil response can cause mistimed exhaust valve operation, risking combustion and turbocharger performance issues
Varnish buildup in control valve clearances can eventually cause sticking and erratic valve actuation
outcomes: If uncorrected, exhaust valve timing deviations can worsen, affecting combustion efficiency and potentially causing valve damage
If corrected via filter replacement and oil conditioning, exhaust valve response returns to normal
key_facts: Hydraulic/control oil circuits require a tighter ISO 4406 XX/16/13 cleanliness standard than the general LO system
HCO filter type (Alfa Laval or Hydac) determines whether the RW connection is used

trace.situation: A failure in the turbocharger's sealing air system increases back-pressure in the turbocharger oil drain line, causing air to be pushed into the lubricating oil bottom tank below the oil surface instead of being released above it, resulting in oil foaming and aeration in the tank.
trace.trigger: Visible foaming/aerated oil observed at the bottom tank sight glass or sudden LO pump suction pressure instability without a change in tank level

procedures.action: Inspect the turbocharger drain outlet arrangement in the bottom tank to confirm air is being released above the oil level as designed.
procedures.why: If the drain outlet geometry or sealing air pressure has changed, air may bubble through the oil instead of venting above it, causing aeration.

procedures.action: Check turbocharger sealing air supply pressure and filter condition for abnormal back-pressure.
procedures.why: Elevated sealing air pressure increases the volume of air carried into the drain line, overwhelming the intended above-level release design.

procedures.action: Allow the tank time to de-aerate with reduced circulation rate if possible, and verify LO pump suction pressure stabilizes before resuming full load.
procedures.why: Aerated oil entering the pump suction can cause unstable discharge pressure and reduced lubrication effectiveness at the bearings.

constraints: Turbocharger drain outlet in the bottom tank must release sealing air above the oil level by design
Maximum circulation rate design is 18 times per hour; excess aeration effectively increases apparent turnover and reduces settling/deaeration time
regulations: Engine builder turbocharger drain and bottom tank venting arrangement requirement
warnings: Persistent oil aeration can cause erratic lubricating oil pressure and reduced bearing protection under load
Foaming oil reduces the effective deaeration capacity of the bottom tank, risking further air entrainment at the pump suction
outcomes: If uncorrected, unstable LO pressure may develop into a low-pressure trip under load
If corrected, oil returns to a properly deaerated condition and pump suction stabilizes
key_facts: Turbocharger drain oil is pressurized by sealing air and must vent above the oil surface per the bottom tank design
Aerated oil at the pump suction is a known cause of unstable LO discharge pressure

known_issue.detection_method: visible foaming at tank sight glass / unstable LO pump suction pressure

trace.situation: Progressive abrasive wear of a crosshead bearing shell goes undetected by temperature sensors because the thermocouple is slightly displaced from the hottest wear zone, while periodic oil analysis begins to show a steady rise in iron, tin, and copper wear-metal content.
trace.trigger: Laboratory oil analysis report showing wear-metal trend exceeding baseline threshold over consecutive samples

procedures.action: Cross-reference the wear-metal trend with bearing temperature logs for all units to identify any subtle deviation, even within normal alarm limits.
procedures.why: A bearing beginning to wear abnormally may show only a small temperature deviation that would not alone trigger an alarm, making the oil analysis trend the earlier indicator.

procedures.action: Schedule an inspection of the suspected crosshead/main bearing at the next available opportunity, using available means such as vibration monitoring or borescope if accessible.
procedures.why: Early physical confirmation prevents a minor wear condition from progressing to bearing failure under load.

procedures.action: Increase oil sampling frequency and maintain full-flow and offline filter inspection until wear-metal trend stabilizes or the bearing is inspected/replaced.
procedures.why: More frequent sampling tracks whether the wear rate is accelerating, which would indicate urgency for intervention.

constraints: Regular LO analysis for wear metals (Fe, Sn, Cu, Pb) is a standard condition-monitoring practice recommended by the engine builder
regulations: Engine builder recommendation for lubricating oil condition monitoring via periodic laboratory analysis
warnings: Relying solely on bearing temperature alarms can miss early-stage wear that is only visible through oil analysis trends
An undetected progressing bearing wear condition can lead to sudden bearing failure under load without further warning
outcomes: If uncorrected, progressive wear can reach a point of sudden bearing seizure or wiping under load
If corrected through early inspection, bearing can be reconditioned or replaced during planned maintenance rather than as an emergency repair
key_facts: Wear-metal trend analysis (Fe, Sn, Cu, Pb) in system oil is a key early indicator of bearing wear not always reflected by temperature sensors
Bearing thermocouple placement limitations mean oil analysis can be the earliest detection method for some wear modes

known_issue.detection_method: trending wear-metal content in periodic laboratory oil analysis

trace.situation: During an extended period at low load or dead ship recovery, the lubricating oil circulation rate falls to a point where sediment and sludge begin to settle out and accumulate in low points of the bottom tank faster than the separator can remove it, gradually reducing effective tank volume and settling capacity.
trace.trigger: Decreasing available tank volume noted during tank soundings/gauging compared to as-built capacity, with increasing separator sludge discharge volume

procedures.action: Arrange for tank sludge/sediment removal during the next dry-dock or tank entry opportunity, following gas-free and enclosed space entry procedures.
procedures.why: Accumulated sediment physically reduces the usable tank volume designed for deaeration and settling, which cannot be corrected without physical removal.

procedures.action: Increase separator operating hours and verify discharge intervals are appropriate for the sludge loading rate.
procedures.why: More frequent separator discharge helps manage the ongoing contamination load even though it does not remove historical sediment.

procedures.action: Recalculate the current effective circulation rate against the 18 times per hour design maximum using the reduced usable tank volume.
procedures.why: A reduced usable volume effectively increases circulation rate beyond design intent, reducing settling and deaeration performance further.

constraints: Maximum recommended lubricating oil circulation rate is 18 times per hour based on minimum tank volume
Enclosed space entry for tank cleaning must follow classification society and company safety procedures
regulations: Classification society enclosed space entry requirements
Engine builder bottom tank design circulation rate guideline
warnings: Reduced usable tank volume increases effective circulation rate, degrading settling and deaeration performance, which can accelerate contamination-related bearing wear
Entering the bottom tank for cleaning requires strict gas-free certification due to oil mist and low-oxygen risk
outcomes: If uncorrected, reduced settling capacity leads to progressively dirtier circulating oil and increased bearing wear risk
If corrected via tank cleaning, design settling/deaeration performance and circulation rate margin are restored
key_facts: Bottom tank minimum volume is based on CEAS pump capacity divided by the 18 times/hour maximum circulation rate
Sediment accumulation in the bottom tank physically reduces usable settling volume over time

known_issue.failure_mode: bottom tank sediment accumulation reducing usable settling volume
known_issue.detection_method: tank sounding trend versus as-built capacity and separator sludge discharge rate

trace.situation: A relief/overflow safety valve integrated into the turbocharger lubricating oil positive displacement pump begins to leak internally due to a worn seat, causing reduced net pump discharge pressure to the turbocharger inlet under high ambient temperature conditions.
trace.trigger: Gradually declining TC lube oil supply pressure trend without any change in filter DP or cooler performance

procedures.action: Confirm pump discharge pressure against the specified 4 bar pump head and 5 barg maximum discharge pressure design values.
procedures.why: Establishes the magnitude of the pressure shortfall relative to design specification.

procedures.action: Inspect and overhaul or replace the pump's built-in overflow safety valve if internal leakage past the seat is confirmed.
procedures.why: A worn relief valve seat allows continuous internal bypass, reducing net delivered pressure even though the pump itself may be mechanically sound.

procedures.action: Switch to the standby TC lube oil pump if fitted while the affected pump is repaired.
procedures.why: Maintains reliable turbocharger lubrication while corrective maintenance is carried out.

constraints: TC lube oil pump head (Ph) is 4 bar with maximum discharge pressure 5 barg
Pump flow capacity must be maintained within 100%-112% of CEAS stated capacity
regulations: Engine builder TC lube oil pump specification and classification pressure test requirements
warnings: Reduced TC lube oil supply pressure under high load/ambient conditions can lead to inadequate turbocharger bearing lubrication
Delaying investigation risks a sudden further pressure drop and turbocharger bearing damage
outcomes: If uncorrected, turbocharger bearing lubrication margin continues to shrink, risking bearing wear or failure at high load
If corrected via relief valve overhaul, design discharge pressure and lubrication margin are restored
key_facts: TC lube oil pump design head is 4 bar with a maximum discharge pressure of 5 barg
The pump has a built-in overflow safety valve whose condition directly affects net delivered pressure

known_issue.detection_method: declining TC lube oil supply pressure trend

trace.situation: The offline fine filtration unit serving the separate turbocharger lubricating oil system, sized to clean one-fifth of tank volume per hour through 3 µm deep-bed cartridges, has its cartridges saturated prematurely due to bunkering of new TC lube oil directly into the tank without passing through the fine filter unit as required.
trace.trigger: Unusually rapid rise in offline fine filter differential pressure shortly after a TC lube oil top-up/bunkering operation

procedures.action: Confirm whether the recent TC lube oil addition was introduced via the fine filter unit inlet as required, or added directly to the tank.
procedures.why: Bypassing the required filling route defeats the purpose of pre-cleaning new oil before it enters the clean tank, rapidly loading the fine filter.

procedures.action: Replace the saturated 3 µm deep-bed cartridge elements and verify correct filling procedure with engine room staff/bunkering party.
procedures.why: Restores filtration capacity and prevents recurrence by correcting the non-standard filling practice.

procedures.action: Sample the TC lube oil tank for particle count to confirm cleanliness has not been compromised by the improper filling method.
procedures.why: Confirms whether contamination has already entered the tank bulk volume requiring extended offline cleaning.

constraints: All TC lube oil filling/top-up operations must be performed via the fine filter unit inlet per engine builder requirement
Offline fine filter capacity is sized to clean 1/5 of tank volume per hour using 3 µm absolute deep-bed cartridge filtration
regulations: Engine builder TC lube oil system filling and offline filtration requirement
warnings: Repeated improper filling practices will continue to prematurely load the fine filter and can allow contaminated new oil to degrade turbocharger bearing clearances
Failure to correct the filling procedure will cause recurring unplanned filter element consumption
outcomes: If uncorrected, recurring premature filter saturation and potential turbocharger bearing contamination risk continue
If corrected, proper filling procedure restores expected filter service life and tank cleanliness
key_facts: All operations adding oil to the TC lube oil tank must be performed via the fine filter unit per engine builder instruction
Offline fine filter unit capacity is designed to clean 1/5 of tank volume per hour at 3 µm absolute fineness

known_issue.detection_method: rapid filter DP rise correlated with recent top-up/bunkering event

trace.situation: A positive displacement main lubricating oil pump develops excessive internal wear over time, reducing its effective volumetric efficiency, so that at high engine load the delivered flow falls toward the lower boundary of the acceptable 100%-112% capacity range and engine inlet pressure trends toward the low alarm limit.
trace.trigger: Gradually declining LO inlet pressure trend at high engine load over several months, approaching but not yet reaching the low-pressure alarm

procedures.action: Trend-log LO inlet pressure against engine load over an extended period and compare to commissioning baseline data.
procedures.why: Distinguishes a genuine pump wear trend from short-term fluctuations caused by temperature or filter condition.

procedures.action: Check pump internal clearances against maker tolerances at the next planned overhaul, and inspect for abnormal wear on rotors/gears.
procedures.why: Positive displacement pump wear directly reduces volumetric efficiency and delivered flow, which is the root cause of the declining pressure trend.

procedures.action: If pressure approaches the low alarm setpoint before overhaul is possible, verify standby pump readiness and consider early changeover to the standby pump to maintain margin.
procedures.why: Ensures continued adequate lubrication supply while the worn pump awaits scheduled maintenance.

constraints: Pump flow capacity must remain within 100%-112% of CEAS stated capacity
Engine inlet LO pressure must remain within the 'Guidance Values for Automation' normal service range at the 1,800 mm reference location
regulations: Engine builder pump flow rate specification and Guidance Values for Automation
warnings: Continuing to operate near the low-pressure alarm threshold with a worn pump reduces margin against a sudden trip under transient conditions
A sudden further drop in pump output at high load could trigger a low LO pressure shutdown
outcomes: If uncorrected, the pump may eventually fail to maintain minimum required pressure at high load, risking an automatic engine shutdown
If corrected via planned overhaul or pump changeover, adequate pressure margin is restored across the load range
key_facts: Pump flow capacity must be maintained within 100%-112% of the CEAS-stated design capacity
Engine inlet LO pressure reference location is 1,800 mm above crankshaft centerline per engine builder specification

known_issue.detection_method: trending LO inlet pressure decline at high load over extended operating period
