trace.situation: The oil mist detector (OMD) begins issuing intermittent crankcase mist alarms during normal steady-state operation, with no corresponding rise in bearing temperatures or vibration. Investigation points to contamination of the sampling optics or moisture ingress into the sampling pipework rather than an actual mist event.
trace.trigger: Repeated OMD alarm resets without any abnormal bearing temperature or BWM trend

procedures.action: Isolate the affected cylinder's sampling point and inspect/clean the OMD measuring chamber and sampling tubes per maker instructions (Visatron/Graviner/etc.).
procedures.why: Dust, oil fouling or condensation on the optical measuring track causes false opacity readings unrelated to actual mist.

procedures.action: Check sampling pipe routing for water traps or blockages and verify rotary sampling head operation.
procedures.why: Blocked or wet sampling lines give erratic or delayed opacity signals.

procedures.action: Re-calibrate the detector against reference (clean air) and log the result before returning to service.
procedures.why: Confirms the unit is reading true opacity, restoring reliable crankcase explosion protection.

constraints: OMD must remain connected to the shutdown system during shop trials per Everllence requirement
Germanischer Lloyd requires a shutdown (not slowdown) response to OMD alarm
regulations: Classification society requirement for OMD fitment on all two-stroke engines since 1990
IACS common recommendation for crankcase oil mist protection
warnings: Never disable or bypass the OMD to suppress nuisance alarms; the engine may be exposed to an undetected crankcase explosion risk.
Repeated manual resets without root-cause investigation can mask a genuine early-stage bearing failure.
outcomes: If root cause is not identified, crew may become desensitized to the alarm and miss a genuine mist event, risking a crankcase explosion.
Proper cleaning and recalibration restores reliable early warning with no loss of engine availability.
key_facts: The OMD measures opacity of crankcase atmosphere samples against reference air.
A slowdown is the standard OMD alarm response; GL class requires shutdown.
Sensor XS 8813 is oil mist in crankcase; XS 8814 indicates oil mist detector failure.

known_issue.detection_method: OMD optical opacity alarm with no corroborating BTM/BWM trend

trace.situation: The oil mist detector reports a sensor fault (XS 8814) rather than a mist alarm, indicating the detector itself has failed rather than detecting actual mist. This removes the primary crankcase explosion warning while the engine continues running.
trace.trigger: XS 8814 'oil mist detector failure' alarm active on the AMS

procedures.action: Dispatch engineer to inspect OMD unit power supply, sampling pump and optical head for fault codes per maker manual.
procedures.why: Determines whether the fault is electrical, mechanical, or sensor degradation.

procedures.action: If the fault cannot be cleared promptly, increase manual crankcase door temperature checks and visual/thermal inspection rounds.
procedures.why: Compensates for loss of continuous automatic mist detection until the OMD is restored.

procedures.action: Notify class/flag state if the vessel is operating UMS and the OMD cannot be restored before the next port, per the vessel's safety management system.
procedures.why: OMD is a mandatory safety sensor for UMS notation; its unavailability affects unattended operation compliance.

constraints: OMD is a mandatory fitment since 1990 for all Everllence B&W two-stroke engines
UMS notation requires functioning crankcase mist detection
regulations: Classification society UMS requirements for crankcase explosion protection
IACS common recommendation for OMD
warnings: Running UMS with the OMD inoperative removes the primary early-warning protection against a crankcase explosion; manual watchkeeping does not fully substitute.
outcomes: If left unresolved, an undetected bearing wipe could progress to crankcase explosion with no automatic warning.
Prompt repair restores full automatic crankcase explosion protection and UMS compliance.
key_facts: XS 8814 signals OMD unit/sensor failure, common with XS 8813 (mist alarm) circuit.
OMD and BTM are the two primary warning systems against crankcase explosions on two-stroke engines.

question_seeds.text: What should be done if the OMD reports a detector failure rather than a mist alarm?

known_issue.failure_mode: OMD unit/sensor failure
known_issue.detection_method: XS 8814 fault alarm on AMS

trace.situation: The bearing wear monitoring (BWM) system shows a progressive increase in proximity sensor clearance reading on one crank-train bearing over several days, exceeding the first high-wear alarm level but not yet the slowdown threshold.
trace.trigger: BWM first-level high-wear/deviation alarm displayed on alarm panel for a specific cylinder bearing

procedures.action: Record and trend the BWM clearance data for the affected cylinder against historical baseline.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the increase is a genuine mechanical wear trend or sensor drift.

procedures.action: Reduce load on the affected cylinder/engine if the trend is steep, and schedule inspection at next opportunity.
procedures.why: Limits further mechanical stress on a bearing showing accelerated wear before steel-to-steel contact risk.

procedures.action: Plan an open-up inspection of the specific bearing guided by BWM data rather than a blanket unscheduled inspection.
procedures.why: BWM is designed to make unscheduled inspections of all bearings unnecessary by pinpointing the specific affected bearing.

constraints: Second BWM alarm level activates an automatic slowdown
BWM uses two proximity sensors (fwd/aft) per cylinder targeting the guide shoe at BDC
regulations: Everllence design basis: BWM precision sufficient to alarm well before steel-to-steel bearing contact
warnings: Ignoring a rising BWM trend risks progression to the second-level slowdown alarm and potential consequential journal/bearing housing damage.
outcomes: Unaddressed, wear can progress to steel-to-steel contact causing journal and housing damage requiring major repair.
Early trend-based inspection planning limits damage to bearing shell replacement only.
key_facts: BWM monitors main, crank pin and crosshead bearings via proximity sensors inside the frame box.
Two high-wear alarm levels exist: first panel-only alarm, second triggers slowdown.
BWM data is intended to replace manual vertical clearance measurements during service checks.

question_seeds.text: Which bearing's BWM sensor is showing the trending high-wear alarm?
How much load reduction is appropriate when a first-level BWM alarm is trending upward?

known_issue.failure_mode: progressive mechanical bearing wear
known_issue.detection_method: BWM proximity sensor clearance trend, first-level high-wear alarm

trace.situation: Bearing temperature monitoring (BTM) indicates a rising oil outlet temperature on a crosshead bearing, approaching the first alarm threshold, while BWM clearance readings remain normal, suggesting an early lubrication or oil film issue rather than mechanical wear.
trace.trigger: BTM oil outlet temperature deviation alarm on a specific crosshead bearing

procedures.action: Verify lubricating oil inlet pressure and temperature to main engine are within normal limits.
procedures.why: Reduced oil supply pressure/temperature can starve the bearing of adequate cooling/lubrication, raising outlet temperature.

procedures.action: Check for recent water-in-oil alarm history or sample the lube oil for water contamination.
procedures.why: Water contamination causes acute corrosive wear of the crosshead bearing overlayer, which can manifest as localized heating before mechanical wear is detected.

procedures.action: If temperature continues to rise toward the second alarm level, reduce load pre-emptively and prepare to respond to an automatic slowdown.
procedures.why: The second BTM alarm level activates an automatic slowdown to prevent bearing damage.

constraints: Two high-temperature alarm levels apply to BTM oil outlet readings: first panel alarm, second triggers slowdown
Water-in-oil alarm threshold for crosshead bearing protection is aw=0.5 (high) and aw=0.9 (high-high)
regulations: Everllence BTM design requirement for two-level alarm/slowdown protection on main, crank pin, and crosshead bearings
warnings: A rising BTM trend combined with any water-in-oil indication should be treated as a developing crosshead bearing overlayer failure, not just a minor cooling issue.
outcomes: If ignored, acute corrosive wear of the crosshead bearing overlayer can progress rapidly to bearing failure.
Early correction of lube oil supply or water contamination prevents irreparable bearing damage.
key_facts: BTM monitors main, crank pin and crosshead bearing shell/housing or oil outlet temperatures.
Crosshead bearings have an overlayer vulnerable to acute corrosive wear from water contamination.
Water content exceeding ~50% of saturation point (aw 0.5) risks crosshead bearing damage.

question_seeds.text: Why is the crosshead bearing oil outlet temperature rising while BWM shows no wear?
What checks should be done before the BTM second-level slowdown alarm activates?

known_issue.failure_mode: developing oil film/lubrication breakdown at crosshead bearing
known_issue.detection_method: BTM oil outlet temperature deviation alarm

chapter_title: Monitoring And Alarms -- synthesized domain knowledge

trace.situation: The water-in-oil monitoring (WIOM) system records a steady rise in water activity (aw) approaching the high alarm level of 0.5, indicating lubricating oil contamination from an unidentified water source such as a cooler leak or condensation ingress.
trace.trigger: WIOM high alarm at aw = 0.5

procedures.action: Take a manual lube oil sample and send for laboratory water content confirmation while continuing WIOM trending.
procedures.why: Confirms the aw sensor reading against an independent method before taking major corrective action.

procedures.action: Inspect lubricating oil coolers, piston cooling oil system, and any steam/condensate interfaces for leaks into the LO system.
procedures.why: Coolers and heat exchangers are common sources of water ingress into lubricating oil.

procedures.action: If water activity continues rising toward 0.9 within a short time, treat this as indication of an active water leak and isolate the suspect component immediately.
procedures.why: A rapid rise from 0.5 to 0.9 specifically indicates an active ingress source requiring urgent isolation, per system design intent.

constraints: WIOM high alarm level: aw = 0.5 (approx. 0.2% water content)
WIOM high-high alarm level: aw = 0.9
regulations: Everllence standard requirement for WIOM fitment on all B&W two-stroke engines
warnings: Free water in lubricating oil exceeding the saturation point causes acute corrosive wear of crosshead bearing overlayers; the higher the water content, the faster the wear rate.
outcomes: If the water source is not found and isolated, rapid crosshead bearing overlayer wear and bearing failure can result.
Prompt source identification and oil treatment/purification restores safe lubrication condition.
key_facts: The aw-type sensor measures water activity on a 0-1 scale, independent of oil age or degradation.
aw 0.5 corresponds to roughly 50% of the oil's saturation point for water.
Main, thrust and crank pin bearings can also suffer irreparable damage from water contamination, though less acutely than crosshead bearings.

trace.situation: The liner wall monitoring (LWM) system registers increasing and fluctuating temperatures on one cylinder liner's manoeuvring-side sensor relative to the calculated average of all cylinders, an early indicator of cylinder oil film breakdown before visible scuffing occurs.
trace.trigger: LWM deviation alarm on one cylinder liner exceeding the preset maximum allowed deviation from the multi-cylinder average

procedures.action: Review the cylinder lubrication (Alpha/ME lubricator) feed rate and timing for the affected cylinder, checking ZV 8281/ZT 8282 feedback status.
procedures.why: Inadequate or mistimed cylinder oil feed is the most common cause of localized oil film breakdown and liner temperature rise.

procedures.action: Reduce load on the affected unit if practicable and increase cylinder lubrication feed rate per maker guidance until the temperature trend stabilizes.
procedures.why: Restores adequate oil film thickness to protect against liner/piston ring scuffing.

procedures.action: If temperatures continue to rise or fluctuate erratically, plan for inspection of the liner and piston rings at the earliest safe opportunity.
procedures.why: Confirmed oil film breakdown left unaddressed leads to scuffing damage to the liner and rings, a major mechanical failure.

constraints: LWM alarm and deviation levels are individually optimized per engine during commissioning, based on at least one week of logged data
LWM sensors are located near piston skirt TDC position on manoeuvring and exhaust sides
regulations: Everllence recommendation for LWM data logging over a minimum one-week period or full round trip for calibration
warnings: Increased and fluctuating liner temperature is a recognized precursor sign of oil film breakdown; ignoring it risks consequential scuffing of cylinder liner and piston rings.
outcomes: Unaddressed oil film breakdown can progress to liner/piston ring scuffing, requiring major overhaul.
Early lubrication adjustment based on LWM trend prevents scuffing damage.
key_facts: LWM uses two sensors per liner (manoeuvring and exhaust side) near piston skirt TDC.
Alarm is based on absolute maximum temperature or deviation from the average of all cylinder sensors.
Oil film breakdown signs are increased and fluctuating liner temperatures.

known_issue.failure_mode: localized cylinder oil film breakdown
known_issue.detection_method: LWM temperature deviation alarm from multi-cylinder average

trace.situation: The axial vibration monitor (AVM) registers an abnormal vibration level on the crankshaft axial damper during ahead running above the barred speed range, suggesting possible degradation of the vibration damper itself rather than a torsional resonance condition.
trace.trigger: AVM alarm while engine is running ahead above the barred speed range

procedures.action: Confirm the engine is outside the barred speed range and not running astern before accepting the AVM alarm as valid.
procedures.why: AVM alarm and slowdown functions are intentionally disabled in the barred range and during astern running to prevent nuisance tripping at torsional resonances.

procedures.action: Perform the mechanical guide functional check of the axial vibration damper per maker instructions.
procedures.why: Determines whether the damper itself has degraded (e.g., loss of damping fluid/mechanical wear) causing the elevated vibration.

procedures.action: If the slowdown function activates, allow the configured holding time to elapse before expecting automatic reset, and avoid manual load changes that could cause rapid hunting.
procedures.why: The holding time function is designed to prevent rapid hunting of engine speed following a slowdown event.

constraints: AVM alarm/slowdown must be enabled only when running ahead above the barred speed range
AVM is mandatory for all ME-C10/9 engines including GI/LGI variants
regulations: Everllence requirement for AVM filtration of alarm/slowdown functions to prevent tripping at torsional resonances
warnings: A genuine axial vibration damper failure left unaddressed can lead to severe torsional/axial vibration damage to the crankshaft and bearings.
outcomes: If the damper fault is not corrected, excessive axial vibration can cause crankshaft or bearing damage over time.
Prompt inspection and damper servicing restores normal vibration damping and protects the crank-train.
key_facts: AVM includes a mechanical guide for functional checking of the vibration damper condition.
AVM alarm/slowdown functions are disabled in the barred speed range and during astern running by design.
A holding time delays automatic reset after a slowdown to prevent speed hunting.

known_issue.detection_method: AVM alarm above barred speed range, ahead running

trace.situation: On a plant fitted with exhaust gas bypass (EGB) and a power-management handshake to a waste heat recovery system, the turbocharger speed sensor registers an overspeed condition following an unexpected EGB valve excursion, and the protective response must escalate from slowdown to shutdown per the plant's handshake configuration.
trace.trigger: Turbocharger overspeed alarm (ZT 8801/XS 8817) with WHRS handshake active

procedures.action: Confirm whether the power management/WHRS handshake interface is active and allowing the delayed response (up to 120 s) before shutdown.
procedures.why: Plants with WHRS or shaft generator handshake are designed to use a non-cancellable shutdown rather than a simple slowdown for turbocharger overspeed protection.

procedures.action: Check the EGB valve position feedback and actuator for correct operation during the overspeed event.
procedures.why: A stuck or erratic EGB valve diverting excess exhaust energy to the turbocharger is a primary cause of sudden overspeed.

procedures.action: After the shutdown/slowdown resolves, inspect the turbocharger rotor and bearings for overspeed-related damage before restarting.
procedures.why: Turbocharger overspeed events can cause rotor imbalance or bearing damage even if shutdown occurred within the design margin.

constraints: For EGB/variable TC/power turbine/hybrid TC plants with WHRS or shaft generator handshake, overspeed protection must be a non-cancellable shutdown, not a simple slowdown
Handshake interface may delay the slowdown/shutdown response by up to 120 seconds
regulations: Everllence turbocharger overspeed protection table (Table 18.06.03) defining required protection by plant configuration
warnings: Failure to upgrade overspeed slowdown to a non-cancellable shutdown on handshake-equipped plants can allow turbocharger overspeed to persist beyond safe limits, risking catastrophic rotor failure.
outcomes: If protection logic is misconfigured or ignored, turbocharger overspeed can escalate to rotor burst with risk to personnel and major collateral damage.
Correctly configured non-cancellable shutdown prevents turbocharger destruction and protects the exhaust/scavenge air system.
key_facts: EGB, variable TC, power turbine, hybrid TC, and TC cut-out plants all require turbocharger overspeed slowdown as a minimum.
With WHRS or shaft generator power-management handshake, the required response escalates to a non-cancellable shutdown.
The handshake interface may delay response by up to 120 seconds by design.

known_issue.detection_method: turbocharger speed sensor overspeed alarm (ZT 8801/XS 8817)

trace.situation: On an engine fitted with the load-dependent cylinder liner (LDCL) cooling water system, one cylinder's liner outlet temperature sensor fails, causing the alarm system to lose its ability to apply the correct load-dependent alarm and slowdown breakpoints for that cylinder.
trace.trigger: Loss of signal or erratic reading from a cylinder's LDCL liner outlet temperature sensor

procedures.action: Verify sensor wiring and connections at the affected cylinder's liner outlet temperature transmitter.
procedures.why: A broken or shorted sensor circuit is the most likely cause of signal loss, rather than an actual process upset.

procedures.action: If the sensor cannot be restored quickly, manually monitor the local thermometer for that cylinder liner outlet and compare against the expected 70-130°C load-dependent range.
procedures.why: Provides a manual substitute for the automatic load-dependent alarm/slowdown monitoring on that cylinder until the sensor is repaired.

procedures.action: Avoid rapid load changes on the affected cylinder until the sensor is repaired and automatic protection is restored.
procedures.why: Without the sensor, the breakpoint-based alarm/slowdown logic specific to LDCL cannot react to load-dependent cooling water deviations.

constraints: LDCL liner outlet temperature range may span roughly 70-130°C and is load-dependent
LDCL alarm system must support both upper fixed limits and load-dependent limits with at least one breakpoint
regulations: All 95-50ME-C10/9/-GI/-LGI engines are standard-fitted with LDCL cooling water monitoring
warnings: Operating with a failed LDCL sensor removes automatic protection against overheating or under-cooling of that cylinder liner, risking liner cracking or excessive thermal stress.
outcomes: If uncorrected, loss of load-dependent cooling control on one cylinder can lead to liner thermal stress cracking or accelerated wear.
Prompt sensor repair restores automatic load-dependent protection and even cooling across all cylinders.
key_facts: Each LDCL cylinder liner has its own outlet temperature sensor for load-dependent control.
The LDCL alarm scheme requires two alarm limits and two slowdown limits per cylinder (upper fixed and load-dependent).
LDCL outlet temperature setpoints are commissioned individually per plant, as cooling water temperature is plant-dependent.

known_issue.detection_method: loss of signal/erratic reading on LDCL transmitter

trace.situation: The common fuel oil leakage drain box level alarm activates, indicating leakage collected from one or more high-pressure fuel pipes across the cylinders, but the common drain design does not identify which specific cylinder is leaking.
trace.trigger: Drain box high-level alarm (LS 8006) for fuel oil leakage

procedures.action: Visually inspect each cylinder's high-pressure fuel pipe connections and sealing glands at the earliest safe opportunity, working systematically from cylinder 1.
procedures.why: Since the drain box is common to all cylinders, physical inspection is required to localize the specific leaking connection.

procedures.action: Check for any recent maintenance history (fuel pump/injector work) on specific cylinders that could indicate a torque or seal issue.
procedures.why: Recent disturbance of HP fuel connections is a common cause of a new leak.

procedures.action: Tighten or renew the leaking HP pipe connection/seal per maker torque specifications, and verify the drain box clears after corrective action.
procedures.why: Confirms the leak source has been correctly identified and repaired.

constraints: The fuel oil leakage drain box level alarm (LS 8006) is a mandatory basic-design sensor on all Everllence B&W engines
regulations: IACS/Everllence requirement for HP fuel pipe leakage alarm as standard fitment
warnings: High-pressure fuel oil leakage presents a fire hazard around hot exhaust and turbocharger surfaces; do not delay inspection once the alarm activates.
outcomes: If the leak source is not found and repaired, continued fuel leakage increases fire risk and fuel consumption losses.
Prompt identification and repair of the leaking connection removes the fire hazard and restores normal fuel system integrity.
key_facts: All cylinders share a common HP fuel pipe leakage drain box with a single level alarm (LS 8006).
The alarm does not by itself identify which cylinder is leaking; physical inspection is required.

trace.situation: The piston cooling oil outlet flow switch (FS 8114) on one cylinder fails in the 'flow detected' position, masking an actual loss of piston cooling oil flow that would otherwise trigger a slowdown, creating a risk of undetected piston overheating.
trace.trigger: No flow alarm present despite other indications (rising piston/liner related exhaust temperature) suggesting reduced piston cooling

procedures.action: Cross-check the piston cooling oil outlet temperature (TE 8113) trend for the same cylinder against the flow switch status.
procedures.why: A temperature sensor reading that disagrees with the flow switch status (e.g., rising temperature with no low-flow alarm) indicates the switch may be stuck or failed.

procedures.action: Physically inspect and function-test the flow switch, including manual flow verification if possible, during the next safe opportunity (reduced load/stop).
procedures.why: Confirms whether the switch mechanism is stuck in the 'flow present' position or has a wiring/signal fault.

procedures.action: If the flow switch cannot be confirmed reliable, reduce load on the affected cylinder and increase manual monitoring of piston cooling oil outlet temperature until repaired.
procedures.why: Compensates for loss of the automatic piston cooling oil flow protection (which normally triggers a slowdown on loss of flow).

constraints: FS 8114 (piston cooling oil outlet flow) is a mandatory alarm and slowdown sensor per IACS/Everllence requirements
regulations: IACS and Everllence requirement for piston cooling oil flow switch as alarm and slowdown sensor
warnings: Loss of piston cooling oil flow without detection can rapidly lead to piston crown overheating, seizure, or burn-through if not caught by an alternate means.
outcomes: If undetected, loss of piston cooling flow can cause severe piston damage requiring major repair or replacement.
Early detection through cross-checking with temperature trends and switch testing prevents piston damage.
key_facts: FS 8114 and TE 8113 both monitor piston cooling oil outlet per cylinder and are intended to be cross-checked.
Loss of piston cooling oil flow is normally designed to trigger an automatic slowdown.

known_issue.failure_mode: stuck/failed flow switch masking loss of piston cooling flow
known_issue.detection_method: cross-check of flow switch status against piston cooling oil outlet temperature trend

trace.situation: The lubricating oil differential pressure switch across the main LO filter (PDS 8140) trends upward over several days, indicating progressive filter clogging, well before reaching the alarm setpoint.
trace.trigger: Gradually rising differential pressure reading across the lube oil filter, trending toward the PDS 8140 alarm setpoint

procedures.action: Check filter backflush/cleaning cycle operation (automatic filter type) and verify it is cycling correctly.
procedures.why: Automatic self-cleaning filters that fail to backflush properly will show a steadily rising differential pressure.

procedures.action: Schedule manual cleaning or element replacement of the lube oil filter before the differential pressure reaches the alarm threshold.
procedures.why: Proactive cleaning prevents an unplanned high-differential-pressure alarm and potential unfiltered oil bypass.

procedures.action: Verify the filter bypass valve (if fitted) has not been inadvertently left open, which would mask a true differential pressure problem.
procedures.why: A bypassed filter can mask the real clogging condition while allowing unfiltered oil to reach the engine.

constraints: PDS 8140 differential pressure alarm across the LO filter is a mandatory alarm sensor
regulations: Classification society requirement for lube oil filter differential pressure alarm
warnings: If the filter clogs completely and the bypass valve opens (or fails open), unfiltered oil carrying debris can reach main bearings and journals, causing abrasive wear.
outcomes: If the clogging trend is ignored, the filter may eventually force a bypass condition, risking contamination of bearings with unfiltered oil.
Scheduled cleaning based on the trend avoids an unplanned high-differential-pressure event and maintains oil cleanliness.
key_facts: PDS 8140 monitors differential pressure across the lube oil filter and is a standard alarm point.
Many plants use automatic self-cleaning (e.g., Boll & Kirch) filters with their own failure alarm (XC 1231).

When should the filter be cleaned relative to the PDS 8140 alarm setpoint?

known_issue.failure_mode: progressive lube oil filter clogging
known_issue.detection_method: rising differential pressure trend on PDS 8140

trace.situation: The scavenge air box fire alarm (TT 8610) activates on one cylinder, indicating an abnormal temperature rise in the scavenge air space consistent with a scavenge box fire caused by oil deposit ignition, a serious and time-critical event.
trace.trigger: Scavenge air box high temperature/fire alarm (TT 8610) on a specific cylinder

procedures.action: Immediately reduce engine load/speed per the emergency procedure for scavenge box fire and prepare to stop the engine if temperature continues to rise.
procedures.why: Reducing load lowers combustion air flow and heat generation feeding the fire while assessment proceeds.

procedures.action: Stop the engine, cut off fuel to the affected cylinder if possible, and activate fixed fire-fighting means for the scavenge space per the engine's fire procedure.
procedures.why: A scavenge box fire can escalate rapidly and must be extinguished using the dedicated system rather than opened doors, to avoid explosion from sudden air ingress.

procedures.action: After the fire is confirmed extinguished and the space cooled, open up and inspect for oil deposit buildup, damaged piston rings, or liner issues that initiated the fire before restarting.
procedures.why: Identifies and corrects the root cause (typically excess oil deposits or worn piston rings) before returning the cylinder to service.

constraints: Scavenge air box fire alarm (TT 8610) is a mandatory alarm and slowdown sensor per class/IACS requirements
regulations: IACS/Everllence requirement for scavenge air box fire alarm as both alarm and slowdown function
warnings: Never open scavenge space doors while a fire is suspected active; sudden air ingress can cause a violent flare-up or explosion.
Delayed response to a scavenge fire alarm can lead to extensive damage to piston, liner, and scavenge air system components.
outcomes: If not promptly addressed, a scavenge box fire can escalate to severe damage of the piston, cylinder liner, and surrounding structure.
Prompt load reduction, engine stop, and proper fire-fighting procedure limits damage to the affected cylinder components.
key_facts: TT 8610 is both an alarm and slowdown function for scavenge air box fire per cylinder.
Scavenge fires are typically caused by accumulated oil/carbon deposits igniting in the scavenge space.

Why must scavenge space doors not be opened immediately after a fire alarm?

known_issue.detection_method: scavenge air box fire/high temperature alarm (TT 8610)

trace.situation: The shaftline earthing device alarm (XC 8816) activates, indicating failure of the shaft earthing/grounding brush, which can allow stray electrical currents to pass through the main bearings and propeller shaft bearings, causing electrical pitting damage over time.
trace.trigger: Shaftline earthing device failure alarm (XC 8816)

procedures.action: Inspect the earthing brush assembly for wear, loss of spring tension, or carbon brush contamination/breakage.
procedures.why: Worn or broken brushes are the most common cause of loss of continuous electrical contact to the shaft.

procedures.action: Clean the slip ring surface on the shaft and verify brush contact pressure and alignment.
procedures.why: Oil film or carbon dust buildup on the slip ring can prevent proper electrical continuity even with a serviceable brush.

procedures.action: Replace the brush or repair the grounding device as needed and confirm resistance/continuity measurement meets the maker's specification before returning to full service.
procedures.why: Confirms effective electrical grounding has been restored to prevent stray current damage to bearings.

constraints: Shaftline earthing device (XC 8816) is a standard monitored alarm point under 'Miscellaneous' functions
regulations: Classification society requirement for shaft earthing arrangement to prevent stray current bearing damage
warnings: Prolonged loss of shaft earthing allows stray currents (e.g., from cathodic protection systems or electrical induction) to pass through bearing oil films, causing spark erosion/pitting damage to bearing surfaces.
outcomes: If uncorrected, stray current damage can progressively pit main and thrust bearing surfaces, leading to premature bearing failure.
Timely brush/slip-ring repair restores proper grounding and prevents electrical bearing damage.
key_facts: The shaftline earthing device provides a continuous electrical path to prevent stray currents from passing through bearing oil films.
XC 8816 is the monitored alarm point for this device's operational status.

known_issue.failure_mode: earthing brush wear/loss of contact
known_issue.detection_method: shaftline earthing device alarm (XC 8816)

trace.situation: Exhaust gas temperature readings after the exhaust valve (TT 8702) show one cylinder deviating significantly above the average of all cylinders, a slowdown-relevant condition indicating possible fuel injection timing fault, injector wear, or combustion imbalance on that unit.
trace.trigger: Exhaust gas temperature deviation alarm for one cylinder relative to calculated average of all cylinders

procedures.action: Cross-check the PMI Auto-tuning cylinder pressure data (pmax, pcomp) for the affected cylinder against the engine control system reference values.
procedures.why: Combustion pressure deviation data from PMI directly indicates whether fuel injection or valve timing is causing the imbalance.

procedures.action: Inspect fuel injection valve condition and exhaust valve timing/sealing for the affected cylinder at the next opportunity.
procedures.why: Worn injector nozzles or an exhaust valve not seating/timing correctly are common root causes of localized exhaust temperature rise.

procedures.action: If the deviation continues to increase toward the slowdown threshold, reduce engine load to limit thermal stress on the affected cylinder until repairs can be made.
procedures.why: High exhaust gas temperature deviation risks exhaust valve and turbocharger inlet overheating if combustion imbalance is not corrected.

constraints: Exhaust gas temperature deviation alarm and slowdown (TT 8702) compares individual cylinder reading against calculated average of all cylinders
regulations: Everllence/class requirement for exhaust gas temperature deviation alarm and slowdown per cylinder
warnings: Persistent uncorrected exhaust temperature deviation can lead to exhaust valve burning, turbocharger inlet overheating, or further combustion-related damage.
outcomes: If the imbalance is not corrected, localized overheating can damage the exhaust valve, piston crown, or turbocharger over time.
Timely injector/valve correction restores balanced combustion across all cylinders and protects hot-section components.
key_facts: TT 8702 (exhaust gas after exhaust valve) has both an absolute high alarm and a deviation-from-average alarm/slowdown function.
PMI Auto-tuning provides continuous cylinder pressure data used to cross-check combustion-related exhaust temperature deviations.

known_issue.failure_mode: cylinder combustion imbalance (injector/valve related)

trace.situation: The common alarm system power supply unit reports a battery discharging condition (XC 2910) without yet losing the main supply, indicating the backup battery charger has failed and the alarm system's uninterruptible backup capability is degrading.
trace.trigger: Battery discharging alarm (XC 2910) on the alarm system power supply unit

procedures.action: Verify main AC supply to the alarm system power unit is present and check charger output voltage/current against specification.
procedures.why: A failed battery charger, not necessarily a main supply loss, is the most common cause of a discharging battery alarm while main power is still present.

procedures.action: Inspect battery condition (terminal voltage, electrolyte/age) and replace if due for renewal per maintenance schedule.
procedures.why: Aged or degraded batteries lose capacity and will discharge even under normal float charging if near end of life.

procedures.action: If the charger cannot be restored promptly, treat the alarm system as having reduced backup autonomy and avoid relying on UMS unattended periods until resolved.
procedures.why: Loss of battery backup capability means a main supply failure (XC 2909) would immediately disable the alarm system with no bridging power.

constraints: Power supply units to the alarm system must include monitored main supply failure, battery discharging, and battery protective device tripped alarms (XC 2909/2910/2911)
regulations: Classification society requirement for alarm system power supply monitoring including battery backup status
warnings: Running UMS with a degraded alarm system battery backup risks total loss of alarm monitoring capability during any subsequent main power interruption.
outcomes: If uncorrected, a subsequent main power failure combined with a depleted battery can cause complete loss of engine alarm monitoring.
Prompt charger/battery repair restores full backup redundancy for the alarm and monitoring system.
key_facts: XC 2909 indicates main power supply failure; XC 2910 indicates battery discharging; XC 2911 indicates battery protective device tripped.
The alarm system design relies on battery backup to maintain monitoring during a main supply interruption.

question_seeds.text: What should be checked first when the alarm system battery discharging alarm activates?
Why is a battery discharging alarm significant even while main power is still available?

known_issue.failure_mode: battery charger failure / backup power degradation
known_issue.detection_method: battery discharging alarm (XC 2910)

trace.situation: The turbocharger lubricating oil outlet temperature (TT 8117) trends upward independent of overall engine load, suggesting developing turbocharger bearing distress rather than a normal load-related temperature rise.
trace.trigger: Turbocharger lube oil outlet temperature alarm (TT 8117) not correlating with engine load changes

procedures.action: Check turbocharger lube oil inlet pressure (PT 8103) and verify adequate supply flow to the turbocharger.
procedures.why: Reduced oil supply pressure or flow is a common cause of rising outlet temperature due to inadequate bearing cooling.

procedures.action: Listen/inspect for abnormal turbocharger noise, vibration, or rotor imbalance indicators, and check turbocharger speed trend (ZT 8801) for irregularities.
procedures.why: Bearing distress often presents with both rising oil outlet temperature and changes in rotor dynamic behavior.

procedures.action: If temperature continues rising toward the alarm threshold, reduce engine load to lower turbocharger speed and thermal loading, and plan for turbocharger bearing inspection.
procedures.why: Reducing speed/load lowers heat generation at the bearing while inspection and repair are arranged, preventing bearing seizure.

constraints: TT 8117 (turbocharger lube oil outlet temperature) is a mandatory alarm sensor; some configurations also apply this as a slowdown function
regulations: Class/IACS requirement for turbocharger lubricating oil outlet temperature alarm
warnings: Undetected turbocharger bearing distress can progress rapidly to bearing seizure, rotor-to-casing contact, and catastrophic turbocharger failure.
outcomes: If the trend is ignored, turbocharger bearing failure can cause extensive rotor and casing damage, potentially trapping debris in the exhaust/air path.
Early load reduction and bearing inspection based on the temperature trend prevents catastrophic turbocharger failure.
key_facts: TT 8117 monitors turbocharger lubricating oil outlet temperature, varying by turbocharger design (some makers monitor differently).
Turbocharger bearing distress often correlates with abnormal lube oil outlet temperature rise independent of engine load.

known_issue.failure_mode: developing turbocharger bearing distress
known_issue.detection_method: turbocharger lube oil outlet temperature trend (TT 8117) independent of load

trace.situation: The crankcase oil mist detector's rotary sampling head intermittently fails to complete a full sampling cycle across all cylinders, resulting in delayed detection times for any given cylinder's crankcase atmosphere, even though the unit itself reports no fault.
trace.trigger: Extended or irregular sampling cycle time observed during routine OMD function test, without an active fault or mist alarm

procedures.action: Perform the maker's recommended functional/cycle-time test on the OMD rotary sampling mechanism.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the sampling head is mechanically binding or the drive motor is degraded, which extends detection latency per cylinder.

procedures.action: Inspect and lubricate/service the rotary sampling head drive mechanism per the maintenance schedule.
procedures.why: Mechanical wear or lack of lubrication in the rotary mechanism is a common cause of slowed or irregular sampling cycles.

procedures.action: If cycle time cannot be restored to specification, treat the OMD as degraded and increase manual engine room rounds focusing on crankcase door temperature checks until repaired.
procedures.why: Compensates for the increased time-to-detection risk posed by a slow sampling cycle.

constraints: OMD sampling cycle time across all cylinders must meet the maker's specified detection response time for UMS compliance
regulations: Classification society UMS requirement for timely crankcase mist detection across all cylinders
warnings: A slowed sampling cycle increases the time between an actual mist event occurring in a given cylinder and the alarm being raised, reducing the safety margin before an explosion risk.
outcomes: If left unresolved, delayed detection could allow a developing crankcase event in one cylinder to progress further before being alarmed.
Restoring normal sampling cycle time returns the OMD to its designed detection response time, maintaining full crankcase explosion protection.
key_facts: Rotary-type OMD units sample each cylinder's crankcase atmosphere sequentially via a rotating sampling head.
Detection latency increases if the sampling cycle time extends beyond the maker's design specification.

question_seeds.text: How is OMD sampling cycle time verified to be within specification?
Why does a slow rotary sampling head matter even if no mist alarm has occurred?

known_issue.failure_mode: degraded rotary sampling head extending detection latency
known_issue.detection_method: routine OMD cycle-time functional test

trace.situation: The EMS network interface between the PMI Auto-tuning system and the Engine Control System drops intermittently, interrupting the closed-loop adjustment of fuel injection and valve timing based on measured cylinder pressures, causing the engine to revert to default/open-loop combustion settings.

procedures.action: Check the EMS network topology (LAN connections, switches, EMS MOP industrial PC) for loose connections or hardware faults per the EMS manager diagnostic screen.
procedures.why: The EMS manager is specifically designed to provide network and interface status monitoring to pinpoint connectivity faults.

procedures.action: Restart the affected EMS application or the EMS MOP per the vendor's recommended recovery procedure, verifying PMI online cylinder pressure readings resume after restart.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the fault is a software/communication hang rather than a hardware wiring fault.

procedures.action: If the interface cannot be restored, confirm the ECS has correctly reverted to its default/open-loop combustion reference values and monitor cylinder pressures manually via local PMI readings until repaired.
procedures.why: Ensures the engine continues operating safely without closed-loop auto-tuning, using manual oversight of combustion parameters instead.

constraints: PMI Auto-tuning provides closed-loop input to ECS for fuel injection and valve timing adjustment to maintain target pmax
EMS is implemented as a hardened platform intended to be robust against interface faults
regulations: Everllence EMS design requirement for continuous performance tuning integration with ECS
warnings: Extended operation without PMI Auto-tuning closed-loop correction can allow cylinder pressure deviations between units to go uncorrected, risking uneven combustion loading.

trace.situation: The jacket cooling water differential pressure measurement across the engine (PDT 8403) trends downward, indicating reduced cooling water flow likely due to partial blockage or scale buildup in the jacket cooling circuit, well before reaching the slowdown-relevant alarm threshold.
trace.trigger: Gradual decline in jacket cooling water differential pressure across the engine over an extended period

procedures.action: Verify jacket cooling water pump performance and confirm pump discharge pressure/flow is within normal design parameters.
procedures.why: A declining pump condition can mimic a blockage by reducing overall system flow and differential pressure.

procedures.action: Inspect and clean strainers/filters in the jacket cooling water circuit and check for scale buildup in heat exchangers or cylinder jackets based on water treatment chemistry records.
procedures.why: Scale deposits from inadequate cooling water treatment are a common cause of progressively reduced flow/differential pressure.

procedures.action: Review and correct cooling water treatment dosing (corrosion inhibitor/anti-scale chemicals) per the maker's water quality specification.
procedures.why: Addresses the root cause of scale formation to prevent recurrence of reduced cooling flow.

constraints: PDT 8403 (jacket cooling water across engine) is a mandatory alarm sensor, calculated from PT 8401 and PT 8413 for non-LDCL engines
regulations: Class/IACS requirement for jacket cooling water pressure/differential pressure monitoring
warnings: Continued decline in cooling water flow can lead to localized overheating of cylinder liners and covers, risking cracking or exhaust valve burning if not corrected.
outcomes: If scale buildup is not addressed, cooling flow may degrade further to the point of triggering alarm/slowdown and risking thermal damage to cylinder components.
Proper water treatment correction and strainer cleaning restores normal cooling flow and protects cylinder liners/covers from thermal stress.
key_facts: PDT 8403 is derived from jacket cooling water inlet (PT 8401) and outlet common pipe (PT 8413) pressures for non-LDCL engines.
Cooling water treatment chemistry directly affects scale formation rate in the jacket cooling circuit.

How is scale buildup in the jacket cooling circuit confirmed and corrected?

known_issue.detection_method: declining jacket cooling water differential pressure trend (PDT 8403)

trace.situation: A redundant sensor pair for a critical shutdown parameter (e.g., main starting valve position, ZS 1111-A/B) shows disagreement between the A and B channels, indicating one sensor has failed while the galvanically separated redundancy is masking the fault from a simple single-channel alarm view.
trace.trigger: Disagreement/deviation alarm between redundant A/B sensor channels for a safety-critical function

procedures.action: Identify which of the A/B channels is reading incorrectly by comparing against an independent local indicator or manual verification of the actual physical state.
procedures.why: Confirms which sensor has failed so the correct one can be relied upon and the faulty one isolated/repaired.

procedures.action: Report the faulty channel to the responsible engineer and schedule replacement/repair without delay, keeping the system on the confirmed-good channel in the interim if the control logic allows.
procedures.why: Maintains the safety function via the remaining good sensor while restoring full redundancy as soon as possible.

procedures.action: Verify the shutdown/safety system's independent electrical separation requirement is still met after any temporary wiring changes.
procedures.why: Classification rules require shutdown sensors to be electrically separated from other systems, or to use galvanically separated circuits even when physically combined; any repair must preserve this separation.

constraints: Shutdown system sensors must be electrically separated from other systems, or use galvanically separated circuits sharing a common sensor
Redundant sensors for the same measuring point are identified with suffix letters A, B, C, etc.
regulations: IACS/classification requirement for electrical separation of shutdown sensor circuits
warnings: Operating on a single remaining channel without timely repair of the failed redundant sensor leaves the safety function with no further backup if that channel also fails.
outcomes: If the faulty channel is not repaired, a subsequent failure of the remaining good sensor would leave the safety-critical function entirely unmonitored.
Prompt repair restores full redundant protection for the safety-critical function.
key_facts: Redundant sensors sharing a measuring point use suffix letters (A, B, C) per the engine's instrument identification scheme.
Shutdown sensors must be electrically separated or galvanically isolated even when sharing a physical sensor housing.

Why is electrical separation required between redundant shutdown sensor channels?

known_issue.failure_mode: disagreement between redundant A/B safety sensor channels
known_issue.detection_method: redundant channel comparison/deviation alarm

trace.situation: The CoCoS-EDS data logging application stops recording engine condition trend data due to a storage or database fault on the EMS MOP, silently degrading the ability to perform condition-based troubleshooting and preventive maintenance planning, while real-time alarms continue to function normally.
trace.trigger: Absence of expected trend data/reports from CoCoS-EDS during a routine review, with no corresponding AMS alarm since real-time alarm functions are unaffected

procedures.action: Check the EMS MOP storage capacity, database service status, and any logged error messages for CoCoS-EDS.
procedures.why: Storage exhaustion or a database service crash is a common cause of silent data logging failure that does not affect live AMS alarms.

procedures.action: Restart the CoCoS-EDS application/service per vendor procedure and verify new data points are being logged and retrievable.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the issue was a recoverable software fault rather than a hardware storage failure.

procedures.action: If data loss has occurred, document the gap period and rely on local instrument logs/manual readings for that interval during any subsequent troubleshooting or maintenance review.
procedures.why: Ensures continuity of engine condition records despite the logging gap, supporting future preventive maintenance decisions.

constraints: CoCoS-EDS is intended for data logging, condition monitoring/reporting, and operational troubleshooting support, separate from the real-time AMS alarm function
regulations: Everllence EMS design intent for CoCoS-EDS as a preventive maintenance and troubleshooting support tool
warnings: A logging outage does not stop the engine from running safely (real-time alarms still function), but it removes historical trend visibility needed to catch slowly developing problems between inspections.
outcomes: If unresolved, loss of trend data reduces the ability to detect slow-developing issues (e.g., gradual wear trends) before they reach alarm thresholds.
Prompt restoration of CoCoS-EDS logging preserves the full condition-monitoring history needed for effective preventive maintenance.
key_facts: CoCoS-EDS performs data logging, condition monitoring/reporting, and troubleshooting support, distinct from the AMS real-time alarm function.

trace.situation: During a routine scavenge space inspection, the crew finds an abnormal film of oil on the piston rod and scavenge air receiver walls below the stuffing box. The oil scraper rings in the lower housing are suspected to have lost sealing effect, allowing cylinder/crankcase oil to migrate upward into the scavenge air space.
trace.trigger: Oil residue and sludge accumulation observed on scavenge space floor during routine inspection

procedures.action: Shut down and isolate the unit, open the stuffing box inspection cover, and withdraw the oil scraper ring set for visual inspection.
procedures.why: Direct inspection confirms whether scraper ring wear, broken segments, or loss of spring tension is causing the oil carryover.

procedures.action: Measure scraper ring radial clearance and spring tension against maker tolerances; renew any ring segment outside limits.
procedures.why: Worn or weak scraper rings cannot maintain contact with the piston rod surface and allow oil to pass into the scavenge space.

procedures.action: Check piston rod surface finish for scoring or corrosion pitting in way of the scraper ring travel.
procedures.why: A damaged rod surface will rapidly re-wear new rings and must be polished or the rod replaced before re-commissioning.

constraints: Oil scraper ring radial clearance must be within maker tolerance (typically 0.3-0.5 mm) before re-assembly
Scavenge space must be kept free of accumulated oil to avoid scavenge fire risk
regulations: MAN B&W Instruction Book - Piston Rod Stuffing Box maintenance interval and inspection requirement
Classification society requirement for scavenge space fire-risk housekeeping
warnings: Accumulated oil in the scavenge space combined with hot surfaces can lead to a scavenge space fire
Continued operation with worn scraper rings accelerates crankcase oil loss and contaminates scavenge air system
outcomes: If uncorrected, oil accumulation in the scavenge space increases scavenge fire risk and oil consumption rises
Renewing worn scraper rings restores the oil-return path to the crankcase sump and eliminates scavenge contamination
key_facts: The oil scraper ring set returns cylinder/crankcase oil draining down the piston rod back to the crankcase
Scavenge space oil accumulation is a recognized precursor to scavenge fires on two-stroke engines

trace.situation: While running at normal load, the oil mist detector registers an increased opacity difference in the atmosphere sample from one crankcase compartment, consistent with early frictional heating of a bearing surface generating fine oil mist before any catastrophic failure occurs.
trace.trigger: OMD high oil mist density alarm on a specific cylinder/crankcase compartment

procedures.action: Respond immediately to the OMD slowdown (or shutdown if GL-classed) and reduce load without delay.
procedures.why: Rising oil mist density indicates localized overheating that can precede a crankcase explosion.

procedures.action: Do not open crankcase inspection doors until the mandatory cooling/venting period has elapsed.
procedures.why: Opening doors while hot surfaces and mist-laden air are still present risks triggering a secondary explosion.

procedures.action: After cooling, open the crankcase and visually inspect bearings, guide shoes and crank webs for scoring, discoloration or metal debris.
procedures.why: Visual inspection identifies which component generated the mist and the extent of damage.

procedures.action: Cross-check BWM and BTM trend data for the affected unit before returning to service.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the event was mechanical wear, lubrication starvation, or a sensor anomaly.

constraints: OMD alarm response (slowdown, or shutdown for GL-classed vessels) is mandatory and cannot be bypassed
Crankcase doors must remain closed for the specified minimum cooling-down period after an OMD alarm
regulations: Everllence has required OMD fitment on all two-stroke plants since 1990 for crankcase explosion prevention
Germanischer Lloyd requires shutdown (not slowdown) on OMD alarm
warnings: Opening the crankcase immediately after an OMD alarm risks a secondary explosion from residual hot gases
Ignoring an OMD alarm can lead to a full crankcase explosion with fire, severe injury, and total engine loss
outcomes: If ignored, localized bearing overheating can progress to steel-to-steel contact and crankcase explosion
If corrected promptly, the mechanical fault is caught and repaired before catastrophic bearing seizure
key_facts: The OMD compares the opacity of sampled crankcase atmosphere against reference atmospheric air
OMD response is a slowdown by default, upgraded to shutdown for GL class and for shop trials
OMD units are located on the manoeuvring side of the engine for personnel safety

trace.situation: The oil mist detector's sampling heads and pipework become fouled with oil residue and carbon over time, causing either repeated nuisance alarms unrelated to actual bearing condition, or a detector failure state that leaves the crankcase without reliable mist detection.
trace.trigger: XS 8814 oil mist detector failure alarm, or repeated OMD alarms with no corresponding bearing wear/temperature trend

procedures.action: Isolate and clean the OMD sampling heads, pipework and optical measuring track per maker instructions.
procedures.why: Fouling on the optical path is the most common cause of erratic readings and false failure states.

procedures.action: Check sampling pipe routing for condensate traps or blockages.
procedures.why: Moisture or oil accumulation in sample lines distorts opacity readings.

procedures.action: Verify calibration against clean reference (atmospheric) air.
procedures.why: Confirms the detector baseline has not drifted.

procedures.action: Replace the detector optics/sensor module if drift or repeated failures persist after cleaning.
procedures.why: A degraded sensor cannot be trusted to detect a genuine mist event.

constraints: OMD must remain operational and connected to the shutdown system for shop trials, and to alarm/slowdown in service
UMS certification requires functioning crankcase explosion protection at all times
regulations: Everllence policy mandates OMD on all plants since 1990
Classification societies require functioning OMD for UMS notation
warnings: Operating with a degraded or unreliable OMD leaves the crankcase without explosion-precursor detection
Disabling or bypassing a nuisance-alarming OMD without root-cause correction is not permitted
outcomes: If left uncorrected, a genuine mist event could go undetected until catastrophic bearing failure occurs
If corrected, reliable early-warning protection against crankcase explosion is restored
key_facts: XS 8814 specifically alarms OMD detector failure, separate from XS 8813 mist detection alarm
Fouled sampling optics is the most frequent cause of OMD reliability issues
Several OMD makes exist (Graviner, Visatron, MD-SX, etc.) with similar maintenance needs

trace.situation: Bearing wear monitoring proximity sensors on one crank-train unit show a gradual increase in measured clearance over several weeks, approaching the first high-wear alarm threshold, indicating progressive mechanical wear in a main, crank or crosshead bearing well before any audible or thermal symptoms appear.
trace.trigger: BWM first-level high-wear/deviation alarm shown on the alarm panel for a specific cylinder unit

procedures.action: Review the BWM trend history for the affected unit over the preceding weeks.
procedures.why: Establishes the rate of wear progression and whether it is linear or accelerating.

procedures.action: Cross-check bearing temperature monitoring (BTM) data and lube oil cleanliness/water-in-oil readings for the same unit.
procedures.why: Correlating data helps identify whether wear is due to lubrication starvation, contamination, or surface fatigue.

procedures.action: Reduce load on the engine if the trend approaches the second (slowdown) alarm level.
procedures.why: Reducing bearing loading slows the wear rate and buys time before steel-to-steel contact.

procedures.action: Plan a crankcase inspection of the affected bearing at the next safe opportunity.
procedures.why: Confirms actual condition and allows corrective bearing renewal before journal damage occurs.

constraints: BWM has two alarm levels: first level panel-only, second level activates automatic slowdown
Everllence states unscheduled open-up inspections are unnecessary if BWM is installed and trusted, but confirmation inspection is still prudent at alarm
regulations: BWM is standard fitment on ME/ME-C/-GI/-LGI engines per Everllence design
warnings: If wear is allowed to progress past the second alarm level without action, steel-to-steel contact can damage the journal and bearing housing irreparably
outcomes: If ignored, progressive wear leads to bearing seizure, journal scoring, and a major unscheduled overhaul
If corrected, the bearing can be renewed on a planned basis before journal damage occurs
key_facts: BWM uses two proximity sensors (forward/aft) per cylinder unit targeting the guide shoe bottom end at BDC
BWM precision is sufficient to alarm well before steel-to-steel contact
Available BWM systems include XTS-W (AMOT), BDMS (Dr. E. Horn), BWCM (Kongsberg), among others

trace.situation: The bearing temperature monitoring system shows a steadily rising oil outlet temperature from a crosshead bearing, exceeding the first alarm level, likely caused by a partial restriction in the bearing's lube oil supply or the onset of surface distress on the bearing overlayer.
trace.trigger: First-level high-temperature alarm on crosshead bearing oil outlet (BTM)

procedures.action: Verify lube oil supply pressure and flow to the affected crosshead bearing.
procedures.why: A restricted supply line directly reduces cooling/lubrication to the bearing surface.

procedures.action: Check lube oil cleanliness and water-in-oil readings for signs of contamination.
procedures.why: Water contamination accelerates corrosive wear of the crosshead overlayer, raising local temperature.

procedures.action: Reduce engine load to lessen bearing loading while investigation continues.
procedures.why: Lower load reduces frictional heat generation and buys time before the second (slowdown) threshold is reached.

procedures.action: Schedule an inspection of the bearing at the next opportunity if the temperature does not stabilize.
procedures.why: Confirms whether surface wiping or overlayer damage has already occurred.

constraints: Two BTM alarm levels apply: first level panel alarm, second level activates slowdown
regulations: BTM is an approved crankcase/bearing protection system recognized by classification societies alongside OMD and BWM
warnings: Continuing to operate with rising crosshead bearing temperature risks wiping of the white-metal/overlayer surface and subsequent catastrophic bearing failure
outcomes: If uncorrected, bearing overlayer wiping can progress to crosshead pin seizure
If corrected, early intervention prevents irreversible bearing damage and allows planned repair
key_facts: BTM measures either bearing shell/housing temperature directly or sampled return oil temperature depending on system design
Crosshead bearings are uniquely vulnerable to water-contamination corrosion due to their overlayer design
Two alarm levels apply to both shell/housing and oil-outlet temperature measurement methods

trace.situation: The water-in-oil monitoring system shows a rising water activity (aw) value on the main lubricating oil system, crossing the 0.5 high alarm threshold and continuing to climb toward 0.9 within a short period, consistent with an active water leak into the LO system rather than slow accumulation.
trace.trigger: WIOM aw = 0.5 high alarm, rapidly trending toward aw = 0.9 high-high alarm

procedures.action: Take a manual oil sample and send for laboratory water-content confirmation while continuing to monitor the WIOM trend.
procedures.why: Confirms the sensor reading and quantifies actual water content for decision-making.

procedures.action: Inspect jacket cooling water coolers, piston cooling oil coolers and any LO cooler for internal leakage into the oil side.
procedures.why: These are the most common sources of water ingress into the LO system.

procedures.action: Run the lube oil purifier/centrifuge continuously to remove free water while the source is traced.
procedures.why: Reduces active water content and protects bearings while repairs are organized.

procedures.action: Isolate and repair the identified leak source before resuming normal operation.
procedures.why: Eliminates the root cause rather than only treating the symptom.

constraints: aw = 0.5 corresponds to approximately 0.2% water content and 50% of the saturation point
aw = 0.9 is the high-high alarm level indicating near-saturation and imminent free water risk
regulations: WIOM with aw-type sensor is standard fitment on all Everllence B&W engines
warnings: If aw reaches saturation (free water present), acute corrosive wear of the crosshead bearing overlayer can occur rapidly
outcomes: If uncorrected, free water in the LO system causes rapid, irreparable crosshead bearing corrosion damage
If corrected promptly, bearing damage is avoided and the oil can be reconditioned
key_facts: The aw sensor measures water activity on a 0-1 scale independent of lube oil age or additive package
A fast rise from aw=0.5 to aw=0.9 is itself diagnostic of an active leak rather than gradual condensation
Main, thrust and crank pin bearings can also suffer irreparable water damage, though by a different, less acute mechanism than crosshead bearings

trace.situation: Liner wall monitoring sensors on one cylinder show increasing and fluctuating temperature readings deviating from the average of all units, an early indicator that the cylinder oil film is beginning to break down on that liner before any scuffing has occurred.
trace.trigger: LWM deviation alarm on one cylinder liner, temperature trend fluctuating above the calculated fleet average

procedures.action: Increase the cylinder lubrication feed rate for the affected unit per the lubricator's load-dependent program.
procedures.why: Restores adequate oil film thickness to prevent metal-to-metal contact.

procedures.action: Check cylinder oil quality, feed timing and lubricator (Alpha/ME) solenoid valve function for that unit.
procedures.why: A malfunctioning lubricator feed is a common root cause of localized oil film breakdown.

procedures.action: Reduce load on the engine if temperature fluctuation does not stabilize after feed rate adjustment.
procedures.why: Lower load reduces thermal and mechanical stress on the liner while the film re-establishes.

procedures.action: Inspect the liner and piston rings for early scuffing marks at the next opportunity.
procedures.why: Confirms whether damage has already begun despite the corrective feed adjustment.

constraints: Alarm/deviation thresholds are individually commissioned per cylinder using at least one week of logged baseline data
regulations: LWM system interfaces to the ship alarm system per Everllence design for early scuffing-risk warning
warnings: If oil film breakdown is not corrected, consequential scuffing of the liner and piston rings can occur, potentially seizing the piston
outcomes: If ignored, localized oil film failure can progress to liner scuffing and major cylinder unit damage
If corrected, increased lubrication restores the oil film and avoids mechanical damage
key_facts: LWM uses two sensors per liner near TDC piston skirt position on manoeuvring and exhaust sides
Rising and fluctuating temperature is the characteristic signature of oil film breakdown, not a steady rise
Alarm setpoints are optimized per engine during commissioning by logging normal operating temperature trends

procedures.action: Verify the AVM filtering/disable logic settings for the barred speed range and astern running in the alarm and safety system.

procedures.why: Rules out an actual damper fault as the cause of elevated readings.

procedures.action: Recalibrate or correct the AVM interface logic with the safety system per Everllence specification.
procedures.why: Ensures the holding-time and barred-range filtering function as designed to prevent nuisance trips.

trace.situation: The plant is fitted with an exhaust gas bypass turbocharger and has a power management system handshake with the shaft generator/WHRS, but the turbocharger overspeed protection was left configured as a cancellable slowdown rather than the required non-cancellable shutdown, discovered during a safety system function test.
trace.trigger: Safety system audit/function test reveals turbocharger overspeed function configured as slowdown instead of shutdown on a handshake-equipped plant

procedures.action: Reconfigure the safety system so turbocharger overspeed triggers a non-cancellable shutdown rather than a slowdown, per the applicable plant configuration table.
procedures.why: Handshake delays of up to 120 seconds for WHRS/shaft generator trips mean a cancellable slowdown may not act in time to prevent overspeed damage.

procedures.action: Test the handshake interface between the power management system and the engine safety system to confirm correct delay and override behavior.
procedures.why: Verifies the interface does not inadvertently suppress the shutdown command.

procedures.action: Verify turbocharger speed sensor (ZT8801/XS8817) calibration and alarm threshold settings.
procedures.why: Accurate speed sensing is essential for the protection function to activate at the correct limit.

constraints: Plants with EGB, variable turbocharger, power turbine, hybrid turbocharger, turbocharger cut-out, or EGR combined with a power management handshake require turbocharger overspeed protection upgraded to non-cancellable shutdown, not slowdown
regulations: Everllence turbocharger overspeed protection requirement per plant configuration table 18.06.03
warnings: A cancellable slowdown on a handshake-equipped plant may be overridden or delayed, allowing the turbocharger to reach destructive overspeed and risking rotor burst
outcomes: If uncorrected, a handshake delay combined with an incorrectly configured slowdown risks turbocharger overspeed damage or rotor failure
If corrected, the non-cancellable shutdown reliably protects the turbocharger regardless of handshake delay
key_facts: Handshake interfaces with WHRS or shaft generator may delay slowdown response by up to 120 seconds
EGR system trips can cause a sudden energy surge to the turbocharger requiring overspeed protection

procedures.action: Allow the automatic slowdown (or shutdown if GL-classed) to take effect and do not override it.

procedures.why: These components are the typical sources of frictional heat that vaporize lubricating oil into mist.

procedures.action: Verify lubricating oil supply pressure and flow to the affected bearing, and check filter condition.
procedures.why: Oil starvation or restricted flow is a common root cause of localized overheating generating oil mist.

constraints: OMD is mandatory standard equipment on all plants since 1990

Prompt slowdown, cooling period, and inspection isolates the frictional source before mist reaches explosive concentration

procedures.why: Engine safety is not dependent on EMS; however extended loss of CoCoS-EDS condition monitoring reduces troubleshooting and preventive maintenance capability.

constraints: EMS is a condition monitoring and data logging layer; basic engine safety/control remains with ECS independent of EMS
regulations: EMS manager provides network and interface monitoring per Everllence EMS design specification
warnings: Extended EMS outage reduces early-warning condition monitoring capability, increasing the risk of undetected gradual engine degradation
outcomes: If uncorrected, loss of CoCoS-EDS trending and PMI feedback integration can delay detection of developing engine problems
Restoring the EMS network re-establishes full condition monitoring, data logging, and closed-loop tuning feedback
key_facts: EMS is executed on a dedicated industrial PC (EMS MOP) designed to be robust against virus threats and unauthorized access
EMS includes PMI Auto-tuning, CoCoS-EDS, and EMS manager applications, with an optional interface to the ship's AMS

Why does an EMS network fault not necessarily compromise basic engine safety and control?

trace.situation: A sensor used commonly for alarm, slow down, and remote indication functions fails in a way that masks a genuine upper-limit exceedance, such as the lubricating oil inlet pressure transmitter, raising concern over whether the shutdown system's galvanic separation is still intact and reliable.
trace.trigger: Discrepancy between local pressure gauge reading and remote alarm/shutdown system indication for lubricating oil inlet pressure

procedures.action: Cross-check the local pressure gauge (PI 8108) against the remote transmitter reading (PT 8108) and the separate shutdown sensor (PS/PT 8109) for the same measuring point.
procedures.why: The shutdown function requires either an independent sensor or a common sensor with galvanically separated terminals; comparing readings verifies whether the discrepancy is in the alarm channel, the shutdown channel, or both.

procedures.action: If only the alarm/remote indication channel is faulty while the shutdown channel reads correctly, continue safe operation but flag the alarm channel for repair.
procedures.why: The galvanic separation design ensures the shutdown protection function can remain intact even if the alarm/indication channel fails.

procedures.action: If both channels show discrepancy or the shutdown channel itself is suspect, reduce load and arrange manual monitoring of lube oil pressure until the sensor is repaired or replaced.
procedures.why: Loss of reliable shutdown protection for a critical parameter requires compensating manual surveillance to maintain engine safety.

procedures.action: Test and recalibrate the affected sensor/terminal circuit according to the sensor manufacturer's procedure before returning to full automatic reliance.
procedures.why: Confirms the galvanic separation and signal integrity are restored before trusting the automatic shutdown function again.

constraints: Shutdown sensors must be electrically separated from alarm/monitoring sensors, either independently or via galvanically separated terminals on a common sensor
regulations: IACS requirement allows common sensors for alarm, slow down, and remote indication, but shutdown sensors require independent circuits or galvanic separation
warnings: A fault that compromises the galvanic separation between alarm and shutdown circuits can lead to a single-point failure disabling both protective functions simultaneously
outcomes: If uncorrected, a genuine low lubricating oil pressure event could fail to trigger the shutdown, risking severe bearing damage from oil starvation
Verifying and restoring proper sensor separation ensures the shutdown function remains independently reliable
key_facts: PT 8108 serves alarm/remote indication while PS/PT 8109 is the dedicated shutdown sensor for lubricating oil inlet pressure and thrust bearing
Shutdown circuits must use independent sensors or galvanically separated terminals per class design requirement

question_seeds.text: Why must the shutdown sensor circuit be galvanically separated from the alarm/indication circuit even when using a common sensor?
What is the correct response if a discrepancy is found between the lube oil pressure alarm channel and the shutdown channel?
Which specific sensors are involved in lubricating oil inlet pressure alarm versus shutdown monitoring?

known_issue.system: monitoring and alarms - shutdown system sensor integrity
known_issue.failure_mode: compromised galvanic separation or fault in shared alarm/shutdown sensor circuit
known_issue.detection_method: cross-check discrepancy between local gauge, alarm transmitter, and shutdown sensor readings

trace.situation: The scavenge air box fire alarm activates on a cylinder, indicating abnormally high temperature in the scavenge air space that is a known early warning sign of a scavenge air fire, typically caused by accumulated oil deposits igniting from piston ring blow-by or lubrication excess.
trace.trigger: Scavenge air box fire alarm, cylinder-specific (TE 8610)

procedures.action: Immediately reduce engine load per the slowdown function and prepare to stop the engine if temperature continues to rise.
procedures.why: Reducing load lowers combustion gas blow-by and heat generation, which can arrest an incipient scavenge fire before it intensifies.

procedures.action: Stop the engine and isolate the affected cylinder's scavenge air space if temperature continues to climb despite load reduction.
procedures.why: A fully developed scavenge fire can damage the piston, liner, and scavenge air receiver if allowed to continue.

procedures.action: Once cooled and safe, inspect the scavenge air ports, piston skirt, and liner for oil deposit buildup or fire damage.
procedures.why: Identifies the root cause, typically excess cylinder lubrication or worn piston rings allowing blow-by and oil accumulation.

procedures.action: Review cylinder lubrication feed rate and piston ring condition before returning the cylinder to service.
procedures.why: Prevents recurrence by correcting the lubrication or ring wear issue that led to oil deposit accumulation.

constraints: Scavenge air box fire alarm (TE 8610) is a universal UMS alarm and slowdown requirement across all classification societies
regulations: Scavenge air box fire alarm and slowdown function is required per Table 18.04.02 and 18.04.03 for all classification societies
warnings: Failure to respond promptly to a scavenge air box fire alarm can allow the fire to spread, risking severe damage to the piston, liner, and scavenge air receiver, and potential injury to personnel nearby
outcomes: If uncorrected, a developing scavenge fire can cause major mechanical damage requiring extensive repair and extended off-hire
Prompt load reduction, shutdown if necessary, and lubrication correction prevents fire escalation and recurrence
key_facts: Scavenge air box fire alarm is both an alarm and a slowdown function per classification requirement
Scavenge fires are typically caused by accumulated oil deposits igniting due to excess lubrication or piston ring blow-by
