trace.situation: An auxiliary blower motor bearing begins to deteriorate, producing increasing vibration and noise during operation, which if left unaddressed can lead to sudden blower failure during a critical low-load maneuvering period.
trace.trigger: Abnormal vibration or noise reported from the auxiliary blower during routine engine room rounds, with no electrical alarm yet present

procedures.action: Record vibration levels and compare with baseline readings from commissioning or last survey if portable monitoring equipment is available.
procedures.why: Establishes the severity and rate of bearing degradation to prioritize the urgency of intervention.

procedures.action: Schedule bearing replacement during the next planned engine stoppage, prioritizing it ahead of other deferred maintenance if trend is worsening rapidly.
procedures.why: Prevents an unplanned failure of the blower, which would reduce redundancy to the single remaining unit.

procedures.action: In the interim, verify the second auxiliary blower is fully operational and consider restricting maneuvering in areas requiring frequent low-load operation.
procedures.why: Reduces reliance on the degrading blower until replacement can be completed.

constraints: Blower motor heaters (if fitted) should be verified functional to prevent condensation-related bearing damage during idle periods
regulations: Manufacturer planned maintenance system requirement for auxiliary blower bearing inspection intervals
warnings: Ignoring progressive bearing wear risks sudden blower seizure, which could occur during a critical maneuvering sequence when both blowers are needed
outcomes: Unaddressed bearing wear can cause blower seizure and loss of redundancy at an inopportune time
Scheduled bearing replacement avoids unplanned failure and maintains full redundancy
key_facts: Each auxiliary blower is controlled by its own starter panel allowing individual control and protection
Heaters for blower motors are available as an option to prevent condensation damage during standby periods

question_seeds.text: How should I prioritize a developing auxiliary blower bearing fault against other maintenance?

known_issue.failure_mode: auxiliary blower motor bearing wear
known_issue.detection_method: vibration/noise observation during rounds

trace.situation: The auxiliary blower control logic fails to stop a blower after the engine has been stopped for the designated time, keeping the blower running continuously and risking thermal overload of the motor due to extended duty beyond its rated continuous running profile at standstill.
trace.trigger: Auxiliary blower still running alarm or observed continuous operation well beyond 30 minutes after engine stop

procedures.action: Manually stop the affected blower from the ECR panel in manual mode.
procedures.why: Immediate manual intervention prevents further unnecessary thermal loading on the motor while the automatic logic fault is investigated.

procedures.action: Check the engine control system logic and timer function responsible for the 30-minute automatic shutdown of blowers after engine stop.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the fault is a software/logic timer issue or a stuck output relay in the control system.

procedures.action: Correct the control fault or arrange temporary manual control procedures until the automatic function is restored and verified.
procedures.why: Ensures blowers are not left running indefinitely, which the system design specifically prevents to avoid overheating.

constraints: Auxiliary blowers are designed to stop automatically 30 minutes after engine stop to prevent motor overheating
regulations: Manufacturer control system design requirement for automatic blower shutdown timing
warnings: Continuous unplanned running beyond the designed duty cycle can overheat the blower motor and shorten insulation life, risking premature failure
outcomes: Uncorrected logic fault risks repeated motor overheating events and reduced blower service life
Restoring correct automatic control protects blower motor longevity
key_facts: The engine control system automatically stops auxiliary blowers 30 minutes after engine stop specifically to prevent overheating
Manual mode allows individual blower control from the ECR panel irrespective of engine condition

question_seeds.text: What should be checked if an auxiliary blower continues running well past the normal 30-minute post-stop shutdown?

known_issue.failure_mode: auxiliary blower automatic stop logic failure
known_issue.detection_method: observed continuous blower running beyond designed post-stop duration

trace.situation: Scavenge air receiver pressure fluctuates erratically at mid-load, causing the auxiliary blowers to cycle on and off repeatedly instead of smoothly handing over to turbocharger-only operation. This is caused by a faulty or drifting scavenge air pressure sensor feeding the blower control logic.
trace.trigger: Repeated short-cycling of auxiliary blower start/stop commands observed in the alarm history log around the 30-40% load transition point

procedures.action: Compare the scavenge air pressure sensor reading against a calibrated reference gauge at the same load point.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the sensor is reading accurately or has drifted, causing false crossing of the preset hysteresis thresholds.

procedures.action: If drift is confirmed, recalibrate or replace the pressure transmitter feeding the auxiliary blower control logic.
procedures.why: Restores accurate pressure feedback so the blower start/stop hysteresis functions as designed without short-cycling.

procedures.action: Temporarily switch the affected blower to manual control to prevent excessive cycling while awaiting sensor replacement.
procedures.why: Protects the blower motor and starter contactors from excessive wear due to frequent start/stop cycling.

constraints: Auxiliary blowers cut in below approx. 25-35% load and cut out above approx. 30-40% load with built-in hysteresis to prevent short-cycling under normal sensor conditions
regulations: Manufacturer design intent for hysteresis-based blower control to avoid excessive motor cycling
warnings: Repeated blower short-cycling accelerates contactor and motor wear, increasing the risk of a subsequent failure to start when actually needed
outcomes: Uncorrected sensor drift leads to accelerated wear of blower starter equipment and potential nuisance trips
Sensor recalibration restores smooth automatic blower handover and reduces equipment wear
key_facts: The blower cut-in/cut-out logic includes a hysteresis band based on recent pressure history to prevent short-cycling
Pressure feedback for blower control comes from a dedicated scavenge air pressure sensor integrated into the engine control system

question_seeds.text: Why would the auxiliary blower short-cycle repeatedly near the 30-40% load range?

known_issue.failure_mode: scavenge air pressure sensor drift affecting blower control
known_issue.detection_method: alarm history pattern of repeated blower start/stop cycling

trace.situation: Chemical cleaning residue from a scavenge air cooler cleaning operation is not fully flushed and partially blocks the spray pipe nozzles or the drain filter, reducing the effectiveness of subsequent cleaning cycles and risking contamination carryover into the drain water system.
trace.trigger: Reduced spray pattern or pressure observed at the cleaning unit during a subsequent scheduled cooler cleaning

procedures.action: Check the circulation pump discharge pressure against the rated 3 bar specification during the cleaning cycle.
procedures.why: A pressure below rated value indicates a restriction in the spray pipe or filter rather than a pump fault.

procedures.action: Inspect and clean the spray pipe nozzles and the drain filter in the return line from 'AM' to the chemical cleaning tank.
procedures.why: These are the common blockage points where residue and sludge accumulate between cleaning cycles.

procedures.action: Verify chemical tank capacity and concentration are per the manufacturer's guidance for the engine's cylinder count before the next cleaning.
procedures.why: Ensures the correct volume and mixture are used to achieve effective cleaning and minimize residue buildup.

constraints: Air cooler cleaning must be performed with the engine at standstill
Circulation pump capacity and chemical tank size are specified per engine cylinder count
regulations: Manufacturer specification for air cooler cleaning unit capacity by cylinder count
warnings: Repeated ineffective cleaning cycles leave fouling uncorrected, perpetuating high scavenge air temperature trends
outcomes: Blocked nozzles or filter render cleaning cycles ineffective, masking true cooler condition
Clearing residue restores full cleaning effectiveness and accurate assessment of cooler fouling
key_facts: The air cooler cleaning unit circulation pump is rated to deliver at 3 bar per the engine's cylinder count specification
Polluted grease dissolvent returns through a filter to the chemical cleaning tank for reuse

question_seeds.text: What should be checked if the air cooler cleaning spray pressure is below the rated 3 bar?

known_issue.failure_mode: cleaning system residue blockage (nozzle/filter)
known_issue.detection_method: reduced spray pressure during scheduled cleaning cycle

trace.situation: Uneven cylinder scavenging develops across units due to a combination of minor piston ring blow-by and uneven turbocharger airflow distribution, resulting in a spread of exhaust gas temperatures between cylinders even though overall scavenge air pressure appears normal.
trace.trigger: Increasing spread between highest and lowest cylinder exhaust gas temperatures noted on the engine performance report

procedures.action: Review recent cylinder condition reports, including ring/liner wear data and lubrication feed rates for the affected units.
procedures.why: Blow-by from worn piston rings is a common contributor to localized scavenging inefficiency and elevated exhaust temperature on specific units.

procedures.action: Inspect scavenge ports on the units with the highest exhaust temperature for carbon buildup restricting port area during the next opportunity.
procedures.why: Port restriction from deposits reduces effective scavenging on that cylinder, compounding any ring wear effect.

procedures.action: Correct findings through port cleaning, ring/liner inspection, and lubrication adjustment as required, then re-verify temperature spread at the same load.
procedures.why: Confirms the corrective actions have restored balanced scavenging across all units.

constraints: Exhaust gas temperature spread between cylinders should remain within the manufacturer's recommended deviation band at steady load
regulations: Manufacturer performance monitoring guideline for cylinder exhaust temperature deviation limits
warnings: Persistent uneven scavenging can mask developing ring or liner damage on specific units, risking progression to a scavenge fire if deposits continue to accumulate
outcomes: Uncorrected imbalance can progress to localized overheating, increased wear, or scavenge fire risk on the affected unit
Addressing port and ring condition restores balanced combustion and reduces fire risk
key_facts: Exhaust temperature spread across cylinders is a standard indicator of relative scavenging and combustion balance
Carbon buildup in scavenge ports reduces effective port area and local scavenging efficiency

question_seeds.text: Which cylinder-specific factors should be checked when exhaust temperature spread increases without an overall scavenge pressure change?

known_issue.failure_mode: uneven cylinder scavenging (port fouling / ring blow-by)
known_issue.detection_method: cylinder exhaust gas temperature spread trend on performance report

trace.situation: The automatic oil content monitor on the overboard drain water disposal system malfunctions, either failing to detect oil content above the discharge limit or giving false high readings that unnecessarily divert clean water to the oily bilge holding tank, affecting environmental compliance or tank capacity management.
trace.trigger: Oil content monitor alarm inconsistent with visual inspection of drain water clarity, or no alarm despite visible sheen in the collecting tank

procedures.action: Take a manual sample of the drain water from the collecting tank and compare visually and, if available, with a portable oil-in-water test kit.
procedures.why: Provides an independent check of actual oil content against the automatic monitor reading to confirm or rule out instrument fault.

procedures.action: If the monitor reading is confirmed inaccurate, divert all drain water to the oily bilge holding tank manually until the monitor is recalibrated or repaired.
procedures.why: Prevents any out-of-specification discharge overboard while the automatic protection is unreliable.

procedures.action: Arrange calibration or replacement of the oil content monitor sensor and verify correct operation before resuming automatic overboard discharge.
procedures.why: Restores reliable automatic compliance monitoring for the discharge system.

constraints: Oil content of drain water must be below 15 ppm before overboard discharge; otherwise it must be routed to the oily bilge water holding tank
regulations: MARPOL Annex I 15 ppm oil content discharge limit for machinery space drainage
warnings: Discharging drain water overboard based on a faulty oil content monitor reading above the limit is a MARPOL violation risking detention and penalties
outcomes: Continued reliance on a faulty monitor risks an illegal discharge or unnecessary loss of holding tank capacity
Monitor repair restores reliable automatic compliance with discharge regulations
key_facts: The automatic pump overboard system is optional and includes oil content monitoring per owner specification
Drain water above 15 ppm oil content must be led to the oily bilge water holding tank rather than discharged overboard

question_seeds.text: What should be done if the automatic oil content monitor reading does not match a visual check of the drain water?

known_issue.failure_mode: oil content monitor malfunction (drain water disposal)
known_issue.detection_method: discrepancy between automatic monitor alarm and manual sample inspection

trace.situation: A sudden drop in scavenge air receiver pressure occurs at high engine load, well above the auxiliary blower cut-in range, indicating a turbocharger-side problem such as compressor fouling or a developing turbocharger bearing issue rather than an auxiliary blower fault.
trace.trigger: Low scavenge air pressure alarm at high load with auxiliary blowers confirmed stopped and not expected to run at that load

procedures.action: Check turbocharger speed, exhaust gas temperature before/after turbine, and compressor outlet pressure against normal performance curves for the load.
procedures.why: Determines whether the turbocharger itself is underperforming due to fouling, surge, or bearing degradation rather than a scavenge air system component.

procedures.action: Reduce load if pressure continues to fall and instability indicators (such as surge noise) are present.
procedures.why: Reducing load lowers the risk of turbocharger surge or further mechanical damage while root cause is investigated.

procedures.action: Plan for turbocharger compressor/turbine cleaning or inspection at the next opportunity based on findings, coordinating with class/manufacturer guidance if bearing wear is suspected.
procedures.why: Addresses the root cause at the turbocharger rather than the scavenge air system itself, since the receiver pressure drop is a downstream symptom.

constraints: Scavenge air pressure at high load should track the manufacturer's performance curve within an acceptable tolerance band for the given fuel index/load
regulations: Manufacturer performance monitoring requirement for turbocharger efficiency tracking
warnings: Continuing at high load with a degrading turbocharger risks surge, mechanical failure, and consequential damage to the scavenge air cooler or receiver from debris
outcomes: Unaddressed turbocharger degradation can lead to sudden surge events and potential mechanical failure requiring major repair
Early identification and load reduction allows planned turbocharger maintenance without consequential damage
key_facts: Auxiliary blowers are not expected to operate above approximately 30-40% load, so a pressure drop at high load points to the turbocharger or cooler rather than blower operation
Turbocharger performance should be benchmarked against manufacturer curves for the given load and ambient conditions

question_seeds.text: Why would scavenge air pressure drop at high load when the auxiliary blowers are not expected to be running?

known_issue.failure_mode: turbocharger-induced low scavenge air pressure at high load
known_issue.detection_method: low scavenge air pressure alarm correlated with turbocharger performance deviation

trace.situation: A crack or gasket failure develops in the scavenge air receiver or associated ducting downstream of the cooler, causing a continuous external air leak that reduces effective scavenge air pressure delivered to the cylinders and produces an audible hissing noise near the affected joint.
trace.trigger: Audible hissing noise near the scavenge air receiver or ducting combined with a slight but persistent scavenge air pressure deficit compared to the turbocharger compressor output

procedures.action: Conduct a visual and acoustic inspection along the scavenge air receiver and ducting joints to localize the leak source.
procedures.why: Pinpointing the exact leak location is necessary before any repair or temporary sealing can be attempted safely.

procedures.action: Assess whether the leak is from a gasket joint that can be tightened/resealed at reduced load or requires a full stop for a cracked casting repair.
procedures.why: Determines the urgency and method of repair; gasket leaks may allow a controlled temporary fix, while structural cracks require engine stoppage.

procedures.action: Repair the joint or crack per manufacturer repair procedures and pressure-test the area before returning to full load operation.
procedures.why: Confirms the leak has been fully eliminated and receiver pressure delivery is restored to design values.

constraints: Scavenge air receiver and ducting joints must maintain pressure integrity per design to ensure correct air delivery to all cylinders
regulations: Manufacturer structural integrity requirement for scavenge air receiver and ducting components
warnings: A worsening leak can lead to localized overheating of the receiver casing material and eventual larger structural failure if not repaired promptly
outcomes: Continued leakage reduces delivered scavenge air pressure and engine efficiency, and risks escalating to a larger structural failure
Prompt repair restores full receiver pressure integrity and engine performance
key_facts: Scavenge air receiver pressure should correspond closely to turbocharger compressor discharge pressure minus normal cooler losses
External air leaks are typically identified by audible hissing and a measurable pressure deficit

question_seeds.text: How can I localize a suspected scavenge air receiver leak before deciding on repair urgency?

known_issue.failure_mode: scavenge air receiver/ducting leak
known_issue.detection_method: audible leak detection combined with pressure deficit measurement

trace.situation: During prolonged standby or reduced manning periods, the optional heaters for the auxiliary blower motors fail, allowing condensation to accumulate inside the idle blower motor windings. This creates a risk of insulation breakdown or short circuit when the blower is next called upon to start.
trace.trigger: Insulation resistance test during routine maintenance shows a declining trend on an idle auxiliary blower motor, or the blower trips on earth fault shortly after a long standby period

procedures.action: Check the blower motor heater circuit for continuity and confirm it is energized during standby periods.
procedures.why: A failed heater is the most likely cause of condensation buildup in an idle motor in a humid engine room environment.

procedures.action: Perform an insulation resistance (megger) test on the affected motor before attempting to run it under load.
procedures.why: Confirms whether moisture ingress has degraded insulation to an unsafe level before re-energizing the motor under normal starting current.

procedures.action: If insulation resistance is low, dry out the motor using appropriate low-heat methods or arrange for motor service/replacement before relying on it, and repair the heater circuit.
procedures.why: Prevents an insulation failure or earth fault trip at a critical moment when the blower is needed for engine starting or low-load running.

constraints: Motor insulation resistance should meet the manufacturer's minimum acceptable value before the motor is returned to service
regulations: Manufacturer recommendation for motor heater use on idle auxiliary blower motors in humid environments
warnings: Starting a motor with degraded insulation from moisture ingress risks an earth fault trip or winding failure at the moment the blower is critically needed
outcomes: Unaddressed heater failure risks loss of a blower exactly when redundancy is needed most, such as during standby-to-sea transition
Heater repair and insulation verification ensures the standby blower is reliably available when called upon
key_facts: Heaters for auxiliary blower motors are available as an option specifically to prevent condensation-related insulation issues during idle periods
Insulation resistance testing is the standard method to verify motor condition before returning an idle machine to service

question_seeds.text: When should insulation resistance be checked on an auxiliary blower motor after an extended standby period?

known_issue.failure_mode: auxiliary blower motor heater failure leading to condensation/insulation degradation
known_issue.detection_method: insulation resistance (megger) test trend / earth fault trip on start attempt

trace.situation: One of the two auxiliary scavenge air blowers trips on motor overload while the engine is running at low load (below ~30% MCR), leaving only a single blower to supply scavenge air. The remaining blower can maintain emergency running, but with reduced margin before the engine must reduce load or stop.
trace.trigger: Auxiliary blower No.1 trip alarm / blower running hours imbalance noted on ECS

procedures.action: Confirm the second blower has automatically taken over and scavenge air pressure is stable within normal range for current load.
procedures.why: The system is designed so the healthy blower continues supplying scavenge air without manual valve adjustment.

procedures.action: Check motor overload relay, insulation resistance, and bearing temperature of the tripped blower before attempting reset.
procedures.why: Resetting an overload without identifying the cause can lead to repeat trip or motor burnout.

procedures.action: If reset is unsuccessful, inform bridge/ECR and restrict load increase until the second blower is confirmed serviceable or repaired.
procedures.why: Running on a single blower reduces redundancy; losing the second blower would force an emergency slow-down or stop.

constraints: Auxiliary blowers must cover scavenging up to approx. 25-35% engine load before turbocharger takes over
Minimum two blowers required per engine per maker design
regulations: Class requirement for engine auxiliary blower redundancy
Manufacturer emergency-running provision for single blower operation
warnings: If the remaining blower also fails, the engine cannot be started or maneuvered safely at low load and may need to be stopped
outcomes: Loss of both blowers forces an uncontrolled stop or failure to start, risking blackout during maneuvering
Prompt isolation and repair restores full blower redundancy and safe starting/maneuvering capability
key_facts: Auxiliary blowers start automatically when blower inlet pressure drops below a level equivalent to approx. 25-35% load
Blowers stop automatically 30 minutes after engine stop to prevent motor overheating
Non-return valves between cooler and receiver close automatically when blowers run, no manual valve action needed

question_seeds.text: What should I check first if one auxiliary blower trips on overload during maneuvering?
Why does losing one auxiliary blower not immediately stop the engine?

known_issue.failure_mode: auxiliary blower motor overload trip
known_issue.detection_method: blower trip alarm and scavenge air pressure monitoring

trace.situation: A non-return valve between the scavenge air cooler and the scavenge air receiver fails to close fully when the auxiliary blowers start, allowing scavenge air to leak back through the idle blower casing. This reduces blower delivery efficiency and can cause erratic scavenge pressure readings during the low-load starting phase.
trace.trigger: Scavenge air pressure fluctuating or lower than expected despite both blowers running normally

procedures.action: Verify blower running status and amperage against normal values, then inspect the non-return valve flap for free movement via inspection hatch when engine is stopped.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the pressure anomaly is due to blower performance or valve malfunction.

procedures.action: Clean and check the valve seat and hinge for carbon deposits or corrosion causing it to stick.
procedures.why: Fouling or corrosion is the most common cause of non-return valves failing to seat properly.

procedures.action: Replace the valve flap or spring if wear or deformation is found, then verify closure by air pressure test before restart.
procedures.why: A properly seating valve is required to prevent backflow and maintain correct receiver pressure during blower-only operation.

constraints: Non-return valves must close automatically and fully when auxiliary blowers are supplying air
Scavenge air receiver pressure must remain stable for safe low-load combustion
regulations: Manufacturer design requirement for automatic non-return valve operation with auxiliary blowers
warnings: Continued leakage can cause uneven scavenging, incomplete combustion, and increased risk of scavenge fire from unburned fuel residues
outcomes: Unchecked valve leakage leads to poor low-load combustion, smoking, and possible misfiring
Repair restores correct receiver pressure and stable low-load operation
key_facts: Non-return valves are located between scavenge air cooler and scavenge air receiver
They close automatically once auxiliary blowers start supplying air

question_seeds.text: How can I confirm a non-return valve is the cause of unstable scavenge pressure at low load?
Which component should be inspected first when scavenge pressure fluctuates with both blowers running?

known_issue.failure_mode: non-return valve failing to seat
known_issue.detection_method: scavenge pressure fluctuation and visual inspection

trace.situation: The air side of the scavenge air cooler becomes progressively fouled with oil and carbon deposits, reducing heat transfer efficiency. Scavenge air temperature after the cooler rises above normal while scavenge air pressure for a given load falls, indicating restricted airflow through the cooler matrix.
trace.trigger: Scavenge air temperature after cooler alarm (high) combined with falling scavenge pressure trend at constant load

procedures.action: Confirm cooling water inlet temperature and flow are normal to rule out a cooling water side problem.
procedures.why: Eliminates cooling water supply issues before concluding the fault is air-side fouling.

procedures.action: Plan and execute an air-side chemical cleaning of the cooler using the grease-dissolving media injected via the spray pipe, with the engine at standstill.
procedures.why: Cleaning must be done with engine stopped and is the designed method for removing oil/carbon buildup from the air side.

procedures.action: After cleaning, verify scavenge air temperature and pressure return to normal values at same load before declaring the system clear.
procedures.why: Confirms the fouling has been removed and heat transfer efficiency restored.

constraints: Cooler cleaning must be carried out with the engine at standstill
Scavenge air temperature after cooler must stay within manufacturer-specified limit to avoid efficiency loss and condensation issues
regulations: Manufacturer scavenge air cooler cleaning procedure
warnings: Prolonged operation with a fouled cooler increases thermal load on pistons/liners and raises risk of knocking or scavenge fire from unburned deposits
outcomes: Continued fouling raises fuel consumption, exhaust temperatures, and risk of thermal overload on cylinder components
Timely chemical cleaning restores design cooling performance and engine efficiency
key_facts: Air-side cleaning is done by injecting grease-dissolving media through a spray pipe above the cooler element
Cleaning requires engine standstill
Cooler cleaning unit tank capacity and pump flow vary by cylinder number per maker table

question_seeds.text: When should an air-side scavenge cooler cleaning be scheduled based on temperature trend?
Why does a fouled scavenge air cooler reduce scavenge pressure even though the blowers are working correctly?

known_issue.failure_mode: air-side cooler fouling
known_issue.detection_method: scavenge air temperature and pressure trend monitoring

trace.situation: A scavenge air cooler tube bundle develops a leak on the water side, allowing cooling water to enter the air side and subsequently the scavenge air receiver. Water carryover into the cylinders risks hydraulic shock on the piston crown and dilution of lubricating oil film.
trace.trigger: Water mist catcher drain tank level switch alarm (high level) or unusually high water quantity observed in cooler drain

procedures.action: Reduce load and monitor drain water quantity from the water mist catcher and cooler drain box.
procedures.why: Confirms whether water ingress is abnormal cooling water leakage rather than normal condensate.

procedures.action: Isolate the suspect cooler (if multiple coolers fitted) or shut down the engine for inspection if leakage is confirmed and quantity is excessive.
procedures.why: Prevents continued water entry into the scavenge air receiver and cylinders.

procedures.action: Pressure test the cooler water side to locate the leaking tube(s) and plug or repair as required before returning to service.
procedures.why: Identifies and seals the specific leak path to stop further water ingress.

constraints: Drain box level switch must indicate excessive water promptly
Scavenge air space must remain free of significant water accumulation to avoid cylinder liner washing and ring damage
regulations: Manufacturer requirement for drain box level monitoring of scavenge air cooler water mist catcher
warnings: If undetected, water carryover can cause loss of lubricating oil film on liners, accelerated wear, and potential hydraulic lock risk in cylinders
outcomes: Unaddressed tube leakage leads to liner/ring wear, oil contamination, and possible major overhaul
Early leak detection and repair avoids collateral cylinder damage
key_facts: Water mist catcher drains sludge/condensate through a dedicated line to the drain water collecting tank
Drain box is fitted with a level switch for excessive water level indication
AL drain line also provides permanent water mist catcher drain during running, via an orifice to limit air loss

question_seeds.text: What is the first check when the scavenge drain box level alarm activates unexpectedly?
How do I confirm a scavenge air cooler tube leak versus normal condensate accumulation?

known_issue.failure_mode: scavenge air cooler tube leak (water side to air side)
known_issue.detection_method: drain box level switch alarm and water quantity inspection

trace.situation: Accumulated oil and carbon deposits in the scavenge air space ignite, producing a scavenge box/piston underside fire. This is typically caused by poor combustion, cylinder oil over-lubrication, or ring blow-by depositing unburned fuel/oil residues in the scavenge spaces.
trace.trigger: Rapid rise in scavenge air space temperature sensors or scavenge fire detection alarm, sometimes with visible smoke from scavenge drain or box

procedures.action: Immediately reduce engine load/slow down and prepare to stop the engine per emergency scavenge fire procedure.
procedures.why: Reducing load lowers heat input and limits fire spread while assessment is made.

procedures.action: Activate the scavenge air space fire extinguishing system (steam, water mist, or CO2 as fitted) once engine is stopped.
procedures.why: Introducing the extinguishing medium smothers the fire by displacing oxygen and cooling the space.

procedures.action: After the fire is extinguished and space has cooled, open inspection covers to assess damage to piston skirt, liner, and scavenge ports before restarting.
procedures.why: Confirms no further ignition source remains and identifies any component damage from the fire.

constraints: Steam fire extinguishing pressure 3-10 bar, quantity approx. 2.2 kg/cyl.
Water mist system minimum 3.5 bar, approx. 1.7 kg/cyl.
CO2 system test pressure 150 bar, approx. 4.3 kg/cyl.
Engine must be stopped before activating extinguishing system
regulations: Class requirement for fitted scavenge air space fire extinguishing system
Manufacturer emergency procedure for scavenge fire
warnings: Opening scavenge space covers before the fire is confirmed out and cooled risks reflash and crew injury from residual heat/smoke
outcomes: Unchecked scavenge fire can escalate to piston seizure, liner cracking, or major mechanical damage requiring in-dock repair
Prompt extinguishing and inspection limits damage to a single unit and allows faster return to service
key_facts: Scavenge air space fire can be extinguished by steam (basic), water mist, or CO2 depending on system fitted
Drain pipes and fire extinguishing pipes are both routed in the scavenge air space

question_seeds.text: What is the correct sequence of actions when a scavenge space fire alarm activates?
Why must the engine be stopped before activating the scavenge air space fire extinguishing system?

known_issue.failure_mode: scavenge box/piston underside fire
known_issue.detection_method: scavenge air space temperature sensors and fire detection alarm

trace.situation: The continuous scavenge air box drain line becomes partially blocked by accumulated sludge, causing drain tank level to rise and restricting normal drainage from the scavenge spaces. If unresolved, sludge and oil can back up into the scavenge air box itself.
trace.trigger: Drain tank high-level alarm or reduced/no flow observed at drain sight glass

procedures.action: Apply steam assist (if fitted via the BV connection) to help liquefy and clear sludge blocking the drain path.
procedures.why: Steam heating reduces sludge viscosity, restoring flow through the drain line.

procedures.action: If steam assist does not clear the blockage, isolate and mechanically clean the drain line and drain tank during next opportunity at reduced load or standstill.
procedures.why: Physical removal of hardened sludge is required when heating alone is insufficient.

procedures.action: Inspect and verify free flow to the sludge tank and reset the drain tank level switch before resuming normal watch routine.
procedures.why: Ensures the drain path is fully restored and future high-level alarms reflect genuine conditions.

constraints: Drain tank capacity sized per cylinder count (e.g., 0.3-0.8 m3 depending on engine size)
Continuous drain must not be directly connected to sludge tank due to pressure differential
regulations: Manufacturer requirement for pressurized drain tank design per steam/air system pressure rating
warnings: If sludge backs up into the scavenge box, it can accumulate near hot surfaces and increase the risk of a scavenge space fire
outcomes: Persistent blockage leads to sludge accumulation in the scavenge box, degraded drainage, and elevated fire risk
Clearing the blockage restores normal drainage and reduces fire risk in the scavenge spaces
key_facts: Scavenge air box drains continuously via AV connection to a small pressurised drain tank
Steam can be applied via BV connection to facilitate draining
Drain tank should be located close to the engine to minimize blockage risk from long piping runs

question_seeds.text: How do I clear a blocked scavenge air box drain line using the steam assist connection?
When should the scavenge drain tank be mechanically cleaned rather than just steam-assisted?

known_issue.failure_mode: scavenge air box drain blockage
known_issue.detection_method: drain tank level alarm / sight glass flow check

trace.situation: The water mist catcher above the scavenge air cooler becomes saturated and its drain orifice partially clogs, allowing excess condensate/oil-laden water to carry over into the scavenge air receiver and cylinders instead of draining to the collecting tank.
trace.trigger: Increased moisture/oil observed at cylinder liner drains or abnormal water quantity noted during routine scavenge space inspection

procedures.action: Inspect and clear the drain orifice and AL drain line for blockage or restriction.
procedures.why: The orifice is sized to limit air loss while permitting continuous condensate drainage; blockage causes water to back up and carry over.

procedures.action: Check water mist catcher element for damage or saturation beyond design capacity.
procedures.why: A damaged or overloaded mist catcher element will not effectively separate water from the scavenge air stream.

procedures.action: Verify drain box level switch operation and drain water quality (oil content) before resuming normal operation.
procedures.why: Confirms the drainage path is functioning and water being discharged meets environmental requirements.

constraints: Oil content of drain water must be measured before overboard discharge; above 15 ppm it must go to oily bilge holding tank
AL drain line orifice sized to prevent major scavenge air loss
regulations: MARPOL Annex I oil content discharge limit (15 ppm) referenced by manufacturer drain water handling guidance
warnings: Continued water carryover into cylinders can wash away lubricating oil film and accelerate liner/ring wear
outcomes: Unresolved mist catcher saturation leads to water-related cylinder wear and potential oil pollution if drain water bypasses monitoring
Restoring drain flow prevents water carryover and ensures compliant drain water disposal
key_facts: Water mist catcher drains sludge via AL to drain water collecting tank with return through AM to chemical cleaning tank
Drain water oil content above 15 ppm requires routing to oily bilge water holding tank rather than overboard discharge

question_seeds.text: What should be checked when water appears to be carrying over past the water mist catcher?
Why is there an orifice fitted on the water mist catcher drain line during running?

known_issue.failure_mode: water mist catcher saturation/drain blockage
known_issue.detection_method: visual inspection of cylinder drains and water quantity monitoring

trace.situation: The auxiliary blower automatic control logic fails to start the standby/required blower when scavenge air (blower inlet) pressure drops below the preset threshold during a load reduction maneuver, leaving the engine temporarily under-scavenged at low load.
trace.trigger: Low scavenge air pressure alarm at a load below approximately 30% MCR without corresponding blower start

procedures.action: Switch the affected auxiliary blower to manual mode from the ECR panel and start it directly.
procedures.why: Manual start bypasses the faulty automatic control logic and restores scavenging immediately.

procedures.action: Check the blower inlet pressure transmitter and automatic control signal path in the Engine Control System for faults.
procedures.why: A failed pressure signal or control logic fault is the likely root cause of the automatic start failure.

procedures.action: Once the blower is confirmed running correctly, restore automatic mode only after the fault is cleared and verified by test.
procedures.why: Returning to automatic mode without fixing the root cause risks a repeat failure to start at the next low-load transition.

constraints: Auxiliary blowers must start automatically when blower inlet pressure drops below the level corresponding to ~25-35% load
Engine start is delayed automatically until blowers confirm running in automatic mode
regulations: Manufacturer ECS automatic blower control logic specification
warnings: Running at low load without adequate scavenge air pressure can cause poor combustion, exhaust smoke, and fouling of exhaust valves and turbocharger
outcomes: Repeated failure to auto-start blowers can force reliance on manual intervention during critical maneuvering, increasing workload and risk
Correcting the control fault restores reliable automatic blower sequencing for safe low-load operation
key_facts: Blowers are controlled via Engine Control System in automatic (default) or manual mode
In manual mode blowers can be controlled individually from the ECR panel irrespective of engine condition

question_seeds.text: How do I manually start an auxiliary blower when the automatic control fails to respond to low scavenge pressure?
Which signal in the Engine Control System should be checked first when auto blower start fails?

known_issue.failure_mode: automatic blower control logic failure
known_issue.detection_method: low scavenge air pressure alarm without blower start confirmation

trace.situation: Both auxiliary scavenge air blowers become unavailable simultaneously (e.g., one under maintenance and the second trips on fault) while the engine is stopped and a start is required for maneuvering. The Engine Control System will not permit engine start without confirmed blower operation.
trace.trigger: Engine start command delayed indefinitely with 'blower not running' indication on ECS panel

procedures.action: Verify status and try to restart the tripped blower from ECR, checking motor protection relays and power supply first.
procedures.why: A quick reset may restore one blower and allow the engine start sequence to proceed.

procedures.action: If neither blower can be restored quickly, inform bridge/master immediately of loss of maneuvering capability and request time to resolve before next required maneuver.
procedures.why: Safe navigation planning depends on knowing the engine cannot start until scavenging is available.

procedures.action: Dispatch engineers to diagnose and repair the fault (electrical, mechanical, or valve-related) on at least one blower as a priority repair.
procedures.why: At least one working blower is mandatory for the ECS to permit engine start.

constraints: Engine start sequence is delayed by ECS until auxiliary blowers are confirmed running
Minimum of two blowers fitted but only one is strictly needed for emergency running
regulations: Manufacturer interlock requiring blower confirmation before engine start
warnings: Total loss of blower capability renders the main engine unable to start, risking loss of propulsion during critical navigation situations
outcomes: Failure to restore at least one blower leaves the vessel without main engine availability, a serious safety and navigational risk
Restoring one blower quickly re-enables engine start capability and maneuvering
key_facts: A minimum of two auxiliary blowers are fitted per engine
ECS delays engine start until blowers have started in the normal sequence
Emergency running is possible on a single blower without manual valve adjustment

question_seeds.text: Who needs to be notified immediately if both auxiliary blowers are unavailable before a scheduled maneuver?
What is the minimum blower condition required for the ECS to permit an engine start?

known_issue.failure_mode: total auxiliary blower unavailability
known_issue.detection_method: ECS engine start interlock / blower status indication

trace.situation: A non-return valve downstream of an idle auxiliary blower fails to close when the turbocharger takes over at higher load, allowing hot scavenge air to recirculate back through the stopped blower casing, overheating the idle blower and its motor bearings.
trace.trigger: High temperature alarm on idle (non-running) auxiliary blower casing or motor bearing while engine is above the load at which blowers normally stop

procedures.action: Confirm which blower is idle and check its casing/bearing temperature locally against the running blower for comparison.
procedures.why: Establishes whether heat is from valve leakage rather than a genuine blower mechanical fault.

procedures.action: Plan to stop the engine or reduce load at the next safe opportunity to inspect and repair the faulty non-return valve.
procedures.why: The valve must be accessed with engine stopped to inspect and repair the sealing surfaces.

procedures.action: Monitor idle blower temperature closely until repair; if it continues rising toward trip setpoint, isolate the blower electrically to prevent motor damage.
procedures.why: Prevents motor winding damage from sustained overheating caused by hot air recirculation.

constraints: Non-return valves must prevent backflow into idle blower casing once turbocharger scavenging takes over above ~30-40% load
Blower motor bearing temperature limits per manufacturer motor data sheet
regulations: Manufacturer design requirement for automatic valve closure to protect idle blower
warnings: Ignoring rising idle blower temperature can lead to motor insulation breakdown and blower failure, reducing redundancy for the next low-load period
outcomes: Unrepaired valve leakage causes premature wear/failure of the idle blower motor, reducing future redundancy
Timely valve repair protects the idle blower and preserves full auxiliary blower redundancy
key_facts: Non-return valves close automatically when auxiliary blowers start supplying scavenge air, and should isolate idle blowers when turbocharger takes over
Idle blower overheating is an indirect but observable symptom of valve backflow

question_seeds.text: Why would an idle auxiliary blower show rising temperature while the engine is running at high load on turbocharger scavenging alone?
When is it safe to inspect a suspected faulty non-return valve on an idle blower?

known_issue.failure_mode: non-return valve backflow heating idle blower
known_issue.detection_method: idle blower casing/bearing temperature monitoring

trace.situation: The scavenge air box drain's pressurised drain tank, connected via steam or compressed air assist, develops a relief/overpressure issue because the tank's design pressure rating does not match the actual steam supply pressure being applied, risking tank deformation or seal failure.
trace.trigger: Abnormal pressure reading or audible relief valve lifting noise at the scavenge air box drain tank

procedures.action: Immediately isolate the steam supply to the drain tank (BV connection) and verify tank pressure drops to safe level.
procedures.why: Removing the overpressure source prevents further risk of tank or pipework failure.

procedures.action: Check the steam reducing valve/regulator setting against the drain tank's actual design pressure rating.
procedures.why: A mismatch between supply pressure and tank design rating is the likely root cause of overpressure.

procedures.action: Correct the regulator setting or replace the relief device, then gradually restore steam assist and confirm stable tank pressure before returning to normal operation.
procedures.why: Ensures the drain tank operates within its intended pressure envelope going forward.

constraints: Drain tank must be designed according to the pressurised system connected to the BV connection (steam or compressed air max working pressure)
Drain tank capacity sized per cylinder count
regulations: Manufacturer design requirement matching drain tank rating to connected steam/air system pressure
warnings: Failure to correct overpressure can result in drain tank rupture, steam release hazard, and loss of scavenge box drainage capability
outcomes: Uncorrected pressure mismatch risks tank failure and a steam/sludge release hazard in the engine room
Correcting the regulator setting restores safe, compliant drain tank operation
key_facts: Steam can be applied via BV connection to facilitate scavenge box draining
Drain tank design pressure must match the connected steam or compressed air system rating

question_seeds.text: What should be checked first if the scavenge air box drain tank shows signs of overpressure?
How is the drain tank pressure rating supposed to relate to the steam assist supply?

known_issue.failure_mode: drain tank overpressure from mismatched steam supply
known_issue.detection_method: pressure gauge reading / relief valve activation at drain tank

trace.situation: Drain water from the scavenge air box and cooler drain system, discharged via the auto pump overboard arrangement, shows an oil content above the 15 ppm limit due to a malfunctioning or bypassed oil content monitor, risking an unlawful overboard discharge.
trace.trigger: Oil content monitor alarm on the drain water auto-disposal system, or visible sheen noted during routine overboard discharge check

procedures.action: Immediately stop the automatic overboard pump-out and divert drain water flow to the oily bilge water holding tank.
procedures.why: Prevents continued discharge of water exceeding the permitted oil content limit.

procedures.action: Inspect and calibrate the oil content monitor, and check upstream separation/filtration in the collecting tank for proper function.
procedures.why: A faulty monitor or ineffective separation is the likely cause of the elevated reading or missed detection.

procedures.action: Record the incident in the Oil Record Book and notify the Chief Engineer/Master per company environmental procedure before resuming automatic discharge.
procedures.why: Ensures proper documentation and compliance verification before returning to automatic operation.

constraints: Oil content of drain water must be measured before overboard discharge; above 15 ppm must be routed to oily bilge water holding tank
Automatic disposal system must include oil content monitoring per owner's installed design
regulations: MARPOL Annex I 15 ppm oil content discharge limit
Oil Record Book entry requirement for bilge/drain water handling
warnings: Continued discharge above the permitted oil content limit constitutes a pollution violation with potential detention and penalties
outcomes: Unchecked monitor failure risks an illegal discharge and regulatory/legal consequences for the vessel
Prompt diversion and monitor repair ensures compliant handling of scavenge drain water
key_facts: Drain water oil content must be measured before overboard pumping; above 15 ppm requires routing to oily bilge holding tank
Dirty water after the water mist catcher is drained via DX to the bilge tank via an open funnel

question_seeds.text: Who should be notified first if the scavenge drain oil content monitor shows a reading above the discharge limit?
What immediate action stops a non-compliant overboard discharge from the scavenge drain system?

known_issue.failure_mode: oil content monitor failure / non-compliant drain discharge
known_issue.detection_method: oil content monitor alarm or visual sheen inspection

trace.situation: Internal corrosion and pitting develop on the scavenge air receiver shell over time due to condensate accumulation and inadequate drainage, eventually creating a small air leak at a weld seam or flange, resulting in a gradual, hard-to-locate loss of scavenge air pressure.
trace.trigger: Slowly declining scavenge air pressure trend at constant load with no corresponding blower or cooler fault found

procedures.action: Conduct a soap-test or ultrasonic leak check around receiver welds, flanges, and inspection covers while engine is stopped and receiver pressurized by auxiliary blower.
procedures.why: Localizes the exact leak point for repair, since receiver leaks are often small and hard to detect by pressure trend alone.

procedures.action: Assess the extent of corrosion/pitting found and arrange temporary sealing (e.g., approved sealant or clamp) if within class-accepted limits, pending permanent repair.
procedures.why: Prevents further air loss and deterioration until a permanent weld repair can be scheduled in port or during planned maintenance.

procedures.action: Schedule permanent repair (welding/plating) by class-approved method and conduct follow-up thickness/pressure testing.
procedures.why: Ensures structural integrity of the receiver is restored to class requirements.

constraints: Scavenge air receiver must maintain design pressure integrity without leakage
Repairs to pressure-containing engine components typically require class surveyor involvement
regulations: Classification society requirement for structural integrity of pressurized engine components
Manufacturer guidance on receiver drainage to prevent condensate-induced corrosion
warnings: Unrepaired receiver leakage reduces scavenge pressure efficiency and can mask other developing faults, delaying correct diagnosis
outcomes: Continued corrosion can progress to a larger structural failure of the receiver, a major repair
Early leak detection and class-approved repair restores full scavenge air efficiency and structural integrity
key_facts: Scavenge air receiver condensate must be properly drained to avoid internal corrosion
Small receiver air leaks typically manifest as a slow pressure decline rather than a sudden alarm

question_seeds.text: How do I localize a small scavenge air receiver leak when pressure is slowly declining with no obvious fault?
When does a scavenge air receiver corrosion repair require class surveyor attendance?

known_issue.failure_mode: scavenge air receiver corrosion/leakage
known_issue.detection_method: slow scavenge pressure decline trend and leak testing

trace.situation: Partial fouling of one scavenge air cooler (on an engine fitted with two or more coolers) causes uneven air distribution between cylinder groups, resulting in one cylinder bank running with noticeably higher exhaust gas temperature than the others at the same load.
trace.trigger: Exhaust gas temperature deviation alarm on specific cylinders while overall scavenge pressure appears within normal range

procedures.action: Compare individual cooler outlet air temperatures (if separately monitored) to identify which cooler is underperforming.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the imbalance originates from one specific cooler rather than a combustion or fuel injection issue.

procedures.action: Schedule chemical cleaning of the underperforming cooler's air side at the next standstill opportunity.
procedures.why: Restores even heat transfer and airflow distribution across all coolers feeding the common receiver.

procedures.action: After cleaning, verify exhaust temperature spread across all cylinders returns to within the normal deviation band at the same load.
procedures.why: Confirms the fouling was the root cause and the imbalance has been corrected.

constraints: Exhaust gas temperature deviation between cylinders should remain within manufacturer-specified band at a given load
Cooler cleaning requires engine standstill
regulations: Manufacturer guidance on cylinder-to-cylinder exhaust temperature balance monitoring
warnings: Ignoring persistent temperature imbalance can lead to localized thermal overload and accelerated wear on the affected cylinder units
outcomes: Continued imbalance risks uneven piston/liner wear and potential for localized overheating damage
Cleaning the fouled cooler restores balanced combustion conditions across all cylinders
key_facts: Larger engines may have two or more scavenge air coolers feeding a common receiver
Cooler fouling is corrected via air-side chemical cleaning with engine stopped

question_seeds.text: Why would only certain cylinders show high exhaust temperature while overall scavenge air pressure looks normal?
Which cooler should be scheduled for cleaning first when cylinder temperature deviation appears on one side of the engine?

known_issue.failure_mode: uneven cooler fouling causing cylinder temperature imbalance
known_issue.detection_method: individual cylinder exhaust temperature deviation monitoring

trace.situation: An auxiliary blower develops a bearing fault (inadequate lubrication or wear) causing abnormal vibration and rising bearing temperature during low-load operation, with risk of sudden seizure if not addressed.
trace.trigger: High bearing temperature alarm or abnormal vibration reading on the running auxiliary blower

procedures.action: Reduce reliance on the affected blower by starting the standby blower (manual mode) and monitoring load share between the two.
procedures.why: Protects against sudden failure of the faulty blower while maintaining scavenging capacity.

procedures.action: Check lubrication system (grease/oil) of the faulty blower bearing and replenish or correct as per maker's schedule.
procedures.why: Inadequate lubrication is a common root cause of rising bearing temperature and vibration.

procedures.action: If vibration/temperature continue to rise despite lubrication correction, stop and isolate the blower for bearing replacement at the next opportunity.
procedures.why: Prevents a catastrophic bearing seizure that could damage the blower impeller/motor and remove redundancy.

constraints: Blower bearing temperature and vibration must remain within manufacturer's motor/blower limits
Standby blower must be available to take over load during maintenance
regulations: Manufacturer blower maintenance and lubrication schedule
warnings: A seized blower bearing can cause impeller contact damage and complete loss of that blower, reducing redundancy to zero if the other blower is also unavailable
outcomes: Ignoring rising bearing temperature risks sudden blower seizure and loss of redundancy at a critical time
Early lubrication correction or bearing replacement preserves blower availability and full redundancy
key_facts: Auxiliary blowers are electrically driven and integrated in the reversing chamber below the scavenge air cooler
Blower heaters are available as an option to protect motors during standstill, separate from running bearing lubrication needs

question_seeds.text: What is the immediate action when an auxiliary blower shows rising bearing temperature during low-load running?
How can I tell if blower vibration is a lubrication issue versus impending bearing seizure?

known_issue.failure_mode: auxiliary blower bearing degradation
known_issue.detection_method: bearing temperature/vibration monitoring

trace.situation: A general low scavenge air pressure alarm occurs at an engine load above the auxiliary blower operating range (turbocharger scavenging zone), caused not by the blowers but by turbocharger compressor-side fouling, reducing the turbocharger's air delivery efficiency.
trace.trigger: Low scavenge air pressure alarm at mid-to-high load with turbocharger speed lower than expected for the given load

procedures.action: Compare turbocharger speed, exhaust gas temperature before/after turbine, and scavenge pressure against the engine's normal performance curve for current load.
procedures.why: Differentiates a turbocharger efficiency problem from an auxiliary blower or cooler issue, since blowers are not active at this load.

procedures.action: Plan turbocharger compressor-side water washing at the next suitable opportunity per maker's washing procedure and interval.
procedures.why: Compressor fouling is a common cause of reduced boost pressure and is correctable by washing without major disassembly.

procedures.action: After washing, confirm scavenge pressure and turbocharger speed return to the expected curve values at the same load.
procedures.why: Validates that fouling was the root cause and performance has been restored.

constraints: Scavenge air pressure must correspond to the engine's load-pressure curve within manufacturer tolerance
Turbocharger washing intervals per maker's recommended schedule
regulations: Manufacturer turbocharger performance monitoring and washing guidance
warnings: Persistent low scavenge pressure from turbocharger fouling increases specific fuel consumption and exhaust temperatures, risking turbine-side damage if left unaddressed
outcomes: Continued fouling degrades fuel efficiency and may push exhaust temperatures toward alarm limits
Compressor washing restores turbocharger efficiency and normal scavenge pressure
key_facts: Above approximately 30-40% load, turbocharger scavenging replaces auxiliary blower operation
Low scavenge pressure at higher loads with blowers inactive points to turbocharger, not blower, performance issues

question_seeds.text: Which parameter distinguishes a turbocharger fouling issue from an auxiliary blower fault when scavenge pressure is low?
When should turbocharger compressor washing be scheduled based on scavenge pressure trend?

known_issue.failure_mode: turbocharger compressor fouling reducing scavenge pressure
known_issue.detection_method: scavenge pressure vs. load curve and turbocharger speed comparison

trace.situation: During a scheduled scavenge air cooler chemical cleaning, the grease-dissolving media is injected while the engine is still rotating on turning gear or not fully isolated, resulting in cleaning chemical carryover into the scavenge air receiver and risk of contaminating cylinder lubrication or causing corrosion inside the receiver.
trace.trigger: Unusual chemical odor or residue noted at scavenge drain, or cleaning procedure deviation noted during the job

procedures.action: Immediately stop the cleaning injection and confirm the engine is fully stopped with turning gear disengaged before resuming.
procedures.why: The procedure explicitly requires the engine to be at standstill; continuing with the engine not properly isolated risks chemical ingress into running components.

procedures.action: Flush and drain the air cooler and receiver thoroughly per the cleaning procedure, verifying all chemical residue is removed via the AL/AM drain and filter path.
procedures.why: Residual cleaning chemical left in the system can corrode internal surfaces or contaminate lubricating oil film at next start.

procedures.action: Inspect scavenge ports and lower cylinder areas for chemical residue before restarting, and verify drain water returned to the chemical cleaning tank is within expected clarity/contamination levels.
procedures.why: Ensures no chemical remains to affect combustion or cylinder lubrication at startup.

constraints: Scavenge air cooler chemical cleaning must be carried out while the engine is at standstill
Cleaning chemical tank capacity and circulation pump rate sized per cylinder count per maker table
regulations: Manufacturer procedure requiring engine standstill during air cooler chemical cleaning
warnings: Chemical residue entering the cylinders at start-up can damage piston rings/liner surfaces and contaminate cylinder lubrication
outcomes: Failure to properly isolate and flush can lead to cylinder liner/ring damage and lubrication system contamination
Correct standstill procedure and thorough flushing prevents any chemical-related engine damage
key_facts: Air-side cleaning media is injected through a spray pipe above the cooler element via connection AK
Polluted grease dissolvent returns through AM via a filter to the chemical cleaning tank
Cleaning must be carried out while the engine is at standstill

question_seeds.text: Why is it critical that the engine be fully stopped, not just on turning gear, during scavenge air cooler chemical cleaning?
What should be checked after a scavenge cooler cleaning to confirm no chemical residue remains before starting the engine?

known_issue.failure_mode: chemical cleaning procedure deviation causing contamination
known_issue.detection_method: chemical odor/residue detection at scavenge drains during or after cleaning

trace.situation: The auxiliary blower starter panel experiences an electrical fault (contactor failure or control wiring fault) that prevents the blower motor from starting even though the Engine Control System commands it, and this is only discovered when the standby blower also fails to engage during a drill or actual low-load transition.
trace.trigger: Blower fails to start on command from ECR panel, no motor hum or current draw observed at the starter panel

procedures.action: Attempt local start at the starter panel and check for contactor engagement, control voltage, and fuse/breaker status.
procedures.why: Isolates whether the fault is in the starter panel electrics or further upstream in the ECS command signal.

procedures.action: If a blown fuse, tripped breaker, or failed contactor is found, replace/reset as appropriate following lockout-tagout procedure before re-energizing.
procedures.why: Addresses the specific electrical fault safely while protecting personnel from electrical hazard.

procedures.action: Test blower start in both manual and automatic mode after repair to confirm full functionality restored before returning panel to automatic default.
procedures.why: Confirms the repair resolves both manual and automatic start paths, not just one.

constraints: Starter panels protect and control blower motors per manufacturer starter panel diagram
Blower must be testable in both automatic and manual mode from ECR
regulations: Manufacturer starter panel design and function specification
warnings: An undetected starter panel fault discovered only during an actual low-load emergency could delay blower response when most needed
outcomes: Undetected starter faults risk a real blower start failure during maneuvering, compromising propulsion
Scheduled testing and prompt electrical repair ensures reliable blower starting when required
key_facts: Each auxiliary blower has its own starter panel controlling and protecting the blower motor
Blowers can be controlled from ECR in manual mode irrespective of engine condition

question_seeds.text: How do I troubleshoot an auxiliary blower that fails to start from both automatic and manual commands?
When should auxiliary blower starter panels be functionally tested to catch latent electrical faults?

known_issue.failure_mode: auxiliary blower starter panel electrical fault
known_issue.detection_method: failed start attempt during drill or operational need, no current draw at panel

trace.situation: The scavenge air space fire extinguishing system (steam, water mist, or CO2 line) is found to be partially blocked or isolated with a closed valve during a routine drill, meaning the system would not have delivered extinguishing medium in a real scavenge fire event.
trace.trigger: No flow or pressure drop observed at the scavenge air space extinguishing outlet during scheduled drill/test

procedures.action: Trace the extinguishing line from the supply source (steam manifold, freshwater pump, or CO2 bank) to the scavenge space connection to locate the closed valve or blockage.
procedures.why: Systematic tracing is needed since the system is rarely used and faults can exist anywhere along the line.

procedures.action: Open any incorrectly closed isolation valves and clear any blockage (scale, debris) found in the piping.
procedures.why: Restores the intended flow path for emergency use.

procedures.action: Re-test the system to confirm correct pressure and quantity delivery at the scavenge space connection, and log the drill result and corrective action taken.
procedures.why: Confirms the system is now fully operational and provides a record for class/safety audit.

constraints: Steam system: 3-10 bar, approx. 2.2 kg/cyl.
Water mist system: min. 3.5 bar, approx. 1.7 kg/cyl.
CO2 system: test pressure 150 bar, approx. 4.3 kg/cyl.
Fire extinguishing system must be tested per ship's safety management system schedule
regulations: SOLAS requirement for functional fire extinguishing systems in machinery spaces
Class/flag requirement for periodic testing of scavenge air space fire extinguishing system
warnings: An inoperative extinguishing system discovered only during a real scavenge fire would leave no means to suppress the fire, risking catastrophic engine damage
outcomes: Failure to detect and correct this before a real fire means no suppression capability when needed most
Regular drilling and prompt valve/line correction ensures the system is ready for an actual emergency
key_facts: Scavenge air space can be protected by steam (basic), water mist, or CO2 extinguishing systems
Extinguishing and drain pipes are both routed through the scavenge air space and must be kept clear

question_seeds.text: When should the scavenge air space fire extinguishing system be functionally tested?
What is the correct procedure if the scavenge fire extinguishing line shows no pressure during a drill?

known_issue.failure_mode: fire extinguishing system line blocked/isolated
known_issue.detection_method: scheduled drill/test showing no flow or pressure at outlet

trace.situation: In cold ambient conditions, the scavenge air box drain line (particularly the exposed external piping run to the drain tank) experiences partial freezing or wax/sludge solidification, reducing drain flow and causing water/sludge to accumulate in the scavenge spaces during prolonged cold weather operation.
trace.trigger: Reduced or stopped flow at the scavenge drain sight glass noted during cold weather routine rounds, with no high-level alarm yet triggered

procedures.action: Apply steam tracing or steam assist via the BV connection to warm and clear the affected drain line section.
procedures.why: Steam application is the designed method to liquefy solidified sludge/condensate and restore flow in cold conditions.

procedures.action: Insulate or lag exposed sections of the drain piping prone to freezing if this is a recurring seasonal issue.
procedures.why: Reduces heat loss from the line and prevents repeat freezing/blockage in cold climates.

procedures.action: Increase frequency of drain flow checks during cold weather transits until the line is confirmed reliably clear.
procedures.why: Early detection prevents sludge/water accumulation in the scavenge box reaching levels that could trigger high-level alarms or affect scavenging.

constraints: Drain tank and piping must be kept clear to maintain continuous scavenge box drainage
Steam assist available via BV connection for facilitating drainage
regulations: Manufacturer recommendation for drain tank placement near engine to minimize long piping runs susceptible to blockage
warnings: Sustained drain blockage in cold weather can lead to sludge/water accumulation in the scavenge box, increasing fire and corrosion risk
outcomes: Unaddressed seasonal freezing/blockage risks repeated drain failures and potential scavenge box contamination buildup
Steam tracing/insulation and increased monitoring maintains reliable drainage through cold weather operation
key_facts: Scavenge air box drains continuously via AV to a pressurised drain tank with steam assist available via BV
Long piping runs between engine and drain tank increase blockage risk, especially in cold conditions

question_seeds.text: Why does the scavenge air box drain line tend to block more frequently during cold weather operation?
How can steam assist be used to clear a partially frozen or solidified scavenge drain line?

known_issue.failure_mode: seasonal drain line blockage from cold-weather solidification
known_issue.detection_method: reduced flow at drain sight glass during routine cold-weather rounds

trace.situation: One of the two starting air compressors runs continuously but fails to build up to the rated 30 bar delivery pressure, indicating internal leakage past worn piston rings or damaged discharge valves on one of the two compression stages.

procedures.action: Confirm receiver pressure trend and compare compressor running hours against normal charging time

procedures.action: Inspect first and second stage discharge valves, piston rings and intercooler for leakage or damage

procedures.action: Overhaul or renew worn components and retest to 30 bar delivery pressure
procedures.why: Restores design capacity before relying on the unit again

Restored full compressor capacity and reliable starting air reserve
key_facts: Starting air compressors are water-cooled, two-stage with intercooling

Receiver volumes are sized for 12 starts (reversible engine) or 6 starts (nonreversible engine)

question_seeds.text: Why is the starting air compressor unable to reach 30 bar despite running continuously?

chapter_title: Starting Control Air -- synthesized domain knowledge

trace.situation: The starting air receiver safety relief valve lifts and discharges to atmosphere at a pressure below its certified set point, pointing to a weakened spring or a leaking valve seat.
trace.trigger: Continuous or repeated venting noise from the receiver safety valve at pressures noticeably under 30 bar + tolerance

procedures.action: Reduce compressor output or isolate the affected receiver if the second receiver can supply the system
procedures.why: Prevents unnecessary venting of start air while the valve is assessed

procedures.action: Inspect the safety valve seat and spring for wear, corrosion or set-point drift
procedures.why: Premature lifting is usually caused by seat damage or spring relaxation

procedures.action: Recalibrate or renew the valve and verify lift pressure on a test bench or in situ with a calibrated test pump
procedures.why: Ensures the valve protects the receiver without wasting starting air capacity

procedures.action: Record the test result and have it verified against class test pressure requirements

trace.situation: Hot carbon deposits and oil residue accumulate on the air cooler fins and scavenge box walls over time, and under certain load conditions can self-ignite, causing a localized fire inside the scavenge air space. trace.trigger: Scavenge air space high temperature alarm or sudden abnormal temperature rise on individual cylinder scavenge air box sensors

procedures.action: Immediately reduce load/stop the engine as per emergency procedure and do not open scavenge drain covers.
procedures.why: Opening covers introduces fresh oxygen and can intensify the fire; reducing load limits further fuel for combustion.

procedures.action: Activate the fixed scavenge air space fire extinguishing system (steam, water mist, or CO2 as fitted).
procedures.why: Steam at 3-10 bar (approx. 2.2 kg/cyl) or equivalent agent smothers the fire by displacing oxygen without needing to open the space.

procedures.action: Keep auxiliary blowers running or stop per fire procedure as specified by maker, and monitor scavenge air temperatures until stable before inspection.
procedures.why: Controlled airflow or isolation prevents re-ignition while cooling occurs; premature opening can cause flashback.

procedures.action: After confirmed extinguishment and cooling, open and inspect scavenge space for damage, residue, and ring/liner condition before restart.

warnings: Opening scavenge drain covers during an active scavenge fire can cause explosive flashback

outcomes: If not controlled quickly, fire can damage piston rings, liner, and cooler, leading to major repair and possible hull/engine room fire spread

procedures.why: Determines whether the corrosion is superficial or has progressed to a structural concern requiring repair.

procedures.action: Review drain system performance (box drains, water mist catcher, drain tank) for any chronic malfunction contributing to excess condensate retention.
procedures.why: Addressing the root drainage deficiency prevents recurrence after repair.

procedures.action: Clean, treat, and if necessary apply protective coating or repair the affected receiver sections per maker's guidance.
procedures.why: Restores structural integrity and corrosion resistance of the affected area.

procedures.action: Increase inspection frequency of the affected area in subsequent overhauls to monitor progression.
procedures.why: Early detection of recurring corrosion prevents unexpected failure of receiver integrity.

constraints: Scavenge air box/receiver drains must function continuously to minimize condensate accumulation
regulations: Class survey requirement for structural inspection of pressure-retaining scavenge air components
warnings: Unaddressed pitting corrosion can progress to through-wall leakage or structural weakness under pressure cycling
Corrosion products can also contaminate scavenge air and accelerate ring/liner wear
outcomes: If uncorrected, advanced corrosion may require receiver section replacement or cause in-service leakage
Early repair and improved drainage practice extends receiver service life
key_facts: Scavenge air box and cooler areas are continuously drained to minimize condensate/sludge accumulation
Drain system design assumes reliable functioning to prevent standing water in the receiver

trace.situation: Excessive piston ring blow-by on one or more cylinders allows combustion gases and additional oil mist to pass into the scavenge air space, resulting in elevated oil content and carbon residue in that cylinder's scavenge drain compared to others, and increasing local fire risk.
trace.trigger: Noticeably higher oil/carbon content or elevated temperature from a specific cylinder's scavenge drain cock during routine sampling or inspection

procedures.action: Sample and compare scavenge drain residue/oil content across all cylinders to identify the outlier cylinder.
procedures.why: Confirms localized blow-by rather than a system-wide lubrication or fouling issue.

procedures.action: Check that cylinder's exhaust temperature, running gear indicator diagrams (if available), and recent piston ring/liner inspection history.
procedures.why: Blow-by is often accompanied by elevated exhaust temperature and altered combustion indicator patterns on the affected unit.

procedures.action: Reduce load on the affected unit if load-dependent adjustment is possible, and plan for liner/ring inspection at the next opportunity.
procedures.why: Limits further wear and fire risk until the unit can be properly inspected and repaired.

procedures.action: Inspect and renew piston rings/liner as needed, and verify cylinder lubrication rate is appropriate for the unit.
procedures.why: Addresses the root mechanical cause of excessive blow-by.

constraints: Scavenge drain oil content should remain consistent across cylinders under normal operation
Cylinder lubrication rate must be within maker's specified range for the given running condition
regulations: Manufacturer guidance on piston ring/liner wear limits and lubrication feed rate
warnings: Excessive and localized oil accumulation in the scavenge space increases risk of a scavenge fire at that cylinder
Unaddressed blow-by accelerates liner and ring wear, risking a major mechanical failure
outcomes: If uncorrected, the affected cylinder may suffer accelerated ring/liner wear and elevated scavenge fire risk
Early identification and repair restores normal combustion sealing and reduces fire risk
