Elevated local oil/carbon content in scavenge drains is a key early indicator of ring or liner wear

trace.situation: The steam supply valve or piping feeding the scavenge air space fire extinguishing system is found to be isolated, blocked, or leaking during a routine test, meaning the system would not be available for use in an actual scavenge fire emergency.
trace.trigger: Failed or inconclusive result during the scheduled fire extinguishing system function/pressure test

procedures.action: Verify the steam supply valve line-up to the scavenge air fire extinguishing manifold matches the required open/standby position.
procedures.why: Many failures are due to an isolation valve being left shut after maintenance rather than a true system defect.

procedures.action: Check steam pressure available at the manifold against the required 3-10 bar range.
procedures.why: Insufficient steam pressure will not deliver the approx. 2.2 kg/cyl needed to extinguish a fire effectively.

procedures.action: Inspect piping and the spray distribution points for blockage, corrosion, or leakage reducing delivered quantity.
procedures.why: Ensures the extinguishing medium will actually reach the scavenge space in sufficient quantity when activated.

procedures.action: Repair/restore the system and re-test, logging the result and reporting to the Chief Engineer and class records as applicable.
procedures.why: Confirms operational readiness of a critical safety system and maintains compliance records.

constraints: Steam pressure for scavenge air fire extinguishing must be maintained between 3-10 bar
Approx. 2.2 kg steam per cylinder required for effective extinguishment
regulations: SOLAS/Class requirement for periodic testing of fixed fire extinguishing systems
Flag/Class survey requirement for scavenge fire system readiness verification
warnings: An unavailable scavenge fire extinguishing system during an actual fire event removes a critical line of defense against major engine damage
Failing to report and rectify this defect may result in a class deficiency finding
outcomes: If uncorrected, an actual scavenge fire event would have no effective suppression, risking catastrophic engine damage
Restoring and verifying the system ensures readiness for emergency use and regulatory compliance
key_facts: Scavenge air fire extinguishing can use steam, water mist, or CO2 depending on system fitted
Steam system design: 3-10 bar supply pressure, approx. 2.2 kg per cylinder
This system should be function/pressure tested periodically per class/owner procedures

trace.situation: On vessels fitted with a CO2-based scavenge air space fire extinguishing system, the CO2 cylinder bank pressure is found below the required test pressure during routine inspection, indicating gas leakage over time and reduced available extinguishing quantity.
trace.trigger: Low pressure reading on CO2 cylinder gauges during scheduled safety equipment inspection, below the expected 150 bar test reference

procedures.action: Weigh or gauge-check each CO2 cylinder in the bank against its rated full charge weight/pressure.
procedures.why: Determines which cylinders have leaked and the total shortfall in available CO2 quantity.

procedures.action: Inspect cylinder valves, connections, and manifold for visible leakage points (frost marks, hissing).
procedures.why: Identifies the leak source for repair rather than simply recharging without fixing the cause.

procedures.action: Arrange recharging of depleted cylinders by an approved service agent and repair/replace faulty valves or seals.
procedures.why: Restores the full approx. 4.3 kg/cyl quantity required for effective fire suppression.

procedures.action: Update the fire safety equipment log and inform the Chief Engineer/Master of the system's status until recharge is complete.
procedures.why: Ensures crew awareness of reduced firefighting capability in the interim and supports compliance recordkeeping.

constraints: CO2 system test pressure reference is 150 bar
Approx. 4.3 kg CO2 per cylinder required for effective scavenge space fire suppression
regulations: SOLAS/Class requirement for periodic inspection and recharge of fixed CO2 fire extinguishing systems
warnings: Reduced CO2 charge may be insufficient to extinguish a scavenge fire, allowing re-ignition or incomplete suppression
Undetected long-term leakage can leave the system effectively empty when needed
outcomes: If uncorrected, an actual scavenge fire may not be fully suppressed, risking major engine damage
Timely recharge and leak repair restores full firefighting capability and regulatory compliance
key_facts: CO2 fire extinguishing system for scavenge air space is tested at 150 bar reference pressure
Required CO2 quantity is approximately 4.3 kg per cylinder

trace.situation: An auxiliary blower starter panel contactor develops worn/pitted contacts over years of cycling, causing intermittent loss of motor power supply, nuisance trips, or failure to de-energize the blower correctly when commanded to stop.
trace.trigger: Intermittent blower start/stop behavior not correlated with scavenge pressure, or arcing/burning smell noticed at the starter panel

procedures.action: De-energize the starter panel and visually inspect the main contactor contacts for pitting, burning, or misalignment.
procedures.why: Worn contactor contacts are a common cause of intermittent electrical supply issues in heavily cycled starter circuits.

procedures.action: Clean or replace the contactor and check coil voltage and auxiliary contact function.
procedures.why: Restores reliable make/break operation of the motor circuit.

procedures.action: Function-test the blower through several start/stop cycles in manual mode before returning to automatic control.
procedures.why: Confirms the repair resolves the intermittent behavior under realistic cycling conditions.

procedures.action: Log the contactor replacement/maintenance and consider inspecting the sister blower's panel for similar wear given equal running hours.
procedures.why: Proactively prevents a similar failure on the other blower's starter panel.

constraints: Starter panel design and protection function must conform to the engine control system interface for each blower motor
regulations: Manufacturer electrical design standard for auxiliary blower starter panels
warnings: Arcing or burning contacts present an electrical fire risk within the starter panel enclosure
Intermittent blower supply can leave the engine without reliable scavenging support at low load
outcomes: If uncorrected, contactor failure may progress to complete loss of blower control or an electrical fire in the panel
Timely contactor renewal restores reliable blower control and removes the fire risk
key_facts: Each auxiliary blower has a dedicated starter panel per OEM design (one panel with starter per blower)
Starter panel design follows the manufacturer's diagram though physical build is yard/owner-specified

trace.situation: Drain water from the scavenge air box and cooler cleaning system, which is directed overboard via an automatic pump-overboard arrangement, is found to have an oil content above the 15 ppm regulatory threshold due to a malfunctioning oil content monitor or bypassed filter, risking an unauthorized oily discharge.
trace.trigger: Oil content monitor alarm on the auto pump overboard system, or visible sheen reported in the overboard discharge during drain pumping

procedures.action: Immediately stop the overboard pump-out and redirect drain flow to the oily bilge water holding tank.
procedures.why: Prevents an unauthorized discharge of oil-contaminated water above the regulatory limit.

procedures.action: Verify the oil content monitor calibration and sensor cleanliness.
procedures.why: A fouled or miscalibrated sensor can give false readings in either direction, so verification confirms the true oil content.

procedures.action: Inspect the upstream filter in the drain return line for bypass or saturation allowing oil carryover.
procedures.why: A saturated or bypassed filter is a common root cause of oil content exceeding the threshold at the monitor.

procedures.action: Record the incident, corrective action taken, and any required reporting per the vessel's SOPEP/SMPEP and oil record book requirements.
procedures.why: Ensures regulatory compliance and proper documentation of the near-miss or actual discharge event.

constraints: Oil content of drain water must not exceed 15 ppm before overboard discharge
Drain water above the threshold must be routed to the oily bilge water holding tank

warnings: Discharging oil-contaminated water above 15 ppm overboard is a MARPOL violation with potential for detention and fines
Ignoring the oil content alarm risks environmental pollution and regulatory non-compliance
outcomes: If uncorrected, continued operation risks an illegal discharge, port state control action, and environmental harm
Prompt rerouting and sensor verification prevents pollution and maintains regulatory compliance

15 ppm is the regulatory oil content threshold before water must be routed to the oily bilge holding tank instead of overboard

trace.situation: Residual grease-dissolving cleaning chemical from the air cooler cleaning process is not fully flushed from the cooler air side or associated drain/filter components after a cleaning cycle, leaving chemical film that attracts new deposits faster or causes localized corrosion on cooler fins.
trace.trigger: Faster-than-expected re-fouling of the scavenge air cooler (temperature rise returning sooner than historical trend) shortly after a cleaning cycle, or visible chemical residue/discoloration noted on inspection

procedures.action: Review the cleaning procedure log to confirm the correct chemical concentration, flush duration, and rinse cycle were followed.
procedures.why: Determines whether the re-fouling is due to an incomplete or improperly executed cleaning/flush cycle.

procedures.action: Perform an additional fresh-water rinse cycle through the spray pipe arrangement to remove residual chemical film.
procedures.why: Residual cleaning chemical left on the fins can act as a deposit-binding film, accelerating subsequent fouling.

procedures.action: Inspect the drain/filter ('AL'/'AM') path for chemical residue buildup and clean/replace the filter element as needed.
procedures.why: A clogged or contaminated filter can recirculate dirty cleaning fluid, undermining cleaning effectiveness.

procedures.action: Adjust the cleaning procedure (concentration, dwell time, flush volume) per maker's recommendation for future cycles.
procedures.why: Prevents recurrence of incomplete chemical removal in subsequent cleaning operations.

constraints: Cleaning must be performed with the engine at standstill
Chemical tank and circulation pump capacity must match the engine's cylinder count per maker's table
regulations: Manufacturer procedure for air cooler cleaning chemical handling and flushing
warnings: Residual aggressive cleaning chemical can accelerate corrosion of cooler fin material over time if not properly rinsed
Incomplete cleaning cycles waste chemical and operational downtime without achieving the intended benefit
outcomes: If uncorrected, repeated incomplete cleaning cycles lead to chronic premature re-fouling and potential fin corrosion
Proper flush and procedure adherence restores expected cleaning intervals and cooler longevity
key_facts: Cleaning chemical tank and circulation pump capacities are sized per cylinder count (e.g., 0.3-1.5 m3 tank, 1-5 m3/h pump depending on engine type)
Cleaning drain/filter path routes used cleaning fluid back to the chemical tank via 'AM'

trace.situation: The scavenge air pressure transmitter used by the Engine Control System to manage auxiliary blower start/stop thresholds drifts or fails, causing erratic or excessive blower cycling (rapid start/stop) rather than smooth operation around the load threshold.
trace.trigger: Auxiliary blower start/stop alarm log shows frequent short-interval cycling not matching smooth load changes

procedures.action: Compare the ECS scavenge air pressure reading against an independent local pressure gauge at the receiver.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the transmitter is reading incorrectly or if pressure is genuinely fluctuating near the threshold.

procedures.action: If the transmitter is confirmed faulty (noisy/drifting signal), switch the affected blower control to manual mode temporarily.
procedures.why: Prevents excessive wear on blower motors and contactors from rapid cycling while the fault is resolved.

procedures.action: Replace or recalibrate the pressure transmitter and verify signal stability across the relevant load range.
procedures.why: Restores accurate automatic control input for the blower start/stop logic.

procedures.action: Return the system to automatic mode and monitor blower cycling behavior over a load transient to confirm normal hysteresis operation.
procedures.why: Confirms the fault has been fully resolved and normal designed hysteresis is functioning.

constraints: Blower start/stop thresholds include built-in hysteresis to prevent rapid cycling near approx. 25-40% load
Manual mode allows individual blower control from the ECR panel irrespective of engine condition
regulations: Manufacturer control system design requirement for blower hysteresis logic
warnings: Frequent rapid cycling significantly shortens blower motor and contactor life
Erratic blower behavior near load transition points can also momentarily affect scavenge pressure stability
outcomes: If uncorrected, rapid cycling accelerates wear and increases risk of a blower failure at a critical moment
Correcting the sensor fault restores smooth, designed hysteresis-based blower operation and extends equipment life
key_facts: The auxiliary blower control hysteresis is designed to prevent rapid cycling near the 25-40% load transition band
Manual mode control is available via the ECR panel as a temporary workaround during sensor faults

trace.situation: During prolonged slow steaming or extended standby at very low load, moisture condensation inside the idle auxiliary blower motor (without heaters, or with failed heaters) leads to insulation degradation, risking an electrical fault the next time the blower is called to start.
trace.trigger: Insulation resistance test on an idle auxiliary blower motor shows a declining trend approaching the minimum acceptable value

procedures.action: Perform a megger (insulation resistance) test on the idle blower motor windings per the planned maintenance schedule.
procedures.why: Early detection of insulation degradation prevents an unexpected failure when the blower is called upon to start.

procedures.action: Verify that the blower motor space heater (if fitted) is energized and functioning correctly.
procedures.why: Space heaters prevent condensation buildup in the motor windings during idle periods, directly addressing the root cause.

procedures.action: If insulation resistance is below the acceptable threshold, dry out the motor using appropriate methods (e.g., low-voltage heating or forced air) before attempting to run it under load.
procedures.why: Running a motor with degraded insulation risks a winding short or ground fault under load.

procedures.action: Repair or install a functioning heater and schedule more frequent insulation checks during extended slow-steaming periods.
procedures.why: Prevents recurrence of moisture-related insulation degradation in future idle periods.

constraints: Blower motor heaters are available as an option and should be functional where fitted
Minimum insulation resistance value per motor manufacturer's standard must be maintained
regulations: Manufacturer/class requirement for periodic insulation resistance testing of standby electrical motors
warnings: Starting a motor with degraded insulation resistance risks an electrical fault, fire, or complete motor failure
Loss of the second blower due to insulation failure removes scavenging redundancy during low-load operation
outcomes: If uncorrected, the blower motor may fail electrically when started, leaving only one blower available
Scheduled insulation testing and functional heaters prevent condensation-related motor failure
key_facts: Heaters for auxiliary blower motors are available as an option specifically to prevent moisture-related issues during idle periods
Insulation resistance testing is a standard preventive check for idle standby motors

trace.situation: During an engine stop-start cycle, the auxiliary blowers fail to complete their mandatory sequential pre-start operation within the expected time window, causing the engine start command to be held up indefinitely by the Engine Control System's interlock, without a clear fault being obviously visible to the watchkeeper.
trace.trigger: Engine start command issued but engine remains in a 'waiting for blowers' state well beyond the normal pre-start delay

procedures.action: Check the ECS diagnostic/alarm page for the specific blower sequence step at which the start is being held.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the issue is with blower 1, blower 2, or a shared interlock/permissive signal.

procedures.action: Verify both blowers are receiving start commands and that sequencing timers/permissives (e.g., non-return valve position feedback) are satisfied.
procedures.why: The sequential start logic depends on confirmed feedback from each blower and associated valves; a missing feedback signal will stall the sequence.

procedures.action: If a specific feedback sensor (e.g., valve position or blower running confirmation) is found faulty, bypass per approved manual procedure only if permitted by the maker/class, or correct the sensor fault directly.
procedures.why: Restores the automatic sequence; unauthorized bypass of safety interlocks should be avoided unless formally approved.

procedures.action: Once the fault is cleared, confirm both blowers complete the sequential start and the engine start proceeds normally before releasing to the bridge/engine control.
procedures.why: Ensures full scavenging capability is actually confirmed before committing to fuel admission and engine start.

constraints: Auxiliary blowers must start sequentially and be confirmed before engine start is permitted to proceed
Engine start is intentionally delayed by design until blowers are confirmed running
regulations: Manufacturer ECS interlock requirement for confirmed blower operation prior to engine start
warnings: Bypassing the blower-confirmation interlock without proper authorization risks starting the engine without adequate scavenging, which can cause a failed start or exhaust fire risk
Repeated manual overrides mask an underlying sensor/sequence fault that needs correction
outcomes: If uncorrected, the engine cannot be started when needed, risking a loss of propulsion/maneuverability at a critical moment
Diagnosing and fixing the sequence fault restores reliable, safe automatic engine starting
key_facts: Auxiliary blowers start consecutively before the engine start and the engine start is delayed until the blowers have started
This sequencing is a built-in safety interlock within the Engine Control System

trace.situation: Over an extended period without maintenance, both auxiliary blower impellers accumulate dust, salt, and oily residue from the intake air, reducing blower aerodynamic efficiency and airflow delivery even though the motors run normally, resulting in marginally lower scavenge air pressure support during low-load and starting conditions.
trace.trigger: Gradual downward trend in scavenge air pressure delivered by the auxiliary blowers at a given load compared to commissioning/reference data, without any individual blower alarm

procedures.action: Trend blower-supported scavenge air pressure at low load over time against commissioning baseline data.

procedures.action: Inspect the blower intake filters/screens and impeller (where accessible) for dust, salt crust, or oily film accumulation.
procedures.why: Confirms fouling as the root cause and identifies which component requires cleaning.

procedures.action: Clean the intake filters/screens and, if accessible without major disassembly, clean the impeller surfaces per maker's guidance.
procedures.why: Restores aerodynamic efficiency and airflow delivery of the blowers.

procedures.action: Re-verify scavenge air pressure trend at low load after cleaning to confirm restored performance.
procedures.why: Validates that fouling was indeed the cause and the corrective action was effective.

constraints: Blower intake air quality and filter condition should be maintained per maker's planned maintenance schedule
regulations: Manufacturer planned maintenance schedule for auxiliary blower intake/impeller cleaning
warnings: Gradual blower efficiency loss can go unnoticed until marginal at very low load or during engine starting, risking a harder start in cold/adverse conditions
Combined fouling of both blowers removes the safety margin that single-blower emergency running relies upon
outcomes: If uncorrected, marginal scavenging support at low load/starting may eventually cause difficult or failed starts, especially in cold conditions
Routine cleaning restores full blower airflow capacity and starting reliability

Blower performance should be periodically verified against commissioning baseline data at known low-load points

trace.situation: One of the two water-cooled, two-stage starting air compressors is taking progressively longer to charge the receivers to the 30 bar cut-out pressure, indicating worn piston rings or leaking suction/discharge valve plates causing internal blow-by between stages.
trace.trigger: Compressor running-hours-per-charge trend increasing; starting air receiver slow to recover pressure after a start

procedures.action: Compare 1st and 2nd stage discharge pressures and intercooler temperature against the maker's performance curve
procedures.why: Identifies which stage is underperforming and whether blow-by or valve leakage is the cause

procedures.action: Stop and open up the suspect stage to inspect piston rings, suction/discharge valve plates and gaskets
procedures.why: Worn rings or pitted valve seats are the most common cause of gradual capacity loss

procedures.action: Renew worn rings/valves and re-torque cylinder head and valve chest fasteners to spec
procedures.why: Restores correct compression ratio per stage and eliminates leakage paths

procedures.action: Run the standby compressor in parallel until repairs are verified
procedures.why: Maintains receiver pressure and starting reserve during downtime of the affected unit

constraints: Compressor delivery pressure must reach 30 bar
Receiver capacity must cover 12 starts (reversible) or 6 starts (nonreversible) at all times

warnings: Failure to restore full compressor capacity risks insufficient starting air during maneuvering, which can prevent timely engine starts in collision-avoidance situations
outcomes: If not corrected: receiver pressure may fall below the number of starts required by class, risking inability to start/reverse the engine when needed
If corrected: full compressor capacity and starting air reserve are restored
key_facts: Starting air compressors are two-stage, water-cooled with intercooling
Delivery pressure is 30 bar
Receiver volumes are sized for 12 starts (reversible engine) or 6 starts (nonreversible engine)

trace.situation: The safety valve fitted to one starting air receiver lifts intermittently at a pressure below its nominal set point, venting air to atmosphere and causing the receiver pressure to cycle erratically.
trace.trigger: Audible venting from receiver safety valve and fluctuating receiver pressure gauge readings well below normal working pressure of 30 bar

procedures.action: Isolate the receiver per permit-to-work and confirm the valve lifts below its stamped set pressure using a test rig or in-situ lifting check

procedures.action: Inspect valve seat and disc for debris, corrosion pitting, or spring fatigue
procedures.why: These are the common causes of premature lifting on receiver safety valves

procedures.action: Lap or renew the seat/disc and reset to the correct lifting pressure per class-approved test pressure
procedures.why: Restores proper sealing and correct set point

procedures.action: Re-certify the valve setting with the class surveyor if required by the vessel's survey status
procedures.why: Safety valve settings on pressure vessels are subject to class verification

constraints: Receiver working pressure 30 bar

regulations: Class rule requirement for periodic testing/certification of air receiver safety valves
warnings: Uncontrolled venting reduces available starting air reserve and may mask a more serious overpressure condition if ignored
outcomes: If not corrected: chronic air loss reduces available starts and may trigger low-pressure alarms during critical maneuvering
If corrected: receiver pressure is stable and safety valve certification remains valid
key_facts: Starting air receiver working pressure is 30 bar
Test pressure is set according to class rule, not a fixed manual value

trace.situation: The control/safety air reduction station, which steps 30-10 bar down to 7 bar, develops a faulty diaphragm or spring in the reducing valve, causing the downstream control air pressure to fall outside the ±10% tolerance band.
trace.trigger: Control air pressure gauge downstream of the reduction station reading below 6.3 bar or fluctuating erratically

procedures.action: Switch over to the standby reduction line using the three isolating valves while the faulty line is worked on
procedures.why: The system is designed with two lines so one can be isolated for maintenance without loss of control air supply

procedures.action: Strip the faulty reducing valve and inspect diaphragm, spring and pilot mechanism
procedures.why: Diaphragm rupture or spring fatigue are the typical causes of unstable downstream pressure

procedures.action: Renew diaphragm/spring and re-set the reducing valve to deliver 7 bar within tolerance
procedures.why: Restores correct regulated pressure required for reliable ME control air functions

trace.situation: The exhaust gas bypass (waste-gate) valve sticks partially open at high load, diverting exhaust gas away from the turbocharger turbine and causing lower-than-expected scavenge air pressure and T/C speed despite normal fuel index.
trace.trigger: Scavenge air pressure lower than expected at high load with bypass valve position feedback not matching commanded position

procedures.action: Check the bypass valve actuator and position feedback against the control system's commanded signal.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the valve is mechanically stuck or the control signal itself is faulty.

procedures.action: Manually operate or free the valve if accessible and safe to do so, checking for seized linkage, actuator air supply fault, or corrosion.
procedures.why: Restores correct exhaust gas routing to the turbine, recovering scavenge air pressure.

procedures.action: If the valve cannot be freed underway, adjust load limitation per the engine's abnormal operation guidance until repair is possible.
procedures.why: Prevents overloading the engine at a scavenge pressure below the safe operating curve.

constraints: Exhaust gas bypass valve position must track commanded signal within maker tolerance
Engine load must be limited if scavenge air pressure falls below the minimum for the commanded fuel index
regulations: Engine manufacturer bypass valve function test procedure (Project Guide reference)
warnings: Running at full load with the bypass valve stuck open risks incomplete combustion, high exhaust temperatures, and turbocharger surge
Forcing load without addressing the valve fault risks engine overload and thermal damage
outcomes: Uncorrected, the condition causes high fuel consumption, high exhaust temperatures and possible turbocharger surge at load changes
Repairing the valve restores design scavenge air pressure and safe load capability
key_facts: Exhaust gas bypass valve diverts gas away from the turbocharger to limit scavenge pressure/turbocharger speed
Position feedback mismatch is the primary diagnostic indicator of valve malfunction

question_seeds.text: When is it safe to continue at full load with the exhaust gas bypass valve malfunctioning?
Why does a stuck-open bypass valve reduce scavenge air pressure at high load?

known_issue.failure_mode: exhaust gas bypass valve malfunction
known_issue.detection_method: position feedback mismatch and scavenge pressure deficit

trace.situation: The sealing air system that prevents lube oil migration into the turbine-side labyrinth seals fails (low sealing air pressure or blocked line), allowing oil to leak into the turbine housing and be visible as smoke or oil residue at the turbine casing drain.
trace.trigger: Oil traces or smoke observed at the turbine casing drain or sealing air pressure alarm

procedures.action: Check sealing air supply pressure and filter condition feeding the turbocharger labyrinth seals.
procedures.why: Low sealing air pressure is the most common root cause of oil migration into the turbine side.

procedures.action: Verify the turbine casing drain is clear and not itself blocked, causing oil to back up into the gas path.
procedures.why: A blocked drain can mimic a sealing air fault by trapping leaked oil in the casing.

procedures.action: Restore sealing air pressure/filter cleanliness and monitor casing drain for recurrence before resuming normal load.
procedures.why: Confirms the fault is corrected and oil ingress into the turbine has stopped.

constraints: Sealing air pressure must be maintained above the minimum differential relative to bearing housing pressure per maker specification
regulations: Turbocharger maker sealing air system specification
warnings: Persistent oil ingress into the turbine side is a fire risk due to oil contacting hot exhaust gas surfaces
Unchecked oil contamination can foul the nozzle ring and exhaust gas boiler downstream
outcomes: If not corrected, oil carbonizes on hot turbine surfaces creating fire risk and accelerated fouling
Restoring sealing air integrity eliminates the oil migration and associated fire/fouling risk
key_facts: Sealing air pressure must exceed bearing housing oil mist pressure to prevent oil migration into the gas path
Oil at the turbine casing drain is a direct indicator of sealing air failure

question_seeds.text: How do I confirm a sealing air fault is causing oil ingress into the turbine casing?
What is the fire risk associated with oil leaking into the turbocharger turbine side?

known_issue.failure_mode: sealing air system failure / oil migration into turbine
known_issue.detection_method: oil residue/smoke at turbine casing drain; sealing air pressure alarm

trace.situation: The automatic/manual turbine water washing system malfunctions, either injecting washing water at the wrong load or failing to inject water at all during a scheduled cleaning cycle, risking thermal shock to hot turbine components or ineffective cleaning.
trace.trigger: Washing cycle completion without expected drop in exhaust gas temperature, or washing water flow alarm during the cycle

procedures.action: Immediately stop the washing sequence if water is being injected outside the permitted load range.
procedures.why: Prevents thermal shock cracking of hot turbine blades and nozzle ring from cold water contact at high metal temperature.

procedures.action: Check washing water supply pressure, solenoid valve operation, and timer/sequence logic for the washing system.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the fault is a water supply issue, valve failure, or control logic error.

procedures.action: Repeat washing manually at the correct load once the fault is corrected, confirming exhaust temperature reduction as evidence of effective cleaning.
procedures.why: Confirms the cleaning was actually achieved and the turbocharger fouling condition addressed.

constraints: Turbine washing permitted only within the maker-specified load window and water temperature range
regulations: Turbocharger maker washing procedure and permitted load window
warnings: Washing outside the permitted load range can crack hot turbine blades or nozzle ring from thermal shock
Skipping washing due to a malfunction allows fouling to progress unchecked
outcomes: Uncorrected washing system faults either cause blade thermal cracking or allow continued fouling with associated efficiency loss
A properly functioning washing system maintains turbocharger efficiency without component damage
key_facts: Turbine washing must only occur within a defined load band to avoid thermal shock
Exhaust gas temperature reduction after washing is the expected confirmation of effective cleaning

question_seeds.text: When should an in-progress turbine washing cycle be aborted due to a malfunction?
How can I verify that a turbine washing cycle was actually effective?

known_issue.failure_mode: turbine washing system malfunction
known_issue.detection_method: washing cycle flow alarm / lack of expected exhaust temperature reduction

trace.situation: The compressor washing system fails to deliver the correct water volume or pressure during a scheduled wash, either overwetting the compressor (risking water ingestion into the scavenge air system) or under-delivering, leaving fouling largely uncleaned.
trace.trigger: Compressor washing cycle alarm for low water flow, or water observed in the scavenge air receiver drain after washing

procedures.action: Stop the washing cycle immediately if excessive water or water carryover into the scavenge air system is observed.
procedures.why: Prevents water damage to scavenge air cooler, non-return valves, and cylinder liners from water ingestion.

procedures.action: Check washing water metering device, nozzle condition, and supply pressure for correct calibration.
procedures.why: Identifies whether the fault is a dosing/metering fault or a blocked/worn nozzle causing poor atomization.

procedures.action: Drain scavenge air receiver and verify no water remains before resuming normal operation.
procedures.why: Ensures no residual water remains that could cause cylinder liner cold corrosion or hydraulic lock risk.

constraints: Compressor washing water quantity and injection rate must follow maker's specified dosing procedure
regulations: Turbocharger maker compressor washing procedure
warnings: Excess water carryover into the scavenge air system risks cylinder liner corrosion and hydraulic effects on piston rings
Under-dosed washing leaves fouling largely in place, giving a false sense of maintenance completion
outcomes: Uncorrected washing system faults either damage downstream components with water ingestion or leave compressor fouling unresolved
A correctly functioning washing system restores compressor efficiency without collateral water damage
key_facts: Scavenge air receiver should be checked and drained after compressor washing to confirm no water carryover
Washing water dosing is maker-specified and should not be manually overridden without justification

question_seeds.text: What should be checked in the scavenge air receiver after a compressor washing cycle?
Why is excess washing water dangerous for the scavenge air system?

known_issue.failure_mode: compressor washing system malfunction / water carryover
known_issue.detection_method: washing flow alarm; water in scavenge air receiver drain

trace.situation: The turbocharger speed sensor (pick-up) develops an intermittent or failed signal, causing erratic or absent T/C rpm readout on the control system. This can mask a real overspeed or underspeed condition and may trigger spurious alarms.
trace.trigger: T/C speed indication dropping to zero or fluctuating erratically while engine load and sound remain steady

procedures.action: Cross-check the actual turbocharger condition by local listening/observation and compare with scavenge air pressure trend, which should remain consistent with real speed.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the turbocharger is actually running normally despite a faulty sensor reading.

procedures.action: Inspect the speed sensor wiring, connector, and air gap/mounting for damage or contamination.
procedures.why: Most speed sensor faults originate from loose connectors, moisture ingress, or mechanical misalignment of the pick-up.

procedures.action: Replace or reseat the sensor as needed and verify stable reading across the load range before relying on it for alarm/trip functions.
procedures.why: Ensures overspeed protection logic is functioning correctly before returning to full operational reliance on the signal.

constraints: Turbocharger overspeed protection depends on a reliable speed signal; redundancy or backup indication should be verified per maker guidance
regulations: Turbocharger maker speed sensor specification and alarm/trip logic
warnings: A failed speed sensor can mask a genuine overspeed trend, delaying protective action
Relying solely on a faulty sensor for load control adjustments can lead to incorrect engine operation
outcomes: If the sensor fault is not resolved, a genuine overspeed event could go undetected until physical damage occurs
Prompt sensor repair restores reliable overspeed protection and accurate performance monitoring
key_facts: T/C speed should correlate closely with scavenge air pressure trend; a mismatch suggests a sensor fault rather than real turbocharger change
Speed sensor faults are commonly connector, wiring, or air-gap related rather than internal mechanical faults

question_seeds.text: How can I verify turbocharger speed is actually normal when the speed sensor reading is erratic?
Why is a failed speed sensor a safety concern even if the turbocharger sounds normal?

known_issue.failure_mode: speed sensor signal failure
known_issue.detection_method: erratic or zero T/C speed readout inconsistent with scavenge pressure trend

trace.situation: The turbocharger rotor exceeds its maximum permissible speed due to a governor/load control fault, rapid unload transient, or exhaust gas bypass valve malfunction, risking centrifugal overstress of the compressor and turbine wheels.
trace.trigger: Turbocharger overspeed alarm or trip activation

procedures.action: Immediately reduce fuel index/load to bring T/C speed back within the normal operating range.
procedures.why: Reduces exhaust gas energy driving the turbine, directly lowering rotor speed.

procedures.action: Verify the exhaust gas bypass valve and governor/load control response are functioning correctly once load is reduced.
procedures.why: Determines whether the overspeed was caused by a control system fault requiring repair before further load increase.

procedures.action: If overspeed trip activated, do not restart/increase load until the root cause is investigated and the rotor condition is confirmed intact by inspection if warranted.
procedures.why: An overspeed event may have induced stress beyond design limits; confirming rotor integrity prevents a later catastrophic failure.

constraints: Turbocharger maximum permissible speed as specified in the maker's data sheet must not be exceeded
Overspeed trip setpoint per maker specification
regulations: Turbocharger maker overspeed trip setpoint and safety system requirement
Classification society requirement for turbocharger overspeed protection
warnings: Sustained overspeed beyond the design limit can cause centrifugal rupture of the compressor or turbine wheel with high-energy debris release
Repeated unresolved overspeed events indicate a control system fault requiring urgent investigation
outcomes: If overspeed recurs without root-cause correction, catastrophic rotor failure and casing rupture may occur
Prompt load reduction and root-cause repair restores safe operation within design speed limits
key_facts: Turbocharger overspeed trip is a dedicated protective function separate from normal speed monitoring
Overspeed is commonly linked to governor/load control faults or bypass valve malfunction during rapid transients

question_seeds.text: What is the immediate action required when a turbocharger overspeed alarm activates?
Why must the root cause of an overspeed event be investigated before resuming full load?

known_issue.failure_mode: rotor overspeed
known_issue.detection_method: overspeed alarm/trip from speed monitoring system

trace.situation: Condensate or cooling water ingress contaminates the turbocharger bearing lube oil, usually due to a leaking water-cooled bearing housing jacket or condensation from ambient conditions in a self-contained oil system turbocharger. Contaminated oil loses lubricating properties and accelerates bearing wear.
trace.trigger: Cloudy/milky appearance of turbocharger lube oil sample or water detected during routine oil draining/check

procedures.action: Drain and sample the turbocharger lube oil sump to confirm water contamination level.
procedures.why: Quantifies the severity before deciding on load restriction or shutdown.

procedures.action: Identify and isolate the source of water ingress, such as a cracked cooling jacket or faulty gasket, and repair as needed.
procedures.why: Removing the ingress source prevents recurrence after oil change.

procedures.action: Change the contaminated oil fully and verify new oil condition before returning the turbocharger to full load service.
procedures.why: Water-contaminated oil cannot adequately lubricate bearings and must be fully replaced, not just topped up.

constraints: Turbocharger lube oil water content must be within maker's specified maximum (commonly very low ppm for self-contained systems)
regulations: Turbocharger maker lube oil quality specification
warnings: Continued operation with water-contaminated oil leads to accelerated bearing wear and potential seizure
Water contamination can also promote corrosion of bearing surfaces even at low concentrations
outcomes: Uncorrected water contamination shortens bearing life significantly and risks unplanned turbocharger failure
Prompt oil change and leak repair restores normal bearing life expectancy
key_facts: A cloudy or milky oil sample is the standard visual indicator of water contamination
Self-contained turbocharger oil systems are particularly sensitive to even small amounts of water contamination

question_seeds.text: How do I confirm water contamination in the turbocharger lube oil and assess its severity?
When is a partial oil top-up acceptable versus requiring a full oil change for water contamination?

known_issue.failure_mode: lube oil water contamination
known_issue.detection_method: oil sample appearance / routine water-in-oil check

trace.situation: An oil mist condition develops within the turbocharger bearing housing due to overfilling, worn seals, or blocked vent, with the potential to ignite on hot turbine-side surfaces, representing a localized fire risk distinct from main engine crankcase oil mist.
trace.trigger: Oil mist or smoke observed emanating from the turbocharger bearing housing vent or casing joints

procedures.action: Reduce load and shut down the turbocharger-affected engine operation if smoke or visible oil mist is confirmed at the bearing housing.
procedures.why: Removes the ignition energy source and allows safe inspection before the condition worsens.

procedures.action: Check bearing housing oil level, vent line patency, and seal condition once safe to access.
procedures.why: Identifies whether overfilling, a blocked vent, or a failed seal is generating the oil mist.

procedures.action: Correct oil level/vent/seal issue and monitor for recurrence before resuming normal load.
procedures.why: Confirms the root cause has been addressed and the fire risk eliminated.

constraints: Turbocharger bearing housing oil level must be maintained within the maker's specified range
Bearing housing vent lines must remain unobstructed per maker design
regulations: Turbocharger maker bearing housing oil system specification
warnings: Oil mist near hot turbine casing surfaces presents an immediate localized fire risk
Ignoring visible smoke from the bearing housing risks fire spreading to surrounding engine room equipment
outcomes: If uncorrected, oil mist ignition can cause a localized turbocharger fire with potential escalation in the engine room
Prompt correction removes the fire risk and protects the bearing from oil starvation caused by overfilling/blocked vent
key_facts: Oil mist at the turbocharger bearing housing is distinct from main engine crankcase oil mist detection and must be identified visually/by smell
Overfilling and blocked vents are common root causes of bearing housing oil mist

question_seeds.text: What immediate actions are required when oil mist/smoke is seen from the turbocharger bearing housing?
Which conditions commonly cause oil mist generation in the turbocharger bearing housing?

known_issue.failure_mode: bearing housing oil mist / localized fire risk
known_issue.detection_method: visual observation of smoke/mist at bearing housing vent or casing

trace.situation: Turbocharger vibration gradually increases over time without a sudden triggering event, consistent with progressive bearing wear or accumulating minor rotor unbalance from gradual blade erosion, rather than a discrete foreign object strike.
trace.trigger: Turbocharger vibration trend showing a steady upward slope over weeks approaching the alarm setpoint

procedures.action: Review vibration trend data over the preceding weeks/months and correlate with running hours since last overhaul/washing.
procedures.why: Distinguishes a gradual wear-related trend from a sudden event requiring different urgency of response.

procedures.action: Schedule borescope inspection of rotor blades and check bearing clearance indicators at the next convenient opportunity before the alarm setpoint is reached.
procedures.why: Allows planned intervention before an automatic alarm/trip forces an unplanned shutdown.

procedures.action: Plan bearing replacement or rotor balancing at the next scheduled maintenance window based on inspection findings.
procedures.why: Addresses the root cause before vibration reaches levels requiring emergency shutdown.

constraints: Vibration trend must be monitored against the maker's alarm and trip thresholds, with planned maintenance before alarm levels are reached
regulations: Turbocharger maker vibration monitoring and planned maintenance guidance
warnings: Deferring inspection once a clear upward vibration trend is established risks an unplanned high-vibration trip during critical operations
A slow trend can mask an accelerating wear mechanism if not periodically reviewed
outcomes: If left unaddressed, the gradual trend can culminate in a sudden vibration trip or bearing failure at an inconvenient time
Planned inspection and repair based on trend analysis avoids unplanned downtime and limits repair scope
key_facts: A gradual vibration trend over weeks is typically wear-related, distinct from a sudden step-change indicating impact damage
Planned maintenance based on vibration trend analysis reduces unplanned turbocharger downtime

question_seeds.text: How should a gradually rising turbocharger vibration trend be managed versus a sudden vibration spike?
When should a borescope inspection be scheduled based on vibration trend data?

known_issue.failure_mode: progressive bearing wear / gradual rotor unbalance
known_issue.detection_method: long-term vibration trend monitoring

trace.situation: At low engine load, interaction between the turbocharger's reduced air delivery and the auxiliary blower cut-in/cut-out logic malfunctions, either leaving the auxiliary blower running unnecessarily at higher loads or failing to cut in when the turbocharger cannot supply sufficient scavenge air, risking insufficient scavenge pressure.
trace.trigger: Scavenge air pressure trending below the minimum required for stable combustion at low load, with auxiliary blower status not matching expected cut-in logic

procedures.action: Check the auxiliary blower cut-in/cut-out setpoint logic against actual scavenge air pressure readings.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the control logic or the pressure sensor feeding it is at fault.

procedures.action: Manually start the auxiliary blower if scavenge air pressure is insufficient and automatic cut-in has failed.
procedures.why: Provides immediate scavenge air support to maintain safe combustion conditions while the fault is investigated.

procedures.action: Inspect blower non-return/flap valves and pressure switch calibration for the auxiliary blower control circuit.
procedures.why: Identifies the specific component causing incorrect cut-in/cut-out behavior for repair.

constraints: Auxiliary blower must cut in automatically below the scavenge air pressure setpoint specified for low-load/maneuvering operation
regulations: Engine manufacturer auxiliary blower control logic specification (Project Guide)
warnings: Insufficient scavenge air pressure at low load risks incomplete combustion, scavenge fire, and exhaust valve overheating
Auxiliary blower running continuously and unnecessarily wastes electrical power and increases blower wear
outcomes: If uncorrected, low-load operation risks poor combustion, slow-speed scavenge fires or exhaust temperature deviation alarms
Correct cut-in/cut-out operation ensures scavenge air pressure is maintained safely across the load range
key_facts: Auxiliary blowers support scavenge air pressure when turbocharger output alone is insufficient at low load
Cut-in/cut-out logic is based on scavenge air pressure setpoints that must be verified against actual readings

question_seeds.text: When should the auxiliary blower be manually started if automatic cut-in fails at low load?
Why is insufficient scavenge air pressure at low load a combustion safety concern?

known_issue.failure_mode: auxiliary blower cut-in/cut-out logic fault
known_issue.detection_method: scavenge air pressure deviation with mismatched blower status

trace.situation: Uneven fuel injection or exhaust valve timing across cylinders causes an abnormal exhaust gas temperature spread entering the turbocharger turbine, subjecting part of the nozzle ring and rotor to localized thermal stress and reducing overall turbocharger efficiency and lifespan.
trace.trigger: Cylinder exhaust gas temperature spread exceeding the normal tolerance band recorded on the engine performance printout

procedures.action: Review individual cylinder exhaust temperature, Pmax, and Pcomp data to identify the outlier cylinder(s).
procedures.why: Localizes the combustion imbalance causing uneven turbine inlet temperature distribution.

procedures.action: Inspect and adjust fuel injection timing/fuel valve condition or exhaust valve condition on the identified cylinder(s).
procedures.why: Corrects the root cause of combustion imbalance feeding uneven thermal load to the turbocharger.

procedures.action: Re-check exhaust temperature spread after adjustment to confirm balance is restored within tolerance.
procedures.why: Confirms the correction was effective and the turbocharger thermal loading is now even.

constraints: Cylinder exhaust gas temperature spread must remain within the engine maker's specified tolerance band
regulations: Engine manufacturer cylinder balancing and exhaust temperature tolerance specification
warnings: Sustained uneven turbine inlet temperature accelerates local nozzle ring and blade thermal fatigue
Ignoring temperature spread can mask a developing fuel injection or exhaust valve fault with broader engine implications
outcomes: Unaddressed imbalance shortens turbocharger component life through localized thermal fatigue
Correcting cylinder balance extends turbocharger component life and restores optimal efficiency
key_facts: Cylinder exhaust gas temperature spread is a standard parameter recorded on the engine performance report
Uneven turbine inlet temperature distribution is a known contributor to localized nozzle ring/blade thermal fatigue

question_seeds.text: Which cylinder parameters should be checked when turbine inlet temperature spread exceeds tolerance?
How does cylinder-to-cylinder combustion imbalance affect turbocharger component life?

known_issue.failure_mode: uneven turbine inlet temperature distribution from cylinder imbalance
known_issue.detection_method: cylinder exhaust gas temperature spread on performance report

trace.situation: The turbocharger's intake silencer/air filter becomes partially blocked by atmospheric dust, salt, or debris, restricting compressor inlet airflow and causing a measurable drop in available scavenge air pressure, particularly noticeable in dusty port environments or heavy weather with salt spray.
trace.trigger: Gradual reduction in scavenge air pressure correlating with recent port calls or heavy weather, with normal T/C bearing and vibration readings

procedures.action: Inspect the turbocharger intake silencer/filter element for visible blockage, salt crust, or debris accumulation.
procedures.why: Confirms intake restriction as the cause rather than an internal turbocharger fault.

procedures.action: Clean or replace the filter element/silencer screen as per maker's maintenance schedule.
procedures.why: Restores design airflow to the compressor inlet.

procedures.action: Verify scavenge air pressure recovery at the same load/fuel index after cleaning.
procedures.why: Confirms the restriction has been fully resolved and no other contributing factor remains.

constraints: Intake air filter/silencer must be inspected and cleaned per the maker's maintenance interval, more frequently in high-dust or high-salinity environments
regulations: Turbocharger maker intake filter maintenance schedule
warnings: A fully blocked intake filter can starve the compressor of air, risking surge and overheating at high load
Operating with a degraded filter in a salty/dusty environment accelerates compressor blade fouling as a secondary effect
outcomes: If uncorrected, intake restriction progressively reduces engine power availability and raises fuel consumption
Cleaning the intake filter promptly restores full scavenge air pressure and engine performance
key_facts: Intake silencer/filter blockage is distinguished from internal turbocharger fouling by inspecting the filter element directly
Dusty port calls and salt spray in heavy weather are common causes of accelerated intake filter fouling

question_seeds.text: How can I distinguish intake filter blockage from internal compressor fouling as the cause of low scavenge pressure?
When should the turbocharger intake filter be inspected after operating in a dusty port or heavy weather with salt spray?

known_issue.failure_mode: intake silencer/filter blockage
known_issue.detection_method: scavenge air pressure deficit with visual filter inspection

trace.situation: During a rapid astern maneuver or crash-stop sequence, the turbocharger experiences a severe thermal and mechanical transient as fuel is cut and exhaust gas flow drops abruptly while the rotor is still at high speed, creating risk of rotor overrun, bearing oil film breakdown, and thermal shock to hot turbine components from sudden gas flow cessation.
trace.trigger: Crash-stop/astern maneuver executed followed by abnormal turbocharger coast-down behavior or unusual noise during spin-down

procedures.action: Monitor turbocharger speed coast-down and listen for abnormal noise immediately following the maneuver.
procedures.why: Early detection of abnormal spin-down behavior allows prompt follow-up inspection before further maneuvering.

procedures.action: Check lube oil supply continuity to the turbocharger bearings through the transient, confirming the standby/auxiliary pump cut in correctly if the main engine-driven supply was interrupted.
procedures.why: Bearing oil film breakdown during rapid speed change is a key risk during crash-stop transients.

procedures.action: After the maneuvering sequence is complete, review turbocharger vibration, bearing temperature, and speed trend data for any anomaly introduced during the transient.
procedures.why: Confirms no lasting damage occurred from the rapid thermal/mechanical transient before resuming normal passage operation.

constraints: Lube oil supply to the turbocharger must remain continuous through all maneuvering transients per the engine's emergency maneuvering procedure
regulations: Engine manufacturer crash-stop/maneuvering procedure regarding turbocharger protection
warnings: Loss of lube oil supply during a high-speed coast-down can cause immediate bearing seizure
Repeated severe maneuvering transients without inspection follow-up can accumulate undetected bearing damage
outcomes: If a transient-induced bearing issue goes undetected, subsequent normal operation can result in sudden bearing failure
Monitoring and verifying oil supply continuity through maneuvering transients protects turbocharger bearing life
key_facts: Crash-stop and rapid reversing maneuvers impose unique thermal/mechanical transients on the turbocharger distinct from steady-state operation
Continuous lube oil supply through the speed transient is critical to prevent bearing oil film breakdown

question_seeds.text: Why is turbocharger lube oil continuity especially critical during a crash-stop maneuver?
What post-maneuver checks should be done on the turbocharger after a crash-stop or rapid astern order?

known_issue.failure_mode: maneuvering transient bearing/thermal stress
known_issue.detection_method: post-maneuver vibration, bearing temperature and coast-down behavior review

trace.situation: Long-term operation without a full turbocharger overhaul leads to progressive wear of internal clearances (compressor/turbine tip clearance, labyrinth seal clearance), gradually reducing efficiency and increasing internal leakage, which manifests as a slow, overhaul-interval-scale decline in overall turbocharger performance rather than any single acute fault.
trace.trigger: Gradual multi-month decline in turbocharger efficiency indicators (scavenge pressure for given fuel index, exhaust temperature margin) approaching the maker's recommended overhaul interval

procedures.action: Compile trend data of scavenge air pressure, exhaust temperature, and T/C speed against fuel index over the preceding overhaul interval.
procedures.why: Establishes whether the decline is consistent with normal wear-out approaching overhaul rather than an acute fault.

procedures.action: Cross-check running hours against the maker's recommended major overhaul interval for the turbocharger model.
procedures.why: Confirms whether the unit is due or overdue for scheduled overhaul based on accumulated running hours.

procedures.action: Plan and execute the scheduled major overhaul, including clearance measurement and component renewal as per maker's overhaul manual, at the next suitable opportunity.
procedures.why: Restores design clearances and performance that cannot be recovered through washing or minor maintenance alone.

constraints: Major turbocharger overhaul must be performed within the maker's specified running-hour interval regardless of apparent performance if due
regulations: Turbocharger maker major overhaul interval and clearance specification
warnings: Deferring a due overhaul based solely on 'acceptable' performance readings risks an underlying clearance or seal condition progressing to an acute failure
Running significantly beyond the recommended overhaul interval may void maker warranty/support terms
outcomes: If overhaul is deferred indefinitely, gradual wear eventually culminates in reduced efficiency, higher fuel consumption, and increased risk of an acute bearing or seal failure
Performing the overhaul on schedule restores full design efficiency and resets the wear-out clock
key_facts: Turbocharger major overhaul intervals are specified in running hours by the maker, independent of apparent day-to-day performance
Gradual performance decline over an overhaul interval is expected wear-out behavior distinct from an acute fault

question_seeds.text: When is a turbocharger major overhaul due based on running hours versus performance trend?
Why can gradual performance decline still require overhaul even if no alarm has activated?

known_issue.failure_mode: progressive internal clearance wear (overhaul-interval wear-out)
known_issue.detection_method: long-term performance trend analysis against running hours

trace.situation: Progressive fouling of the compressor side (diffuser and blades) due to oil mist and salt-laden intake air has reduced compressor efficiency over several weeks of operation. The crew notices scavenge air pressure trending lower for the same fuel index while exhaust temperatures slowly climb.
trace.trigger: Scavenge air pressure 0.2-0.3 bar below normal curve for given load, with TC speed unchanged or slightly reduced

procedures.action: Compare current scavenge pressure, TC speed, and exhaust temperature against the engine's commissioning performance curve for the same load.
procedures.why: Confirms deviation is fouling-related rather than a load or fuel quality issue.

procedures.action: Schedule compressor-side water washing per maker's running (on-load) wash procedure at reduced load.
procedures.why: Dissolves salt and oil deposits on blades/diffuser without stopping the engine.

procedures.action: Inspect washing water drain for deposit color/quantity and repeat wash if heavily contaminated.
procedures.why: Confirms effectiveness and determines if nozzle ring on turbine side is also fouled.

constraints: On-load compressor washing normally limited to loads below ~80% MCR per maker instructions
Wash water must be fresh, not seawater, to avoid additional salt deposition
regulations: MAN B&W maintenance manual washing interval recommendations
warnings: Continued fouling increases specific fuel consumption and exhaust temperature, eventually risking turbine overheating
Washing at high load can cause blade thermal shock and erosion
outcomes: Uncorrected fouling causes falling scavenge pressure, rising exhaust temperatures and reduced engine efficiency, potentially triggering high exhaust temperature alarms
Timely washing restores compressor efficiency and lowers fuel consumption
key_facts: Compressor fouling reduces air mass flow for a given TC speed
Running (on-load) washing is the standard first corrective measure for compressor fouling
Fouling is typically gradual, detected by trend analysis not a single alarm

question_seeds.text: What is the expected scavenge pressure deviation that indicates compressor fouling at this load?
How do we perform an on-load compressor water wash without exceeding the load limit?
Why does compressor fouling raise exhaust temperature even though fuel index is unchanged?

known_issue.failure_mode: compressor blade/diffuser fouling
known_issue.detection_method: performance trend comparison (scavenge pressure vs load curve)

trace.situation: Carbon and ash deposits have built up on the turbine nozzle ring and blades from prolonged low-load operation and incomplete combustion, restricting exhaust gas flow area. Exhaust gas temperature spread between cylinders is widening and TC speed is falling for the same fuel rack position.
trace.trigger: Rising exhaust gas temperature before turbine with falling or static TC rpm, increasing temperature spread between cylinder exhaust outlets

procedures.action: Log exhaust temperatures per cylinder and TC inlet/outlet temperatures, compare to baseline.
procedures.why: Distinguishes nozzle ring fouling from an individual cylinder combustion fault.

procedures.action: Perform turbine-side dry or wet cleaning per maker's procedure while engine is running at reduced load.
procedures.why: Removes carbon deposits restoring nozzle ring flow area without a shutdown.

procedures.action: If cleaning does not restore performance, plan for turbine inspection at next port/dock opportunity.
procedures.why: Severe fouling may require manual cleaning or nozzle ring replacement not achievable underway.

constraints: Exhaust gas temperature before turbine must stay within maker's maximum limit (typically around 500-530°C depending on load)
